areas.title: Is "metric-driven agentic coding" an established term, and what comes up for it?
areas.summary_before_verification: No. "Metric-driven agentic coding" is not an established term. Standard and extended web searches on 2026-11-07, plus close variants ("metrics-driven agentic coding", "metric-driven agentic development", "metric-driven AI coding"), returned no page that uses it as a name. The results were articles on measuring agent productivity or ROI (Warp, CodeRabbit, Larridin, DX) and pages on feeding quality metrics to agents. The only verbatim use found is a Hacker News comment from 2026-05-03 in the "Uncle Bob: It's Over" thread, and it is critical: such refactors "push complexity to outside the scope of the metric". Several adjacent terms are established, each with a clear origin. Metrics-Driven Development comes from DevOps around 2012 and means runtime and business telemetry, not code quality. Architectural fitness functions come from Building Evolutionary Architectures; Thoughtworks Radar listed them at Trial in Nov 2017. Error budgets come from Google SRE. Eval-driven development is OpenAI's term for LLM applications. Quality gates (Sonar, Osmani) and ratchets are long-standing practice. In 2026 a further set of terms appeared that matches Geiger's framing: harness engineering, with guides and sensors (OpenAI, Feb 2026; Böckeler, Apr 2026); back-pressure; agentic fitness functions (InfoQ, Aug 2026); and CodeScene's Code Health guardrails in the agent loop (TechDebt 2026). The literature repeatedly warns, with Goodhart-style arguments, against giving agents a single composite score. Their recommendations are separate signals, ratchets or budgets on changed code, and guidance on what to do about each finding. For Geiger, "fitness functions" (hard gates), "quality gates" and "ratchet/budget on new code" (soft score deltas), and "harness sensors" (feedback to agents) are the recognized vocabulary. "Metric-driven agentic coding" would be a new coinage, and its one existing use is negative.

findings.claim: The exact phrase "metric-driven agentic coding" is not an established term. Standard and extended web searches on 2026-11-07, an extended search limited to github.com, news.ycombinator.com, x.com, linkedin.com, medium.com and substack.com, and a Hacker News Algolia search found no article, paper, tool or talk that uses it as a name. The only verbatim hit is one HN comment (term-2). This conclusion rests on the absence of results in these searches; usage in closed social media cannot be excluded.

sources.title: HN comment by aleyan on 'Uncle Bob: It's Over'
sources.quote: I found metric driven agentic refactors just push complexity to outside the scope of the metric.

findings.relevance: Geiger cannot borrow this phrase as recognized vocabulary. Using it would be a new coinage, and its one prior use is critical.

verdict.corrected_claim: The exact phrase "metric-driven agentic coding" is not an established term. Repeated standard and extended web searches on 2026-11-07, a domain-limited extended search, and HN Algolia found no page that uses the exact phrase. The closest match is one HN comment that says "metric driven agentic refactors" (term-2), so it is a near-match, not a verbatim hit. No cited page defines a related name such as "metric-driven agentic" or "metrics-driven agentic". The conclusion rests only on missing search results; closed social media is not covered.
verdict.evidence: I reran the searches. Standard and extended web searches for "metric-driven agentic coding", the extended search limited to github.com, HN, x.com, linkedin.com, medium.com and substack.com, and an extended search for "metric-driven agentic" OR "metrics-driven agentic" did not surface the phrase. I also downloaded 10 top result pages (CodeRabbit, Warp, Larridin, Port, CallSphere, CodeScene, dekobon agent-feedback, understandingdata, DEV dmitryame, arXiv 2609.04681), the agentic_coding_lab README and the Ronacher gist, and grepped each for 'metrics?[- ]driven agentic': 0 hits. HN Algolia (advancedSyntax) gave "metric-driven agentic coding" 0 hits and "metric-driven agentic" / "metric driven agentic" 1 hit, item 47999904, which reads "I found metric driven agentic refactors just push complexity to outside the scope of the metric." The inference holds. Only the wording "only verbatim hit" overstates: the comment matches part of the phrase, not all of it.

findings.claim: The only located use of the phrase (as "metric driven agentic refactors") is a critical HN comment from 2026-05-03 by user aleyan. It responds to Uncle Bob's push for agents to refactor against metrics: agents move complexity outside what the metric measures and need active guidance to reduce codebase entropy.

sources.title: HN comment on 'Uncle Bob: It's Over' (story 47998601)
sources.quote: I am finding I need to actively guide the agents for the refactors to actually improve things without increasing the entropy of the codebase.

findings.relevance: This is a direct practitioner report of metric gaming in the setting Geiger targets, an agent optimizing CRAP-style metrics from Uncle Bob's tools. Geiger's rules need to anticipate it.

verdict.corrected_claim: The phrase appears only as "metric driven agentic refactors", in a PS to an HN comment by aleyan (2026-05-03T18:29:54Z) on the story "Uncle Bob: It's Over". Most of the comment is about agent-written tests being perfunctory and over-mocked. The PS says, in reaction to Uncle Bob, that metric-driven agentic refactors push complexity outside what the metric measures, and that the commenter must actively guide agents so refactors improve the code without increasing the codebase's entropy. The comment does not name the metrics (not CRAP or any Uncle Bob tool). It does not show that Uncle Bob advocated refactoring against metrics; it only says his post was about agents writing tests and refactoring code.
verdict.evidence: I opened https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47999904. Exact text: "PS. Reacting to Uncle Bob, I found metric driven agentic refactors just push complexity to outside the scope of the metric." and "I need to actively guide the agents for the refactors to actually improve things without increasing the entropy of the codebase." The comment also says "the subject matter, which is about having agents write tests and refactor code." HN Algolia API: created_at 2026-05-03T18:29:54Z, author aleyan, parent story 47998601 "Uncle Bob: It's Over" (a reddit link). The claim's "Uncle Bob's push for agents to refactor against metrics" and "reduce codebase entropy" overstate the source, which says avoid increasing entropy. The relevance note's "CRAP-style metrics from Uncle Bob's tools" is not in the comment. I did not open the linked X post.

findings.claim: Metrics-Driven Development (MDD) is an older DevOps term. InfoQ published Mantas Klasavičius's article on 2012-11-30, based on his DevOpsDays Rome talk. In his usage, metrics are runtime, usage and revenue telemetry that drive development, not static code-quality measures.

sources.title: Metrics Driven Development (InfoQ)
sources.quote: I would define MDD as a practice where metrics are used to drive the entire application development. In a company which uses MDD, everything from performance and usage patterns to revenue is measured.

findings.relevance: "Metrics-driven development" already means production telemetry. Reusing it for code-quality scoring would confuse readers.

verdict.evidence: I opened https://www.infoq.com/articles/metrics-driven-development/. It reads "Nov 30, 2012 ... by Mantas Klasavičius" and "This publication is based on the talk I gave at DevOpsDays in Rome, Italy". The quote "I would define MDD as a practice where metrics are used to drive the entire application development. In a company which uses MDD, everything from performance and usage patterns to revenue is measured." is present. The metrics discussed are business, application, infrastructure (CPU, memory, I/O) and production usage; the page has no static code-quality metrics such as coverage or complexity. Note: the term predates this article (7digital blog post "Metric Driven Development" on HN on 2012-04-19, Wootton on 2012-05-22). The claim does not say InfoQ coined it.

findings.claim: In 2016, Kevin Sookocheff still called Metrics-Driven Development an emerging term derived from CI/CD, DevOps and agile. He defined it by real-time metrics, which confirms the runtime-telemetry meaning. Early HN posts with the term date from 2012 to 2015 (7digital StatsD/Graphite, Librato, Benjamin Wootton).

sources.title: Metrics-Driven Development (Kevin Sookocheff)
sources.quote: Metrics-Driven Development (MDD) The use of real-time metrics to drive rapid, precise, and granular software iterations.

findings.relevance: Supports term-3: the established meaning of MDD is outside static code quality.

verdict.evidence: I opened https://sookocheff.com/post/mdd/mdd/: "August 9, 2016 · Kevin Sookocheff" and "Metrics-Driven Development is an emerging term developing from the practices of continuous integration, continuous delivery, dev ops, and agile software methodologies." The definition "The use of real-time metrics to drive rapid, precise, and granular software iterations" is present. HN Algolia search_by_date found 7digital "Metric Driven Development Fueled by StatsD and Graphite" (2012-04-19), benjaminwootton.co.uk (2012-05-22), a speakerdeck MDD deck (2012-06-29), and Librato posts (2014-07-17, 2014-10-28, 2015-04-02).

findings.claim: "Architectural fitness function" is an established term defined in Building Evolutionary Architectures (Ford, Parsons, Kua; O'Reilly 2017; 2nd ed. 2022 adds Sadalage). Thoughtworks Technology Radar listed it at Trial in Nov 2017 and May 2018.

sources.title: Architectural fitness function (Thoughtworks Technology Radar)
sources.quote: An architectural fitness function, as defined in Building Evolutionary Architectures, provides an objective integrity assessment of some architectural characteristics.

findings.relevance: Geiger's hard gates, such as banning infrastructure-to-domain dependencies or enforcing ECS rules, match this established concept and name.

verdict.evidence: I opened https://www.thoughtworks.com/radar/techniques/architectural-fitness-function. It reads "An architectural fitness function , as defined in Building Evolutionary Architectures , provides an objective integrity assessment of some architectural characteristics" and the history shows "May 2018 Trial" and "Nov 2017 Trial" (the blip is no longer on the current Radar). I downloaded the Thoughtworks free-chapter PDF of the 2nd edition. Its copyright page lists "Neal Ford, Rebecca Parsons, Patrick Kua, and Pramod Sadalage", "October 2017: First Edition" and "December 2022: Second Edition" (first release 2022-11-22). The Radar page shows only the month, not the day given as 2017-11-30.

findings.claim: Birgitta Böckeler (Thoughtworks, on martinfowler.com, 2026-04-02) frames harness engineering for coding agents as guides (feedforward) and sensors (feedback). She names an "architecture fitness harness" that is "basically" fitness functions. Her examples include ArchUnit module-boundary tests run in a coding-agent hook, and computational sensors for duplication and complexity.

sources.title: Harness engineering for coding agent users (Böckeler)
sources.quote: Computational sensors catch the structural stuff reliably: duplicate code, cyclomatic complexity, missing test coverage, architectural drift, style violations.

sources.title: Harness engineering for coding agent users (Böckeler)
sources.quote: This groups guides and sensors that define and check the architecture characteristics of the application. Basically: Fitness Functions .

findings.relevance: "Harness engineering" with computational sensors is the established 2026 term for what Geiger does. Geiger would be a sensor and gate layer in an agent harness.

verdict.evidence: I opened https://martinfowler.com/articles/harness-engineering.html ("02 April 2026 Birgitta Böckeler", Distinguished Engineer at Thoughtworks). Both quotes are present: "Computational sensors catch the structural stuff reliably: duplicate code, cyclomatic complexity, missing test coverage, architectural drift, style violations." and "Architecture fitness harness This groups guides and sensors that define and check the architecture characteristics of the application. Basically: Fitness Functions ." It defines "Guides (feedforward controls)". Its example table lists "A pre-commit (or coding agent) hook running ArchUnit tests that check for violations of module boundaries".

findings.claim: Böckeler's memo from 2026-02-17 summarizes OpenAI's harness-engineering report (Ryan Lopopolo, Feb 2026). In it, architectural constraints were enforced by deterministic custom linters and structural tests, and periodic agents did "garbage collection" against decay. She criticizes the report for lacking verification of behaviour and notes OpenAI's commercial interest. The OpenAI page itself returned 403 and was not read.

sources.title: Harness Engineering - first thoughts (Böckeler)
sources.quote: Monitored not only by the LLM-based agents, but also deterministic custom linters and structural tests.

findings.relevance: This is a high-profile precedent for deterministic architecture gates on agent-written code, close to Geiger's layer-violation gates.

verdict.evidence: I opened https://www.martinfowler.com/articles/exploring-gen-ai/harness-engineering-memo.html ("17 February 2026"). It reads "Architectural constraints : Monitored not only by the LLM-based agents, but also deterministic custom linters and structural tests" and "'Garbage collection' : Agents that run periodically to find inconsistencies in documentation or violations of architectural constraints, fighting entropy and decay". It also says "What I am missing in the write-up is verification of functionality and behaviour" and "OpenAI do have a vested interest in us believing in AI-maintainable code". The memo links openai.com/index/harness-engineering/, which returned 403 to my curl as well. The memo does not name Lopopolo. InfoQ news (https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/02/openai-harness-engineering-codex/, Feb 21, 2026) names "Ryan Lopopolo , member of the technical staff at OpenAI", which supports the Feb 2026 attribution. The memo notes that a later, more considered article superseded it.

findings.claim: InfoQ (2026-08-17; Mahato, Sieczkowski, Kuppusamy) introduced "agentic fitness functions": LLM-judged architecture checks with rubrics. The article states that deterministic fitness functions should stay the primary enforcement for measurable invariants such as dependency direction.

sources.title: Agentic Fitness Functions: Extending Evolutionary Architecture Beyond Deterministic Rules (InfoQ)
sources.quote: Deterministic fitness functions should remain the primary enforcement mechanism for measurable invariants such as dependency direction, contract shape, latency budgets, security posture, and policy checks.

findings.relevance: Supports Geiger's design choice to make layer and dependency rules deterministic hard gates. LLM-judged rules would be a separate, softer category.

verdict.evidence: I opened https://www.infoq.com/articles/agentic-fitness-functions-evolutionary-architecture/: "Aug 17, 2026 ... by Hemant Kumar Mahato Łukasz Sieczkowski Vijayasenthilkumar Kuppusamy". The quoted Key Takeaway is present verbatim. Its definition reads: "An agentic fitness function is an architecture governance check whose evaluator is a calibrated AI agent, whose criteria are expressed as an analytic rubric". The page never says "LLM"; "AI agent" is the source's wording. The article is a capstone of the InfoQ Certified Architect Program. A web search for "agentic fitness functions" found no earlier use, so "introduced" is plausible but not proven.

findings.claim: Neal Ford, co-author of Building Evolutionary Architectures, offers a 2026 workshop on deriving deterministic guardrails for human and AI agents from architecture rules. The page was created on 2026-05-29. Fitness functions are thus being explicitly repositioned for coding agents by their originator.

sources.title: Agents and Architecture training (Neal Ford)
sources.quote: how to define architecture rules embedded within specifications and how to use the same rules to generate deterministic guardrails. Even with the best models, developers should trust but verify

findings.relevance: The original authors of the concept now use "fitness functions" as the vocabulary for agent guardrails.

verdict.evidence: I opened https://nealford.com/training/agentsandarch.html. It reads "This class shows developers and architects how to define architecture rules embedded within specifications and how to use the same rules to generate deterministic guardrails. Even with the best models, developers should trust but verify ." and "you need ways to ensure that agents (either humans or machines) build proper software". The outline includes "fitness function-driven architecture". The footer reads "Author: Neal Ford Created: 2026-05-29". Ford co-authored the book that defined architectural fitness functions. Fitness functions as such come from evolutionary computing, so "originator" means the book's authors.

findings.claim: Error budgets come from Google's SRE book (chapter "Embracing Risk"). The budget is the gap between the SLO and measured reliability. Releases continue while budget remains and halt when it is spent.

sources.title: Site Reliability Engineering, Ch. 3: Embracing Risk
sources.quote: If SLO violations occur frequently enough to expend the error budget, releases are temporarily halted while additional resources are invested in system testing and development

findings.relevance: Geiger's rule of at most 0.2 points per PR and 10 points over 50 PRs is structurally an error budget applied to code quality. This is the closest established analogy.

verdict.evidence: I opened https://sre.google/sre-book/embracing-risk/ (chapter written by Marc Alvidrez per the book; the error-budget section is in this chapter). It reads "The difference between these two numbers is the 'budget' of how much 'unreliability' is remaining for the quarter. As long as the uptime measured is above the SLO—in other words, as long as there is error budget remaining—new releases can b[e pushed]". The quoted sentence "If SLO violations occur frequently enough to expend the error budget, releases are temporarily halted while additional resources are invested in system testing and development" is present. The page also notes that subtler approaches than on/off exist, such as slowing releases. The error-budget analogy to a per-PR score budget is the finding's own inference and is reasonable.

findings.claim: "Technical debt budget" is used informally for the share of team capacity reserved for paying down debt, not for an allowed loss of a quality score. No authoritative percentage exists. A Medium post proposing a debt budget modelled on SRE error budgets was found but returned 403 and was not read.

sources.title: Reserve Sprint Capacity for Improvement and Technical Debt (OneUptime, Nawaz Dhandala)
sources.quote: There is no authoritative Scrum percentage for improvement work or technical debt.

findings.relevance: If Geiger uses "quality budget" or "debt budget", it should define it as a score-loss allowance per change set. The common meaning is time allocation.

verdict.evidence: Opened the OneUptime post (Nawaz Dhandala, 2026-08-12). It contains the quote exactly: "There is no authoritative Scrum percentage for improvement work or technical debt." It never uses "technical debt budget" or "debt budget" (the closest term is "Debt bucket"), so it supports the no-authoritative-percentage part but not the usage claim. A separate source supports the usage: https://tianpan.co/forum/t/the-20-tech-debt-budget-engineering-best-practice-or-investor-red-flag/1540 ("The 20% Tech Debt Budget", cto_michelle, 2026-03-13) quotes "dedicate 20-30% of your engineering capacity to managing technical debt." A search found SRE writing that ties error budgets to debt paydown (Google CRE blog), but no use of the term for an allowed loss of a quality score. That absence comes from a single search and is not proof. The 403'd Medium post could not be checked.
verdict.corrected_claim: "Tech debt budget" is used informally for the share of engineering capacity reserved for debt work (for example a 20% tech debt budget, tianpan.co forum, 2026-03). No authoritative percentage exists (OneUptime, 2026-08-12, which itself does not use the term "debt budget"). One search found no use of the term for an allowed loss of a quality score. Separately, SRE sources link error budgets to when debt gets paid down.

findings.claim: "Eval-driven development" is established in LLM application engineering, and OpenAI's evaluation best-practices guide names it. It means writing evals of model or agent behaviour early. It does not mean scoring the code an agent writes.

sources.title: Evaluation best practices (OpenAI API docs)
sources.quote: Adopt eval-driven development: Evaluate early and often. Write scoped tests at every stage.

findings.relevance: An adjacent term with a different object: it evaluates the model or agent, while Geiger evaluates the repository. Geiger's per-PR delta could serve as an eval signal for comparing agent setups.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evaluation-best-practices. Under "Evals tips" it contains the quote exactly: "Adopt eval-driven development: Evaluate early and often. Write scoped tests at every stage." The guide is about evaluating LLM applications. The claim that the term does not mean scoring the code an agent writes follows from that context.

findings.claim: "Quality gates" is the mainstream term for constraints on agent changes. Addy Osmani (2026-08-08) uses it for tests, mutation testing, and complexity and line-length metrics, together with "back-pressure". He also states that quality is not a single metric.

sources.title: Agentic Code Quality (Addy Osmani)
sources.quote: We call these constraints quality gates, and they take many forms.

sources.title: Agentic Code Quality (Addy Osmani)
sources.quote: Software quality isn’t a single metric. Think of it as a collection of signals of varying importance to you and your team.

findings.relevance: Gives Geiger its hard-gate vocabulary. It also raises a mainstream objection to a single 0-100 score that Geiger must answer with drill-down reporting.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://addyosmani.com/blog/agentic-code-quality/ (Addy Osmani, August 8, 2026). Both quotes are verbatim. The article mentions mutation testing ("They include mutation testing, where we generate variations of code...") and "metrics around code quality, such as cyclomatic complexity and line length". It uses back-pressure several times ("Constraints and back-pressure let agents catch bad work..."). The word "mainstream" is a mild judgement based on one prominent author plus the SonarQube usage.

findings.claim: SonarQube Cloud ships a built-in "Sonar way for agentic AI" quality gate, which replaces the legacy "Sonar way for AI code" gate. Its conditions apply to new code only, for example coverage on new code ≥80% and duplication on new code ≤3%. This is existing tooling for scoring only the changed area.

sources.title: Quality gate for agentic AI (SonarQube Cloud docs)
sources.quote: The Sonar way for agentic AI quality gate is a built-in quality gate optimized for agent centric development lifecycles where AI agents are generating or modifying code.

findings.relevance: This is direct prior art for Geiger's locality requirement (new-code conditions) and its agent focus. Geiger must differentiate from it, for example on Rust, custom architecture rules and score deltas.

verdict.evidence: Opened the SonarQube Cloud docs page. It says the gate is "a built-in quality gate optimized for agent centric development lifecycles" and that "The Sonar way for agentic AI quality gate replaces the Sonar way for AI code quality gate." It states "The quality gate enforces six conditions on new code," including coverage at least 80% and duplication at most 3% on new code. The other conditions cover reliability, security and maintainability issue severities and dependency risks; the dependency-risk check needs Advanced Security on Enterprise.

findings.claim: CodeScene and loveholidays reported at TechDebt 2026 (industry track, 2026-04-12) that they put CodeScene's CodeHealth metric into the Claude Code loop as a guardrail. Agents iterated on low-CodeHealth additions until they reached a threshold of 10, and CodeHealth rose as output grew. The report is co-authored by the vendor and was not peer-reviewed as research.

sources.title: Quality Feedback in the Agentic Loop: Using CodeHealth Guardrails to Agentic Code Improvement (Borg, Caborn)
sources.quote: The agents iterated on any low-CodeHealth code additions until they reached a predefined threshold, intentionally set at a high value (a perfect 10).

findings.relevance: This is the closest existing practice to Geiger: an aggregate code-health score used as a feedback and gating signal for coding agents. It is both a competitor and a precedent.

verdict.evidence: Opened the researchr page with curl and read the full abstract: TechDebt 2026 Industry Track, Sun 12 Apr 2026, 11:20-11:40, by Markus Borg (CodeScene) and Stuart Caborn (loveholidays). Verbatim: "The agents iterated on any low-CodeHealth code additions until they reached a predefined threshold, intentionally set at a high value (a perfect 10)." Also verbatim: "While overall code production increased, our results show that CodeHealth scores increased as well." The page says loveholidays used "primarily using Claude Code", first through the CodeScene CLI and from January 2026 through MCP. It also reports AI-assisted commits rising from 0% to 45% and a 20% velocity gain. Caveats: this is a talk abstract, not a paper, and the "not peer-reviewed as research" label is an inference from the industry-track format.

findings.claim: Practitioners describe ratchets, in which quality may only move in one direction, as a guardrail for coding agents. Gary Pendergast (2026-04-13) uses a coverage ratchet and recommends binary pass/fail signals.

sources.title: Guardrails for Agentic Development (Gary Pendergast)
sources.quote: Ratcheting. Quality should only move in one direction. Coding agents will always skip something they decide is too hard; you need to stop that from happening.

findings.relevance: "Ratchet" is the established name for Geiger's no-regression-per-PR rule. Geiger's 0.2-point tolerance is a ratchet with slack, or a budget.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://pento.net/?p=5839 ("Guardrails for Agentic Development", Gary Pendergast, April 13, 2026). The quote is verbatim with the bold label "Ratcheting." On coverage it says "it enforces a ratchet mechanism where coverage can never go down." Under "Objective" it says "Pass or fail."

findings.claim: Several sources warn that metrics shown to agents get gamed. The big-code-analysis (bca) docs say bare metric feedback leads to score-lowering helper extraction without better readability. The agentic_coding_lab README says that once a prompt names a metric, the metric becomes a compliance signal rather than an independent observation.

sources.title: Feeding metrics to an agentic coding tool (big-code-analysis docs)
sources.quote: Bare metric feedback can encourage changes that lower scores without improving readability, such as extracting helpers with no useful responsibility.

sources.title: agentic_coding_lab README (marcoemrich)
sources.quote: runs of that workflow no longer produce independent observations of that metric — they produce compliance signals.

findings.relevance: Geiger's score will be the agent's target. It needs hidden or holdout metrics (for example mutation score), guidance on what to do about each finding, and anti-gaming rules.

verdict.evidence: Opened the big-code-analysis agent-feedback page. The quote "Bare metric feedback can encourage changes that lower scores without improving readability, such as extracting helpers with no useful responsibility." is present, along with "Do not game the metric." The page is undated and mentions Claude Code "2.1.139 or later". Opened the agentic_coding_lab README. The quote is present, and the README adds "Metrics named in the prompt of a workflow under test are compliance metrics for that workflow." One date detail is off: the latest explicit run date is 2026-07-24, and the "2026-10" entries are lab changes (a corpus migration), not runs. This affects only the source's date field, not the claim.

findings.claim: A long evidence report hosted by Peter Roelants (v1.26, evidence through 2026-08-22, researched by OpenAI Codex under his direction) argues against a universal code-quality score and against using letter grades as an agent reward. It recommends ratchets on changed code. It never uses "metric-driven" or "fitness function" (grep of the raw gist).

sources.title: Code quality in agentic software engineering, v1.26 (Peter Roelants gist)
sources.quote: Five problems make a universal code-quality score misleading.

sources.title: Code quality in agentic software engineering, v1.26 (Peter Roelants gist)
sources.quote: use the dashboard for triage, not its letter grade as the reward function

findings.relevance: This is a direct critique of Geiger's core premise of one 0-100 score as an agent constraint. It points toward per-change ratchets and separate signals as the defensible form.

verdict.evidence: Fetched the raw gist (gist.githubusercontent.com/peterroelants/69029d4100a99e22dbb7df60a14c286b/raw). The header reads "Version 1.26 · Updated 22 August 2026 · Evidence cut-off 22 August 2026" and "Written and researched by OpenAI Codex, under the direction and editorial guidance of Peter Roelants". Line 142 reads "Five problems make a universal code-quality score misleading." Line 289 contains "use the dashboard for triage, not its letter grade as the reward function". Line 432 reads "A ratchet asks whether the new change made a known risk worse." The gist also recommends "changed-code ratchet" in several places. Case-insensitive grep counts: "metric-driven" 0, "fitness function" 0, "fitness" 0.

findings.claim: In ML research, Karpathy's autoresearch (March 2026) popularized an agent loop driven by a single metric: an agent modifies code, runs a fixed 5-minute training run, checks val_bpb, and keeps or discards the change. When people say "metric-driven agent loop", this is a likely association, and it means optimizing an outcome metric rather than preserving code quality.

sources.title: karpathy/autoresearch README
sources.quote: It modifies the code, trains for 5 minutes, checks if the result improved, keeps or discards, and repeats.

findings.relevance: A competing sense of "metric-driven" agentic coding. Geiger's naming should distinguish quality constraints from objective optimization.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://github.com/karpathy/autoresearch. Verbatim: "It modifies the code, trains for 5 minutes, checks if the result improved, keeps or discards, and repeats." The metric is val_bpb (validation bits per byte), and the intro quote is dated "March 2026". A search found wide coverage (DataCamp tutorial, "The Karpathy Loop" newsletter, many blogs), which supports "popularized". The DataCamp tutorial dates the release to 2026-03-07; this comes from a search result I did not open. That people associate "metric-driven agent loop" with autoresearch is a plausible inference, not a measured fact.

findings.claim: Inference from term-1 to term-18: for Geiger, the recognized vocabulary is "fitness functions" or "architecture rules" for hard gates, "quality gates" or "ratchet on new code" for soft score deltas, "quality budget" by analogy with SRE error budgets for the 0.2-point and 10-point allowance, and "harness sensors" or "back-pressure" for feedback to agents. A new label such as "metric-driven agentic coding" would need defining, and its only prior use is critical.

sources.title: Harness engineering for coding agent users (Böckeler)
sources.quote: The term harness has emerged as a shorthand to mean everything in an AI agent except the model itself - Agent = Model + Harness .

findings.relevance: Helps Malte choose naming and positioning that readers will recognize.

verdict.evidence: Opened the Fowler/Böckeler harness-engineering page (2 April 2026). It defines the harness ("Agent = Model + Harness"), uses "sensors" throughout, and links "Fitness Functions". It does not use back-pressure, quality gate, ratchet or budget. "Back-pressure" comes from Osmani. Two parts of the inference do not follow. First, "quality gates" is pass/fail vocabulary in the cited sources: Osmani calls constraints quality gates, Pendergast says "Pass or fail", and Sonar gates block. Assigning the term to soft score deltas is a mismatch. Second, Roelants' gist puts it this way: "Gates fit exact or high-confidence rules" and "Ratchets and budgets fit noisy structural signals". It also says "Exact architecture violations can be gates" (https://gist.github.com/peterroelants/69029d4100a99e22dbb7df60a14c286b, lines 420 and 426-427). Also unsupported: "its only prior use is critical". Exact-phrase searches for "metric-driven agentic coding" found no established use, and Roelants does not use "metric-driven". No critical prior use was shown. The "quality budget" analogy is reasonable, but per term-11 the common meaning of "debt budget" is capacity, so Geiger must define the term.
verdict.corrected_claim: Recognized vocabulary for Geiger: "fitness functions" / "architecture rules" and "quality gates" (pass/fail) for hard gates; "ratchets" on changed or new code and "budgets" for soft score deltas, following Roelants' gate/ratchet-and-budget split ("quality budget" by analogy with SRE error budgets needs an explicit definition because "debt budget" usually means capacity share); "harness sensors" (Böckeler) or "back-pressure" (Osmani) for feedback to agents. "Metric-driven agentic coding" is not an established term; searches found no prior use of the exact phrase, so it would need defining.

areas.title: Products and open-source tools that score or gate code changes, especially changes by AI coding agents
areas.summary_before_verification: No product found implements Geiger's core idea: a 0-100 repository score where each pull request may lower the score by at most a fixed budget, built on deterministic rules that teams write themselves. The market falls into four groups. (a) Deterministic metric platforms with a score: CodeScene Code Health (1-10 per file, LoC-weighted average), SonarQube (A-E ratings and pass/fail quality gates on "new code"), Codacy (A-F grade), Qlty/Code Climate (A-F ratings, technical-debt ratio) and DeepSource (PR Report Card, A-D). (b) LLM reviewers with natural-language rules: CodeRabbit pre-merge checks, Qodo Rules System, Sourcery review rules and Graphite (being acquired by Cursor). These rules are pluggable but judged probabilistically. (c) Agent-loop integrations, mostly from 2025-2026: CodeScene MCP (pre-commit and branch-diff safeguards), Codacy Guardrails MCP, Sonar Vortex with hooks and plugins, the Qlty CLI through git hooks, and the CodeRabbit CLI as a Claude Code plugin. (d) Open-source ratchet and diff primitives: Betterer, Trunk hold-the-line, Codecov thresholds and Danger. The closest match to the per-PR budget is Qlty SlopOne (research preview, 2026-09-27): its `--max-drop` rejects a changed file whose 1-10 score drops by more than N points. It works per file, and the score comes from a hybrid model that combines static-analysis statistics with LLM classifications. The closest match to a 0-100 north-star score is desloppify, which aims for above 98 and has full Rust and GDScript plugins. It scores the full codebase only; diff scoring is not supported. Rust support is uneven. CodeScene supports Rust fully and SonarQube Cloud added first-class Rust on 2026-09-22. Codacy covers Rust only through Opengrep and Trivy. GitHub Code Quality has no CodeQL rules for Rust. Sonar's agentic-AI quality profile, its Vortex agent analysis and its Architecture analysis (intended architecture with forbidden dependencies, the nearest thing to layer gates) all exclude Rust. Evidence that rule-based debt scores predict faults is weak: in the Lenarduzzi et al. 2019 study, only 25 of 202 SonarQube Java rules were found to have relatively low fault-proneness. Geiger should therefore treat its weights as tunable, not authoritative.

findings.claim: CodeScene's MCP server returns a per-file Code Health score from 10.0 (best) to 1.0 (worst). It has two change-scoped gate tools. `pre_commit_code_health_safeguard` reviews staged files. `analyze_change_set` reviews all files that differ from a base ref and returns pass/fail quality gates plus a per-file verdict: improved, degraded or stable.

verdict.corrected_claim: The CodeScene MCP server is not fully open source. Its LICENSE mixes Apache-2.0 open-source components with closed-source components. Its full feature set (hotspots, technical-debt goals, code ownership, usage overview) needs a CodeScene subscription. Local Code Health analysis, including the score, review, pre-commit safeguard and analyze_change_set tools, is also available under a 'standalone' license without a CodeScene subscription. ACE auto-refactoring needs an additional license. Code Health analysis runs locally. Project-insight data is fetched over REST from the user's CodeScene account.
verdict.evidence: The LICENSE quote is present (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/codescene-oss/codescene-mcp-server/main/LICENSE). The docs page https://codescene.io/docs/developer-tools/mcp/codescene-mcp-server.html lists 'An active CodeScene subscription (Cloud or on-prem)' as a prerequisite and says "ACE requires an additional license." It also says "The CodeScene MCP Server runs fully locally." The repo README contradicts the blanket subscription requirement (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/codescene-oss/codescene-mcp-server/main/README.md): "For local Code Health analysis without a CodeScene subscription, you can use the standalone CodeScene Code Health MCP". It also says: "The full feature set — including hotspots, technical debt goals, and code ownership — requires a CodeScene subscription." docs/tools.md marks the analysis and gate tools 'All Users' (standalone or API-connected). The docs page adds: "Analysis results (e.g. hotspots and technical debt goals) are fetched via REST from your own CodeScene account". The relevance note says custom domain rules are impossible. That is an inference, consistent with the rules-config tools, which only enable or disable rules and set thresholds and weights.

findings.relevance: 'Clean as You Code' is the established form of locality, but it gates by thresholds, not by a score delta. The fudge factor shows that ratio metrics on tiny diffs are noisy, which a per-PR budget must also handle.

findings.claim: Qlty SlopOne (free research preview, 2026-09-27) scores each file 1-10 with a model that combines static-analysis statistics with classifications from Typesafe AI's Jev LLM. Its CLI compares changed files against a base ref and rejects a file whose score drops by more than `--max-drop` points (default 1). Triggers include agent, pre-commit and pre-push. Users pay for Jev API calls themselves, and Qlty has not yet published its methodology.

findings.relevance: This is the closest existing match to Geiger's 'no PR may lower the score by more than X'. It differs in three ways: the budget is per file, the score depends partly on an LLM (cost and possible variance between runs), and teams cannot add their own rules to it.

verdict.evidence: https://docs.qlty.sh/cli/commands/slop-one.md (CLI v0.667.0) has the --max-drop quote verbatim. It also documents '--upstream <REF> Compare the files changed since the merge base with REF' and lists trigger values manual, ide, agent, pre-commit, pre-push and build. The blog https://qlty.sh/blog/introducing-slopone (Sep 27, 2026) says "releasing SlopOne as a free research preview" and contains both quotes. It also says "You bring your own API key for Jev". For the 1-10 scale: merged PR https://github.com/qltysh/qlty/pull/2861 (Sep 25, 2026) says "maps the risk to a 1–10 score with a 5.0 cutoff" and that the CLI "exits with code 1 when a file fails the 5.0 cutoff", so there is also an absolute floor besides --max-drop. As of 2026-11-07, Qlty's blog index lists no methodology post after the launch; the next post is 'Automatic coverage setup' (Oct 12, 2026). findings.claim: CodeRabbit's 'Agentic Pre-Merge Checks' include custom checks written in natural language, each set to off, warning or error. An error blocks merges only when Automatic Approvals is enabled, and an 'Inconclusive' result never blocks. Custom checks need the Team plan or higher. findings.relevance: Teams can add rules in plain language, but an LLM judges them, so a hard gate can quietly degrade to 'Inconclusive'. This is weak for Geiger's hard layer or ECS gates.

verdict.evidence: I opened https://docs.coderabbit.ai/pr-reviews/pre-merge-checks.md. It names the feature 'Agentic Pre-Merge Checks' and describes 'Custom Checks with natural language instructions'. The enforcement modes are off, warning and error, where error means 'When paired with Automatic Approvals, block merges until resolved or manually overridden'. The status list includes '❓ Inconclusive — incomplete instructions, insufficient information, or analysis that could not be completed; does not block the pull request' (verbatim). The page also says 'Custom checks are available on the Team plan and above.' findings.claim: Qodo 2.1 (2026-02-17) added a 'Rules System' in beta for GitHub. Rules are versioned entities and may include architectural constraints; an AI review enforces them on every PR. Sourcery's 'review rules' combine path globs with free-form text and check only the lines a PR changes.

sources.title: Introducing Qodo's Rule System: Turning Standards into Systems
sources.quote: Rules encode explicit standards, from architectural constraints to security and domain requirements, and can be applied at the organization or repository level

sources.title: Sourcery - Review rules
sources.quote: A rule only looks at the lines the pull request changes.

findings.relevance: Teams can add domain rules here too, but they produce review comments, not a numeric score, and enforcement depends on an LLM. Qodo's own post says rules injected as plain prompts make enforcement 'probabilistic instead of policy-driven'.

verdict.evidence: I opened https://www.qodo.ai/blog/introducing-qodo-rule-system/ (datePublished 2026-02-17T13:57:20, author Elana Krasner). It contains 'Today, we're excited to release Qodo 2.1 and introduce the first Rules System', 'Each rule is a versioned entity with defined scope, ownership, and lifecycle' and 'Qodo's Rule System is Beta and currently available for GitHub single/multi-tenant users.' The cited quote about architectural constraints appears verbatim. On enforcement, the post says rules become 'an active component of Qodo's agentic review experience, and available for the specialized rules enforcement agent'. One caveat for the relevance note: the phrase 'Enforcement becomes probabilistic instead of policy-driven' describes the status quo of rules injected as prompts in other tools. Qodo claims its own enforcement 'is deterministic rather than probabilistic', which is vendor marketing. The note's 'depends on an LLM' is our inference, not Qodo's wording. https://docs.sourcery.ai/reviews/review-rules.md describes path patterns as globs and the rule as 'up to 3,000 characters of free-form text', and contains 'A rule only looks at the lines the pull request changes.' verbatim. It also says rules post ordinary inline comments, and that security scanners ignore review rules.

findings.claim: GitHub Code Quality runs deterministic CodeQL rules on PRs and can block PRs through rulesets. Its rule-based languages are C#, Go, Java, JavaScript, Python, Ruby and TypeScript; other languages, including Rust, get only AI analysis of recently changed code. It requires GitHub Team or Enterprise Cloud.

sources.title: GitHub Code Quality - GitHub Docs
sources.quote: You can enforce quality and coverage thresholds with rulesets to block pull requests that don't meet your criteria, so new quality debt doesn't accumulate.

findings.relevance: The platform default is threshold gating with no deterministic Rust rules, so it does not cover Geiger's first target.

verdict.corrected_claim: On pull requests, GitHub Code Quality posts only deterministic CodeQL rule findings. Teams can use rulesets with quality and coverage thresholds to block PRs. Rule-based analysis covers C#, Go, Java, JavaScript, Python, Ruby and TypeScript. AI-powered analysis runs on recently changed files on the default branch, not on PRs, and covers languages beyond those rules. The page does not name Rust; that Rust gets only AI analysis is an inference from the language list. Coverage thresholds come from an uploaded Cobertura XML report, so coverage gating can still apply to a Rust project. The feature requires GitHub Team or Enterprise Cloud.
verdict.evidence: I opened https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/concepts/about-code-quality. The cited quote appears verbatim. The page says 'Who can use this feature? GitHub Team or GitHub Enterprise Cloud' and 'On pull requests, Code Quality uses deterministic CodeQL rules to detect known anti-patterns'. It also says 'On the default branch ... AI-powered analysis also runs on recently changed files, flagging issues that fall outside existing rule sets, including languages not yet covered by CodeQL queries.' and 'Note On pull requests, Code Quality posts rules-based CodeQL findings only.' The language list is 'C# Go Java JavaScript Python Ruby TypeScript', and Rust is not mentioned. On coverage: 'If you upload a Cobertura XML coverage report, line coverage metrics show whether a change maintains or reduces coverage.'

findings.claim: Betterer (open source, TypeScript) implements a ratchet. It stores a test's value in a committed `.betterer.results` file, updates the file when the value improves and fails when the value gets worse.

sources.title: Betterer - Introduction
sources.quote: If it gets better, the .betterer.results file will be updated with the new result ✅! If it gets worse, your test will fail and Betterer will throw an error ❌!

findings.relevance: A committed baseline that tolerates no regression is the zero-budget special case of Geiger's per-PR budget. Geiger generalises it to an allowed drop, such as 0.2 points.

verdict.evidence: I opened https://phenomnomnominal.github.io/betterer/docs/introduction (footer: 'Last updated on Nov 12, 2021'). The cited quote appears verbatim: 'If it gets better, the .betterer.results file will be updated with the new result ✅! If it gets worse, your test will fail and Betterer will throw an error ❌!' The results-file docs page (https://phenomnomnominal.github.io/betterer/docs/results-file) says 'It should be commited along with your code', which supports 'committed'. The npm registry shows @betterer/cli with the latest dist-tag 6.0.0-alpha.1, published 2024-12-01, under the MIT license, so the project is open source and has had little release activity since.

Codecov's project status has a `threshold` that lets coverage drop by a set percentage and still pass, which is a per-PR allowed-drop budget for a single metric.

sources.quote: Trunk Code Quality has the ability to ***Hold The Line***, which means it only lints your git diffs; only what you changed on your branch gets linted.

sources.quote: Allow the coverage to drop by <number>% , and posting a success status.

I opened https://docs.codecov.com/docs/commit-status. findings.claim: desloppify is a source-available agent harness. It is free for individuals and open-source companies; commercial use otherwise is paid under its LICENSE. It produces a strict score meant to resist gaming, targets 'above 98', and combines mechanical detectors with LLM review. It has full plugins for Rust and GDScript. It explicitly supports full-codebase scoring only, not diff scoring.

sources.quote: A score above 98 should correlate with a codebase a seasoned engineer would call beautiful.

sources.title: desloppify README

findings.relevance: This is the nearest open-source analogue to Geiger's 98/100 score, and it covers both Rust and Godot. It lacks change-scoped scoring and a per-PR budget.

verdict.corrected_claim: desloppify is a source-available agent harness under the Open Source Native License (OSNL) v0.2, which is not OSI-approved. Anyone may use it free for internal purposes, including commercial companies improving their own code. Payment applies only when a company that is not open source distributes desloppify, or a derivative, in a product or service, or offers it to third parties. The tool combines mechanical detectors with LLM review and produces a strict score designed to resist gaming. The README says diff-only scanning is 'not the supported model yet' and recommends full-codebase CI gating. It also says 'full plugin depth for TypeScript, Python, C#, C++, Dart, GDScript, Go, and Rust' and 'Desloppify is free for any individual — whether working independently or at a company — to use for their own work.' findings.claim: The evidence that rule-based debt scores predict defects is weak. In an empirical study of 21 Java projects, only 25 of 202 SonarQube Java rules were found to have relatively low fault-proneness, and SonarQube's 'bug' violations were generally not fault-prone.

sources.title: Are SonarQube Rules Inducing Bugs? (Lenarduzzi, Lomio, Huttunen, Taibi)
sources.quote: violations considered as "bugs" by SonarQube were generally not fault-prone and, consequently, the fault-prediction power of the model proposed by SonarQube is extremely low.

findings.relevance: Geiger's default weights should not be presented as validated. User-tunable weights (requirement 3) and calibration against the project's own history are justified.

verdict.corrected_claim: Lenarduzzi et al. (SANER 2020, arXiv v2 2019-12-19) studied 21 open-source Java projects. They found that SonarQube's own 'bug' classification predicts faults at about chance level (AUC 50.94%), and that individual violations are poor fault predictors. The abstract's '25 of 202 rules with relatively low fault-proneness' is ambiguously worded; the paper body says 26 violations were found fault-prone by the XGBoost model. The same paper reports that violations taken together in a trained XGBoost model reach an AUC of about 0.83. Its first lesson is that violations 'can be good predictors if considered together', and it recommends a customized model per company. A follow-up on 33 Apache Java projects (JSS 2020) found no difference in fault-proneness between classes with and without SonarQube issues, and only a small difference in change-proneness. So SonarQube's default rules and weights are poorly validated, but the evidence also supports calibrating weights to a project's own history, not abandoning rule-based measurement.
verdict.evidence: I opened https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.00376v2. The cited quote appears verbatim in the abstract, alongside 'Among the 202 rules defined for Java by SonarQube, only 25 can be considered to have relatively low fault-proneness.' (v2 submitted 19 Dec 2019; SANER 2020). In the PDF body: 'Our results show that 26 violations can be considered fault-prone from the XGBoost model.' and 'an AUC of 50.94%, confirming that violations classified as "bugs" almost never resulted in a fault.' It also says 'Lesson 1: SonarQube violations are not good predictors of fault-proneness if considered individually, but can be good predictors if considered together.' with 'XGBoost AUC=83.32%±10%'. The follow-up is https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.11590 (JSS vol. 170, Dec 2020): 'As for fault-proneness, there is no difference between clean and dirty classes.'

findings.claim: Inference: no surveyed tool combines all of the following: (a) one repository-level score with a numeric budget per PR, (b) deterministic, team-written hard-gate rules such as layer or ECS rules alongside soft metrics, and (c) change-scoped scoring for Rust. CodeScene (per-file improved/degraded verdict), Qlty SlopOne (per-file max-drop with an LLM-hybrid score), Codecov (budget for one metric) and Sonar (thresholds on new code; architecture analysis not available for Rust) each cover a part. This rests on findings land-1 to land-19; it does not rule out unindexed tools.

sources.title: slop-one - Qlty Docs
sources.quote: Compare the files changed since the merge base with REF against their versions there

sources.title: CodeScene MCP Server - Tools
sources.quote: Returns quality gates (passed/failed) and per-file verdicts (improved, degraded, or stable).

findings.relevance: This defines Geiger's differentiation: a budget on an aggregate score, pluggable deterministic rules and hard gates, Rust first, run in Dagger.

verdict.evidence: Both cited quotes match the sources I opened. https://docs.qlty.sh/cli/commands/slop-one.md (Qlty CLI v0.667.0) says: "Compare the files changed since the merge base with REF against their versions there" and "Largest score drop allowed before a changed file counts as declined (default: 1)". It makes paid model-provider API calls ("Maximum estimated API spend for this invocation in USD"), which supports a model-based score. The page itself does not say "LLM-hybrid". https://raw.githubusercontent.com/codescene-oss/codescene-mcp-server/main/docs/tools.md says: "Returns quality gates (passed/failed) and per-file verdicts (improved, degraded, or stable)." It scores per file (1.0-10.0) and defines no repository-level budget. code-health-rules.json only tunes thresholds; it does not add layer rules. Sonar: https://docs.sonarsource.com/sonarqube-cloud/architecture-analysis.md lists under 'Supported languages': "C#, Java, JavaScript, Python, and TypeScript." Rust is not listed, so that part holds. Codecov: https://docs.codecov.com/docs/commit-status says "The codecov/project status measures overall project coverage and compares it against the base of the pull request" and has a `threshold` setting. That is a budget on one metric (coverage). I checked one possible counterexample, Qlty Cloud. It has deterministic team-written rules: https://docs.qlty.sh/custom-checks.md says "Custom checks allow you to create and enforce your own static analysis rules" (ast-grep/semgrep/ripgrep). It also has a PR gate: https://docs.qlty.sh/cloud/gates.md says "The Gate can be configured to consider new issues, vulnerabilities, and file maintainability". Its project-level ratings are letter grades, not a numeric per-PR budget. So Qlty covers (b) and per-file (c) but not (a), and the inference still holds. An extended search found no tool that combines all three. The closest result, agent-readiness-action, scores whether a repo is ready for agents, not code quality. Caveat: the finding names Qlty only through SlopOne and leaves out Qlty Cloud's custom checks and gate. Those cover more of (b) than the finding suggests, but they do not change the conclusion. The finding's own hedge, that unindexed tools may exist, is appropriate.
