open_questions: Halstead, NPath, ABC, LCOM variants and fan-in/fan-out were not separately validated in sources read here. Do any primary studies show they add predictive value beyond LOC once size is controlled?
No validation of Robert Martin's instability/abstractness/distance against defects or change effort was found. Is there any, or should Geiger treat these purely as policy rules?

All comprehension validations (cognitive complexity meta-analysis, fMRI, EEG, readability models) use short Java/C/Python snippets. Do any cover Rust, or ownership and lifetime constructs, which add complexity these metrics ignore?
Does LLM per-token surprisal (perplexity) on changed lines outperform n-gram entropy for bug localisation, and is it stable enough between model versions to serve as a scored metric?
Majumder et al. replicated Rahman & Devanbu (arXiv 2008.09569, EMSE 2022) and disagreed on some conclusions. Which conclusions survive?

How do metric thresholds behave when the code author is an AI agent? Agents may game function-length or complexity limits by splitting functions, which raises fan-out and propagation cost instead (Goodhart risk; no empirical source found here).

areas.title: Test-quality, evolution/process and organizational metrics and their validity
areas.summary_before_verification: The evidence does not support any single test-quality number as a reliable score input. Coverage correlates only low-to-moderately with suite effectiveness once suite size is controlled (Inozemtseva & Holmes 2014: 31,000 suites, 5 Java systems). Stronger criteria such as decision coverage and MC/DC-like coverage added no insight in that study. At project level, coverage did not predict post-release bugs across 100 Java projects (Kochhar et al. 2017). Mutation score tracks real faults better than coverage (Just et al. 2014: 357 real faults, 73% coupled to mutants). Papadakis et al. 2018 found this correlation weak once suite size is controlled, and Chen et al. 2020 argue that controlling for size this way is methodologically flawed. A 2026 ISSTA replication on LLM-generated tests finds that coverage and mutation are useful only when the code under test is assumed correct. Google's industrial practice points to diff-scoped measurement: changelist coverage with voluntary thresholds and no global enforcement. Mutation runs only on changed lines; 85% of mutants were initially judged unproductive until heuristic suppression raised the productive rate to 89%. Flakiness is a real noise source for any gate: at Google, 1.5% of runs were flaky and 84% of pass-to-fail transitions involved a flaky test. Process metrics (churn, change count, code age) usually predict defects better than code metrics: Graves 2000, Nagappan & Ball 2005, Moser 2008, Rahman & Devanbu 2013, and Majumder et al. 2021 across 700 GitHub projects. They describe where risk lies, not how good a single PR is. Ownership, developer-count and organizational metrics show strong effects at Microsoft (Bird 2011; Nagappan, Murphy & Basili 2008). Replications conflict: Foucault 2014 (open source), Caglayan 2015 (another enterprise), Koana 2024 (nine Brightsquid projects), and Graves 2000, which found no effect of developer count. CodeScene's Code Red study reports 15x more defects and 124% longer development time in low-Code-Health files. That study uses the vendor's own metric and customers, counts defects per file rather than per line of code, and its authors concede it is correlational with possible reverse causality. For Geiger, coverage, mutation and assertion measures fit best as soft, diff-local signals; process and hotspot data fit best as weights on where a change lands; organizational metrics are weak candidates for agent-facing gates.

findings.claim: Inozemtseva & Holmes (ICSE 2014) generated 31,000 test suites for 5 Java systems (up to 724 KLOC) and found only low-to-moderate correlation between coverage (statement, decision, modified condition) and mutation-based effectiveness once suite size is held constant. Stronger coverage criteria gave no extra insight. Limit: effectiveness was measured with mutants, not real faults.

sources.title: Coverage Is Not Strongly Correlated with Test Suite Effectiveness (ICSE 2014)
sources.quote: We found that there is a low to moderate correlation between coverage and effectiveness when the number of test cases in the suite is controlled for.

sources.title: Coverage Is Not Strongly Correlated with Test Suite Effectiveness (ICSE 2014)
sources.quote: stronger forms of coverage do not provide greater insight into the effectiveness of the suite

findings.relevance: Argues against heavily weighting coverage (or MC/DC) in the 0-100 score; coverage is better used to locate untested code than as a target agents can optimize.

verdict.evidence: Downloaded https://cs.ubc.ca/~rtholmes/papers/icse_2014_inozemtseva.pdf (saved as .local/geiger-research/sources/test-quality/inoz.pdf). Abstract: "we generated 31,000 test suites for five systems consisting of up to 724,000 lines of source code. We measured the statement coverage, decision coverage, and modified condition coverage". Both quotes found verbatim. Effectiveness measured with PIT mutants (Sec. 3.3). Abstract also says coverage is "useful for identifying under-tested parts of a program, should not be used as a quality target", which supports the relevance note. Note: authors were at U. Waterloo. Search budget was exhausted, so I ran no independent search; Chen et al. 2020 (cov-4) is the known methodological critique.

findings.claim: Gopinath, Jensen & Groce (ICSE 2014) studied manual and generated suites from hundreds of real-world open-source projects and found that plain statement coverage predicted mutation kills better than block, branch or path coverage when evaluating a single suite.

sources.title: Code Coverage for Suite Evaluation by Developers (ICSE 2014)
sources.quote: statement (not block, branch, or path) coverage predicts mutation kills best.

findings.relevance: If Geiger includes coverage, cheap line/statement coverage (e.g., cargo-llvm-cov line data) is as informative as costlier criteria.

verdict.evidence: Downloaded https://www.cefns.nau.edu/~adg326/icse14.pdf. Abstract quote verbatim: "statement (not block, branch, or path) coverage predicts mutation kills best." Body: "This paper draws from the evaluation of hundreds of open source projects". Scope caveat to add: only open-source Java/Maven projects on GitHub, generated suites from Randoop, and effectiveness measured by mutation kills ("mutation testing is used, as identifying real faults of hundreds of Java projects was clearly infeasible").

findings.claim: Kochhar, Lo, Lawall & Nagappan (IEEE Trans. Reliability, Dec 2017) measured coverage of 100 large open-source Java projects against post-release bugs. They found an insignificant correlation at project level and none at file level.

sources.title: Code Coverage and Post-release Defects: A Large-Scale Study on Open Source Projects
sources.quote: Our results show that coverage has an insignificant correlation with the number of bugs

findings.relevance: Real-defect evidence that a repository-level coverage number is a weak health signal; quote taken via WebFetch of the abstract, full text not read.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/code-coverage-and-post-release-defects-a-large-scale-study-on-open-source-projects/ (curl). It gives Kochhar, Lo, Lawall, Nagappan, IEEE Transactions on Reliability, Dec 2017, Vol 66(4) pp. 1213-1228. Abstract: "Our results show that coverage has an insignificant correlation with the number of bugs that are found after the release of the software at the project level, and no such correlation at the file level." It covers 100 large open-source Java projects. Only the abstract was read; the full text (SMU/CORE) is still blocked by Incapsula/403. Search budget was exhausted, so I ran no independent search for replications.

findings.claim: Chen et al. (ASE 2020, with Just, Holmes, Ernst, Fraser) argue that test set size is neither a confounder nor a variable to manipulate, and call the random-selection designs of earlier studies flawed. With their own method they find adequacy-based selection beats random selection, and mutation-based selection pays off most after coverage is exhausted.

sources.title: Revisiting the Relationship Between Fault Detection, Test Adequacy Criteria, and Test Set Size (ASE 2020)
sources.quote: mutation-based test selection is most effective when employed after coverage has exhausted its usefulness.

sources.title: Revisiting the Relationship Between Fault Detection, Test Adequacy Criteria, and Test Set Size (ASE 2020)
sources.quote: test set size is neither a confounding variable, as previously suggested, nor an independent variable that should be experimentally manipulated.

findings.relevance: Shows the coverage-validity debate is methodological and unsettled; supports a layered design: coverage first, mutation testing on top.

verdict.evidence: Downloaded https://homes.cs.washington.edu/~mernst/pubs/test-set-size-ase2020.pdf. Authors: Chen, Gopinath, Tadakamalla, Ernst, Holmes, Fraser, Ammann, Just (ASE '20). Both quotes appear verbatim in the abstract. Abstract: "this paper concludes that adequacy-based test selection is superior to random selection". Conclusions: "concluding that the random-selection methodology is flawed." The listed co-authors are correct but incomplete; Gopinath and Ammann are also authors.

findings.claim: Just et al. (FSE 2014) used 357 real faults in 5 Java programs (321 KLOC) and 230,000 mutants. Mutant detection correlated significantly with real-fault detection independently of coverage, and more strongly than statement coverage did. 73% of real faults were coupled to mutants, 10% needed new or stronger operators, and 17% were not coupled.

sources.title: Are Mutants a Valid Substitute for Real Faults in Software Testing? (FSE 2014)
sources.quote: The results show a statistically significant correlation between mutant detection and real fault detection, independently of code coverage.

findings.relevance: Mutation score is the strongest test-quality proxy available, but about a sixth of real faults are invisible to standard operators.

verdict.evidence: Downloaded https://homes.cs.washington.edu/~mernst/pubs/mutation-effectiveness-fse2014.pdf. "357 real faults in 5 open-source applications that comprise a total of 321,000 lines of code"; "230,000 mutants"; "coupling effect for 73% of real faults"; "10% of real faults require a new or stronger mutation operator"; "17% of real faults are not coupled to mutants"; "statistically significant correlation that is stronger than the correlation between statement coverage and real fault detection." The quote is verbatim. Caveat: the paper says it cannot compute the correlation coefficient directly with coverage held fixed. It tests mutation-score differences between suite pairs that have the same coverage.

findings.claim: Papadakis, Shin, Yoo & Bae (ICSE 2018), using CoreBench (C) and Defects4J (Java), found that all mutation-score versus real-fault correlations become weak when suite size is controlled. Selecting suites by higher mutation score still significantly improved fault detection over random same-size suites.

sources.title: Are Mutation Scores Correlated with Real Fault Detection? (ICSE 2018)
sources.quote: all correlations between mutation scores and real fault detection are weak when controlling for test suite size.

sources.title: Are Mutation Scores Correlated with Real Fault Detection? (ICSE 2018)
sources.quote: our data suggest that mutants provide good guidance for improving the fault detection of test suites, but their correlation with fault detection are weak.

findings.relevance: Supports using surviving mutants as actionable findings in the report rather than treating the mutation score as a precise quality number.

verdict.evidence: Downloaded https://mpapad.github.io/publications/pdfs/ICSE2018.pdf. Both quotes appear verbatim in the abstract. It uses CoREBench (4 C programs) and Defects4J (5 Java programs). Abstract: "By measuring the fault detection capability of the top ranked, according to mutation score, test suites (opposed to randomly selected test suites of the same size), we find that achieving higher mutation scores improves significantly the fault detection."

findings.claim: Zhao, Zhou & Cohen (ISSTA 2026, arXiv July 2026) replicated Inozemtseva and Papadakis on LLM-generated test suites. Coverage and mutation give meaningful signals only in regression-style settings where the code under test is assumed bug-free. They become unreliable when the code may already be buggy, and suite size was not a dominant confounder.

sources.title: Do Coverage and Mutation Scores of LLM-Generated Test Suites Correlate with Their Effectiveness? (Replicability Study)
sources.quote: We also find little evidence that test suite size is a dominant confounder for correlations among coverage, mutation, and real-bug detection for LLM-generated tests.

sources.title: Do Coverage and Mutation Scores of LLM-Generated Test Suites Correlate with Their Effectiveness? (Replicability Study)
sources.quote: in another common scenario where the code-under-test may already be buggy and the goal is to expose the bug within the code-under-test, they no longer serve as reliable indicators.

findings.relevance: Directly relevant to agents writing tests for their own code: tests generated from buggy code can score well on coverage and mutation while encoding the bug.

verdict.corrected_claim: Zhao, Zhou & Cohen (Proc. ACM Softw. Eng. 3, ISSTA, Oct 2026; arXiv 2607.22880, 24 Jul 2026) replicated Inozemtseva et al. and Papadakis et al. on test suites that 11 LLMs generated for Defects4J (Java). Coverage and mutation score gave meaningful signals when comparing across models in regression-style settings, where the code under test is assumed bug-free. When the code under test may already be buggy, coverage became unreliable and mutation analysis was not applicable. They found little evidence that suite size is a dominant confounder.
verdict.evidence: Downloaded https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.22880. Both quotes appear verbatim. Abstract qualifier omitted by the claim: "these metrics can provide meaningful signals when comparing across models". Body: "coverage becomes unreliable as an indicator of bug detection effectiveness, and mutation analysis is not applicable." Scope: "we use Defects4J" with "11 state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLMs". Venue: "Proc. ACM Softw. Eng. 3, ISSTA, Article ISSTA002 (October 2026)". The relevance note (tests from buggy code encode the bug) is supported: "tests generated from buggy code can encode faulty behavior that is absent from the bug-free implementation." The finding is about comparing LLMs, not about scoring one repository's suite, so it bears only indirectly on Geiger's per-repository score.

findings.claim: Google (Petrović, Ivanković, Fraser, Just; IEEE TSE 2021) runs mutation testing only on changed lines during code review for over 24,000 developers and 1,000 projects (~17M mutants, 760k changes). Developers initially rated 85% of mutants unproductive. Suppression heuristics built from developer feedback raised the productive share from 15% to 89%.

sources.title: Practical Mutation Testing at Scale: A view from Google
sources.quote: developers at Google initially classified 85% of reported mutants as unproductive.

sources.title: Practical Mutation Testing at Scale: A view from Google
sources.quote: heuristics for mutant suppression that improved the ratio of productive mutants from 15% to 89%.

findings.relevance: Precedent for Geiger's locality requirement: diff-scoped mutation is feasible and actionable, but raw mutation output needs noise filtering, or agents will write brittle change-detector tests.

verdict.evidence: Downloaded https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.11378v2 (22 pp.). Both quotes appear verbatim. "used by more than 24,000 developers on more than 1,000 projects"; "almost 17 million mutants and 760,000 changes"; "considering only changed lines of code"; reports at most one mutant per changed and covered line. The 15%-to-89% improvement came from "feedback of more than 20,000 developers on thousands of mutants over siz [six] years". The arXiv copy is the preprint ("submitted to the IEEE"). https://research.google/pubs/practical-mutation-testing-at-scale-a-view-from-google/ lists it as "IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering (2021)".

findings.claim: Google computes coverage for about 1 billion lines daily in 7 languages and surfaces changelist (diff) coverage in code review. It enforces no codebase-wide threshold; projects opt into voluntary levels such as project ≥60% with changelist ≥70%, up to ≥90%/≥90%. Of 512 survey responses, 60% were positive about coverage and 16% negative.

sources.title: Code Coverage at Google (ESEC/FSE 2019)
sources.quote: Google does not enforce any code coverage thresholds across the entire codebase. Projects (or groups of projects) are free to define their own thresholds and goals.

findings.relevance: Industrial model for Geiger's per-PR delta: changelist-level metrics with team-chosen thresholds rather than a global mandate.

verdict.corrected_claim: Google computes coverage for one billion lines daily in seven languages and surfaces changelist coverage in code review. It enforces no codebase-wide threshold; many projects opt into voluntary levels, from project >=60% with changelist >=70% up to project >=90% with changelist >=90%. The survey went to 3,000 developers and got 512 responses (17%). Of the 286 write-in comments, 60% were positive about coverage, 24% neutral and 16% negative.
verdict.evidence: Downloaded https://homes.cs.washington.edu/~rjust/publ/google_coverage_fse_2019.pdf. The no-threshold quote is verbatim. The 60%/16% figures come from Table 3: "Sentiment towards coverage expressed in the write-in text box"; "60% of responses were generally positive towards coverage, 16% were negative, 24% were neutral." The table total is 286 (173 positive, 46 negative), not 512. Also: "We sent the survey to 3000 randomly chosen developers at Google out of which 512 responded (17%)." Levels in Table 2: "Project coverage at least 60%; Changelist coverage at least 70%" ... "Project coverage at least 90%; Changelist coverage at least 90%". The data is from 2019.

findings.claim: Zhang & Mesbah (ESEC/FSE 2015) built 6,700 suites using 24,000 assertions from 5 Java projects. Assertion count and assertion coverage correlated strongly with effectiveness, and assertion count explains much of the size-effectiveness link. Limit: effectiveness was measured as mutation score.

sources.title: Assertions Are Strongly Correlated with Test Suite Effectiveness (FSE 2015)
sources.quote: the number of assertions in a test suite strongly correlates with its effectiveness, and this factor directly influences the relationship between test suite size and effectiveness.

findings.relevance: Assertion density/coverage is a cheap static proxy that also catches tests without oracles, though agents can easily game the raw assertion count.

verdict.evidence: Downloaded https://people.ece.ubc.ca/amesbah/resources/papers/fse15.pdf. The abstract quote is verbatim. "We compose 6,700 test suites in total, using 24,000 assertions of five real-world Java projects"; "assertion coverage is strongly correlated with effectiveness". Effectiveness is mutation score. Contributions: "assertion quantity can significantly influence the relationship between a test suite's size and its effectiveness". "Explains much of" is a mild paraphrase of "directly/significantly influences". The paper notes Java-only external validity.

findings.claim: Google reported (May 2016) that about 1.5% of all test runs gave flaky results, almost 16% of tests showed some flakiness, and about 84% of observed pass-to-fail transitions involved a flaky test.

sources.title: Flaky Tests at Google and How We Mitigate Them (John Micco, Google Testing Blog)
sources.quote: What we find in practice is that about 84% of the transitions we observe from pass to fail involve a flaky test!

findings.relevance: Any Geiger hard gate or score that depends on test outcomes (including mutation kills) needs reruns or quarantine, or it will penalize PRs for noise.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://testing.googleblog.com/2016/05/flaky-tests-at-google-and-how-we.html (post dated May 27, 2016, John Micco). All three numbers appear: "we see a continual rate of about 1.5% of all test runs reporting a 'flaky' result"; "Almost 16% of our tests have some level of flakiness associated with them!"; "about 84% of the transitions we observe from pass to fail involve a flaky test!" Scope: Google's post-submit CI corpus, as of 2016. I could not run an independent search for newer figures because the session's web-search budget ran out.

findings.claim: Graves et al. (IEEE TSE 2000), studying one very large, long-lived system, found that change-history measures beat product metrics. Change count predicted faults better than length, and complexity metrics added nothing because they tracked LOC. A module one year older had about a third fewer faults. Developer count and co-change coupling did not improve predictions.

sources.title: Predicting Fault Incidence Using Software Change History (IEEE TSE 26(7))
sources.quote: the number of times code has been changed is a better indication of how many faults it will contain than is its length.

sources.title: Predicting Fault Incidence Using Software Change History (IEEE TSE 26(7))
sources.quote: Perhaps surprisingly, there was no evidence that a large number of developers working on a module caused it to be more faulty.

findings.relevance: Code age and change frequency are cheap git-derived signals; also contradicts Bird et al. on developer count, so such metrics need local validation.

verdict.evidence: Opened the graves_tse98.pdf URL (header: IEEE TSE vol. 26, no. 7, July 2000). Quotes: "the number of times code has been changed is a better indication of how many faults it will contain than is its length"; "if a module is, on the average, a year older than an otherwise similar module, the older module will have roughly a third fewer faults"; "many software complexity metrics are also not useful in this context because, within our data set, these metrics are very highly correlated with lines of code"; developer count: "no evidence that a large number of developers working on a module caused it to be more faulty"; co-change: "typical number of other modules changed together with the module, this feature ... also did not appear to be important in our models". Scope: an 80-module, 1.5-million-line subsystem of one telephone switching system, a single-system study.

findings.claim: Nagappan & Ball (ICSE 2005) found on Windows Server 2003 that absolute churn predicts defect density poorly. Churn normalized by component size and time span is highly predictive and separated fault-prone binaries with 89.0% accuracy.

sources.title: Use of Relative Code Churn Measures to Predict System Defect Density (ICSE 2005)
sources.quote: while absolute measures of code churn are poor predictors of defect density, our set of relative measures of code churn is highly predictive of defect density.

findings.relevance: If Geiger uses churn, normalize it (churn/LOC, churn over time); raw lines changed is a poor signal.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/icse05churn.pdf. Quote verified: "while absolute measures of code churn are poor predictors of defect density, our set of relative measures of code churn is highly predictive of defect density." Also: "discriminate between fault and not fault-prone binaries in W2k3-SP1 with an accuracy of 89.0 percent." The relative measures normalize by size and time, e.g. M1 "Churned LOC / Total LOC" and M5 "Weeks of churn / File count". Study system: Windows Server 2003.

findings.claim: Rahman & Devanbu (ICSE 2013) built models across 85 releases of 12 large open-source projects. Code metrics were generally less useful than process metrics and showed high stasis: they barely change between releases, so models keep flagging the same files. Moser et al. (ICSE 2008) reached the same conclusion from a single project (Eclipse), per Majumder et al.

sources.title: How, and Why, Process Metrics Are Better (ICSE 2013)
sources.quote: code metrics, despite widespread use in the defect prediction literature, are generally less useful than process metrics for prediction.

sources.title: Revisiting Process versus Product Metrics: a Large Scale Analysis
sources.quote: Moser et al. [53], Arisholm et al. [7], Kamei et al. [34], Rahman et al. [70], Graves et al. [26] and Giger et al. [25] based their conclusions on 1,1,3,12,15,21 projects

findings.relevance: Static code metrics alone (function length, complexity) are weak defect predictors; this bears on how much weight Geiger's soft code measurements deserve.

verdict.corrected_claim: Rahman & Devanbu (ICSE 2013) built models across 85 releases of 12 large open-source projects. Code metrics were generally less useful than process metrics and showed high stasis, so models kept flagging the same files, which turned out to be comparatively less defect-dense. Majumder et al. list Moser et al. (ICSE 2008) as reaching a similar conclusion from 1 project. Majumder et al. do not name that project. The claim that it was Eclipse comes from outside that source and was not verified here.
verdict.evidence: ICSE 2013 page https://2013.icse-conferences.org/content/how-and-why-process-metrics-are-better.html: "We build many prediction models across 85 releases of 12 large open source projects"; "code metrics have high stasis; they dont change very much from release to release". Majumder PDF https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.09569v3.pdf: "Similar conclusions (about the superiority of process metrics) are offered by Moser et al. [53], Giger et al. [25], and Graves et al. [26]." It gives the project count as "1,1,3,12,15,21 projects", and its text does not mention Eclipse for Moser. Caveat: the same Majumder list attributes 15 projects to Graves et al., but Graves studied one switching-system subsystem. Treat Majumder's per-study counts with caution. Web-search budget was exhausted, so I could not open Moser 2008 directly.

findings.claim: Majumder, Mody & Menzies (EMSE 2021) re-checked process versus product metrics on 722,471 commits from 700 GitHub projects. Process metrics won, with median recall 98% vs 44% and AUC 95% vs 54%. They warn that metric-importance rankings from small studies change dramatically at scale.

sources.title: Revisiting Process versus Product Metrics: a Large Scale Analysis
sources.quote: process metrics are better predictors for defects than product metrics (best process/product-based learners respectively achieve recalls of 98%/44% and AUCs of 95%/54%, median values).

findings.relevance: Strongest large-sample support for process metrics; also cautions against fixed, literature-derived weights in an aggregate score.

verdict.corrected_claim: Majumder, Mody & Menzies (Empirical Software Engineering 27(3), May 2022; arXiv v3 dated 26 Oct 2021) re-checked process versus product metrics on 722,471 commits from 700 GitHub projects. Process metrics won: the best learners reached median recall 98% vs 44% and AUC 95% vs 54%. They warn that metric-importance results from small studies change dramatically at scale.
verdict.evidence: PDF https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.09569v3.pdf. The abstract contains the quoted sentence exactly and "using 722,471 commits from 700 Github projects". It also says "we warn that it is unwise to trust metric importance results from analytics in-the-small studies since those change dramatically". The venue year is wrong in the claim. The arXiv abs page https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.09569v3 gives: "Journal reference: Empirical Software Engineering, Volume 27, Issue 3, May 2022" (DOI 10.1007/s10664-021-10068-4).

findings.claim: Bird et al. (ESEC/FSE 2011) on Windows Vista and Windows 7 found ownership measures (minor-contributor count, top-owner share) related to pre- and post-release failures. Adding them to a size/complexity/churn baseline raised explained variance by +20, +12, +46 and +3 percentage points across the four outcomes.

sources.title: Don't Touch My Code! Examining the Effects of Ownership on Software Quality (ESEC/FSE 2011)
sources.quote: measures of ownership such as the number of low-expertise developers, and the proportion of ownership for the top owner have a relationship with both pre-release faults and post-release failures.

findings.relevance: Ownership is a strong signal in a large commercial setting, but it is unclear what 'ownership' means when AI agents author most commits.

verdict.corrected_claim: Bird et al. (ESEC/FSE 2011) on Windows Vista and Windows 7 found ownership measures (minor-contributor count, top-owner share) related to pre- and post-release failures. Adding the minor-contributor count alone to a size/complexity/churn baseline raised explained variance by +20, +12, +46 and +3 percentage points (Vista pre/post, Win7 pre/post). Adding all ownership measures raised it to 50/44/72/22%, i.e. +24, +15, +48 and +4 points over the 26/29/24/18% baseline.
verdict.evidence: Opened https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/bird2011dtm.pdf. The cited quote is present. Table 2 reads: "Base (code metrics) 26% 29% 24% 18% ... Base + Minor 46%∗ (+20%) 41%∗ (+12%) 70%∗ (+46%) 21%∗ (+3%) ... Base + Minor + Major + Ownership 50%∗ (+2%) 44%∗ (+1%) 72%∗ (+1%) 22% (+0%)". So the +20/+12/+46/+3 gains come from Minor alone, not from the ownership measures together.

findings.claim: Ownership replications conflict. Greiler et al. (MSR 2015, 4 Microsoft products) confirmed Bird et al., reaching median file-level precision 0.74 and recall 0.38. Foucault et al. (EASE 2014, open source) raised doubts. Koana et al. (2024, 9 Brightsquid projects) found no strong link for minor contributors or total developers.

sources.title: Code Ownership and Software Quality: A Replication Study (MSR 2015)
sources.quote: A recent replication study by Foucault et al. [2] on open source software replicate the original results and lead to doubts about the general concept of ownership impacting code quality.

sources.title: Examining Ownership Models in Software Teams: A Systematic Literature Review and a Replication Study
sources.quote: Unlike prior studies, we found no strong correlation between minor contributors and bug numbers.

findings.relevance: Ownership and developer-count metrics do not transfer reliably across contexts and should not be default inputs to a general-purpose score.

verdict.evidence: Greiler et al. PDF (MSR 2015): "The results confirm the original findings by Bird et al. [1] that code ownership correlates with code quality". It also gives "median precision of 0.74 and a median recall of 0.38" at file level, and it covers "four main Microsoft product: Office, Windows, Office365 and Exchange". The cited Foucault quote is present, and ref [2] is in Proc. 18th Int. Conf. on Evaluation and Assessment in SE (EASE 2014). Koana et al. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.15665 (2024): "replicated experiments on nine priority projects at Brightsquid"; "no strong correlation between minor contributors and bug numbers"; "no strong link between the total number of developers modifying a file and bug counts". The claim leaves out that Koana et al. did find a significant correlation between major contributors and bug counts.

findings.claim: Nagappan, Murphy & Basili (ICSE 2008) found organizational metrics predicted failure-prone Windows Vista binaries (3,404 binaries, >50 MLOC) with average precision 0.87 and recall 0.84 over 50 random splits. Caglayan et al. (ICSE 2015) replicated this on other enterprise software: organizational metrics beat churn but lost to pre-release bug metrics.

sources.title: The Influence of Organizational Structure on Software Quality: An Empirical Case Study (ICSE 2008)
sources.quote: The average precision across all 50 random splits was 0.87 or 87% of the predicted failure-prone binaries that were actually failure-prone.

sources.title: Merits of Organizational Metrics in Defect Prediction: An Industrial Replication (ICSE 2015)
sources.quote: models based on organizational metrics performed better than models based on churn metrics but were outperformed by pre-release metric models.

findings.relevance: Organizational metrics are context-dependent and need org-chart data; not a fit for scoring an agent's pull request.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://www.cs.umd.edu/users/basili/publications/proceedings/P125.pdf. It contains "The average precision across all 50 random splits was 0.87", "the average recall value was 0.84" and "3404 binaries which account for a code size above ... 50 Million Lines of Code". The study system is Windows Vista. The Brunel record https://bura.brunel.ac.uk/handle/2438/14620 (ICSE 2015, Caglayan et al., "large-scale enterprise software") contains the quoted sentence exactly.

findings.claim: Logical (change) coupling was introduced by Gall, Hajek & Jazayeri (ICSM 1998) using 20 releases of a telecom switching system. D'Ambros, Lanza & Robbes (WCRE 2009) reported that it correlates with defects in three open-source systems, as described by Wiese et al. 2015. Graves et al. 2000 found co-change connectedness unimportant in their models.

sources.title: Detection of Logical Coupling Based on Product Release History (ICSM 1998)
sources.quote: We present an approach that uses information in a release history of a system to uncover logical dependencies and change patterns among modules.

sources.title: An Empirical Study of the Relation Between Strong Change Coupling and Defects ... Apache Aries
sources.quote: mined historical data from three open source projects and showed that change couplings correlate with defects extracted from a bug repository.

findings.relevance: Change coupling across hexagonal crates (e.g., domain and infrastructure always co-changing) could flag hidden architectural coupling that static layer rules miss; the D'Ambros primary PDF was not reachable.

verdict.evidence: Opened the Gall PDF https://plg.uwaterloo.ca/~migod/846/papers/gall-coupling.pdf. The quote is present, along with "We have developed the approach by working with 20 releases of a large Telecommunications Switching System". The PDF does not print its venue; ICSM 1998 is the standard attribution and was not checked against a second source. Wiese et al. PDF: "D'ambros, Robbles & Lanza [4] mined historical data from three open source projects and showed that change couplings correlate with defects"; ref [4] is "WCRE 2009". Graves: co-change connectedness "also did not appear to be important in our models". The D'Ambros primary paper was not opened, and the claim correctly says it relies on Wiese et al. for that point.

findings.claim: Tornhill & Borg (TechDebt 2022) analyzed 39 proprietary CodeScene-customer codebases (30,737 files, 6-12 months of Jira data). Low-Code-Health files had 15x more defects, 124% longer development time and 9x longer maximum cycle times. Limits: defects are counted per file, not per LOC; the metric is the vendor's own; the authors concede possible reverse causality. Code Health correlated r=-0.58 with resolution time, against r=0.13 for LoC.

sources.title: Code Red: The Business Impact of Code Quality - A Quantitative Study of 39 Proprietary Production Codebases
sources.quote: By analyzing activity in 30,737 files, we find that low quality code contains 15 times more defects than high quality code.

sources.title: Code Red: The Business Impact of Code Quality - A Quantitative Study of 39 Proprietary Production Codebases
sources.quote: Does low quality code lead to additional defects or is the code quality low because of the many defects?

findings.relevance: The closest published evidence for a composite file-level quality score like Geiger's; useful for business framing, but it is correlational and vendor-run.

verdict.corrected_claim: Tornhill & Borg (TechDebt 2022; arXiv 8 Mar 2022) analyzed 39 proprietary CodeScene-customer codebases (30,737 files, 6-12 months of Jira data). Compared with Healthy files, files in the Alert Code Health category averaged 15x more reported Jira defects per file, 124% longer Time-in-Development and up to 9x longer maximum Time-in-Development. Limits: defects are counted per file and not normalized by size; the metric is the vendor's own; the authors concede possible reverse causality. Raw Code Health correlated r=-0.58 with average issue resolution time, against r=0.13 for added LoC (lines added, not file size).
verdict.evidence: Opened https://arxiv.org/pdf/2203.04374. Both quotes are present. It says "Alert code results in 15 times more reported Jira defects than Healthy code" and "needs, on average, 124% longer". It also says "might require up to 9 times longer Time-in-Development" and "development tasks completed over 6-12 months". The LoC comparison is to added LoC: "We found a low Pearson correlation (r=0.13) between added LoC and the average issue resolution time"; Code Health: "We found a higher degree of correlation (r=-0.58)". The per-file-not-per-LOC limitation is the fact-checker's inference. The paper itself frames RQ1 as defect density but compares defects per file.

findings.claim: Borg, Pruvost, Mones & Tornhill (TechDebt 2024, best paper) re-analyzed the Code Red data plus a second public dataset (79 projects in total). The relation between code quality and defects/time is strongly non-linear, with amplified returns at the high-quality end. They recommend preventing code smells in high-churn files.

sources.title: Increasing, not Diminishing: Investigating the Returns of Highly Maintainable Code
sources.quote: the value model suggests strong non-linearities at the extremes of the code quality spectrum. Most importantly, the model suggests amplified returns on investment in the upper end.

findings.relevance: Suggests that a 98-to-88 drop may cost more than a linear score implies; a non-linear mapping, and protecting the upper end, may matter for Geiger's per-PR budget.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.13407 (v1, 24 Jan 2024). The abstract quote is exact. On the data, the paper says "we extend the dataset with another publicly available dataset with a similar structure [4]. In total, our analysis is based on data from 79 proprietary software projects", made up of CodeRed (39 projects) and UOwns (40 projects). On churn, the abstract says it will "recommend organizations to diligently prevent the introduction of code smells in files with high churn". The best-paper award is confirmed on https://conf.researchr.org/home/TechDebt-2024, which lists "Best Paper Award:" for Borg, Pruvost, Mones and Tornhill. Two parts of the claim are overstated. (1) Defects are not strongly non-linear across the scale. Sec. 5.1 says "There are negative trends for CH ≤ 5 and CH ≥ 8. No correlation appears for 5 ≤ CH ≤ 8", and Time-in-Dev shows "a steady decline for CH ≥ 4". The 'strong non-linearities' are in the value-creation model and only 'at the extremes'. (2) The results are file-level and correlational. Sec. 6 says "Extrapolating file-level results to project-wide averages is an important research direction." The paper says file size and churn "are not represented in the merged datasets" and that coupling is not considered. Three of the four authors work at CodeScene, which sells the Code Health metric. I could not run a search for newer replications because the session's web-search budget was used up.
verdict.corrected_claim: Borg, Pruvost, Mones & Tornhill (TechDebt 2024, Best Paper Award; three of the four authors work at CodeScene) combined the Code Red data (39 projects) with a second public dataset, UOwns (40 projects): 79 proprietary projects in total. File-level regressions of CodeScene Code Health (1-10) found two patterns. Defects fall for CH ≤ 5 and for CH ≥ 8, with no correlation between 5 and 8. Time-in-Dev falls steadily for CH ≥ 4. A value-creation model built on these regressions shows strong non-linearities at the extremes and increasing (not diminishing) returns at the top end. The authors recommend preventing code smells in high-churn files. The analysis is correlational and file-level, with no controls for file size, churn or coupling. The authors say extrapolating it to project-wide averages is future work, so it does not directly show how a drop in a repo-level score (e.g. 98 to 88) translates into cost.

findings.claim: CodeScene's documentation says it prioritizes hotspots by first finding files with high change frequency and low Code Health. It then raises priority for files that co-change with many modules or are touched by many developers or teams.

sources.title: CodeScene docs: Technical Debt / Hotspots
sources.quote: CodeScene starts by identifying files with high change frequency and low Code Health. Then CodeScene factors in other aspects.

findings.relevance: An existing hotspot model (change frequency x quality, plus coupling and team spread) that Geiger could replicate with git history to weight local score deltas.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://codescene.io/docs/guides/technical/hotspots.html (page title 'Technical Debt — CodeScene 1 Documentation', accessed 2026-11-07). Under 'Focus on your Refactoring Targets' it says: "CodeScene starts by identifying files with high change frequency and low Code Health. Then CodeScene factors in other aspects." It goes on: "Complicated code that changes often is more of a problem if: The hotspot has to be changed together with several other modules. The hotspot affects many different developers on different teams." A third factor applies too: "likely to be a coordination bottleneck for multiple developers". The claim matches the doc. The doc lists the factors but publishes no formula or weights.

findings.claim: Inference: for per-PR agent gating, Geiger should measure test quality on the diff (changelist coverage, diff-scoped mutation with noise suppression, assertion presence) as soft signals. Process and hotspot metrics should weight where a delta lands rather than score the PR itself, since they need history and do not attribute risk to one change. Ownership and organizational metrics should be optional, because replications conflict and agent authorship changes their meaning.

sources.title: Practical Mutation Testing at Scale: A view from Google
sources.quote: Our approach performs mutation testing on code changes, considering only changed lines of code

sources.title: Code Red: The Business Impact of Code Quality
sources.quote: there can be confounding variables such as differences in process [19] and organizational factors [41].

findings.relevance: Rests on findings cov-1..5, mut-1..4, proc-1..4, own-1..2, org-1, cs-1..3; maps the evidence onto Geiger's locality and hard/soft gate requirements.

verdict.evidence: Google paper (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.11378v2): the quote is exact ("Our approach performs mutation testing on code changes, considering only changed lines of code"). The paper also describes suppression of arid nodes, which raised productive mutants "from 15% to 89%". It supports diff-scoped mutation with noise suppression, but not as a score: Google says a mutation score is "neither concrete nor actionable, and it does not guide testing", and instead surfaces a restricted set of surviving mutants as code-review findings. Code Red quote (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2203.04374): exact ("there can be confounding variables such as differences in process [19] and organizational factors [41]."). It only says confounders exist; it says nothing about conflicting ownership replications or agent authorship. Those parts rest on other findings that I did not check here. 'Assertion presence' and 'changelist coverage' have no support in the two cited sources. The premise that process metrics 'do not attribute risk to one change' is contradicted by just-in-time defect prediction. Kamei et al., IEEE TSE 39(6), 2013 (https://posl.ait.kyushu-u.ac.jp/~kamei/publications/Kamei_TSE2013.pdf) say they "consider defect prediction models that focus on identifying defect-prone (“risky”) software changes instead of files or packages". They use "the number of added lines, and developer experience" and report about 68% accuracy and 64% recall. The hotspot-weighting part does have support: Borg et al. 2024 suggest "churn-based filtering and size-based weighting", and the CodeScene hotspot docs rank by change frequency plus Code Health.
verdict.corrected_claim: Inference, with caveats: for per-PR agent gating, Geiger can measure test quality on the diff. The cited evidence supports diff-scoped mutation testing with noise suppression (Google). Google surfaces surviving mutants as actionable review findings and rejects a mutation score as non-actionable, so any score penalty that Geiger derives from mutants is a design choice the source does not validate. Changelist coverage and assertion presence need their own sources. Hotspot and churn data are well suited to weighting where a delta lands (Borg et al. 2024; CodeScene). Process metrics are not limited to that role: just-in-time defect prediction (Kamei et al. 2013) attributes risk to single changes using change-level metrics such as size and developer experience. Agent authorship weakens the experience and ownership metrics among these, which supports keeping ownership and organizational metrics optional. Change-size and diffusion metrics remain usable for each PR.

open_questions: Does any study validate coverage, mutation or process metrics for Rust specifically (e.g., cargo-mutants, cargo-llvm-cov) or for game/ECS code? None found in this area's sources.
How do ownership, developer-count and churn metrics behave when most commits are authored by AI agents? No study found.
Chen et al. 2020 versus Papadakis et al. 2018: which size-control methodology is correct remains disputed; the 2026 LLM replication sides partly with neither.
Code Red counts defects per file without size normalization; whether the 15x effect survives LOC control is untested in the paper.
What noise floor (run-to-run variance from flaky tests or nondeterministic mutation sampling) would make a 0.2-point per-PR budget meaningful?

areas.title: Inventory of Rust quality-measurement tools
areas.summary_before_verification: Most Rust quality signals Geiger needs already have maintained tools that produce machine-readable output. Clippy (847 stable lints) is the main per-function source. It has configurable thresholds (too_many_lines defaults to 100, too_many_arguments to 7, type_complexity to 250, cognitive_complexity to 25). Its restriction lints count panics (unwrap_used, expect_used, indexing_slicing, panic), lint suppressions (allow_attributes_without_reason) and unsafe hygiene (undocumented_unsafe_blocks). A correction to the brief: cognitive_complexity is no longer in nursery. Clippy moved it to restriction in Rust 1.91 (2025-10-30), and its documentation now warns against using it as a measurement tool. Coverage (cargo-llvm-cov, tarpaulin, grcov), mutation testing (cargo-mutants, which has diff-scoped runs and outcomes.json), flaky-test detection (nextest, through JUnit), supply-chain checks (cargo-deny with JSON/SARIF, cargo-audit with JSON) and API-surface checks (cargo-semver-checks, cargo-public-api) are all released in 2026 and suit automated scoring. Some tools are stale or archived: rust-code-analysis (last release 0.0.25, Jan 2023), mutagen (last crate release 2018), cargo-depgraph (archived) and cargo-bloat (last release May 2024). Commercial platforms now cover Rust. SonarQube computes cognitive and cyclomatic complexity and imports Clippy JSON (Server 2026.5 LTA). CodeQL Rust has been GA since 2025-10-14, Semgrep Rust is GA, CodeScene has full Code Health support, and Qlty and DeepSource are GA. ast-grep (JSON/SARIF output) is the most direct engine for team-defined structural rules such as ECS conventions or counting Rc<RefCell<>> and .clone(), because no Clippy lint covers those two signals. Uncle Bob's crapper supports Rust: it computes CRAP from cyclomatic complexity and LCOV, offers a --changed mode, but has no identity matching across runs. Naming risk: cargo-geiger already uses the Geiger-counter and radiation metaphor for unsafe-code statistics in Rust, which collides with the product name "Geiger".

findings.claim: Clippy has 9 lint groups. clippy::all (correctness, suspicious, style, complexity, perf) is on by default. pedantic, restriction, nursery and cargo are allow-by-default, and the README says restriction should never be enabled wholesale. Thresholds are set in clippy.toml: too-many-lines-threshold (default 100), too-many-arguments-threshold (7), type-complexity-threshold (250), cognitive-complexity-threshold (25), excessive-nesting-threshold (0, meaning off).

Category table lists clippy::all 'all lints that are on by default (correctness, suspicious, style, complexity, perf)' warn/deny, plus correctness, suspicious, style, complexity, perf, pedantic, restriction, nursery, cargo (9 categories). pedantic/restriction/nursery/cargo are 'allow'. The excessive_nesting lint text says it 'will only trigger if a maximum nesting level is defined in the clippy.toml file', so 0 means off. findings.claim: Correction to the brief: cognitive_complexity is no longer in nursery. Clippy moved it from nursery to restriction in Rust 1.91 (released 2025-10-30); it had been in nursery since 2020 (PR #5428). The lint's documentation says it does not measure true cognitive complexity and points to excessive_nesting and too_many_lines instead. The critique goes back to a 2019 comment on issue #3793 by the lint's own author.

findings.claim: Several Rust-specific signals map to Clippy restriction lints that tools can count: panics (unwrap_used, expect_used, indexing_slicing, panic), suppressions (allow_attributes, allow_attributes_without_reason), unsafe hygiene (undocumented_unsafe_blocks, multiple_unsafe_ops_per_block) and Rc<Mutex> (rc_mutex). redundant_clone is in nursery. Inference from scanning the 847 stable lint IDs: no lint flags Rc<RefCell<T>> or counts .clone() calls in general, so those signals need a custom rule, for example in ast-grep.

sources.quote: Checks for unsafe blocks and impls without a // SAFETY: comment explaining why the unsafe operations performed inside the block are safe.

findings.relevance: Clippy can count most of the requested signals (panics, suppressions, unsafe); clone and Rc<RefCell> counts need Geiger's own rules.

verdict.evidence: Downloaded rust-lang.github.io/rust-clippy/stable/index.html and parsed it: 847 <article> lint IDs. Groups: unwrap_used, expect_used, indexing_slicing, panic, allow_attributes, allow_attributes_without_reason, undocumented_unsafe_blocks, multiple_unsafe_ops_per_block and rc_mutex are restriction; redundant_clone is nursery. Both quotes are present ('Checks for attributes that allow lints without a reason.'; 'Checks for unsafe blocks and impls without a // SAFETY: comment explaining why the unsafe operations performed inside the block are safe.'). Only rc_mutex, rc_buffer and arc_with_non_send_sync mention Rc together with RefCell, and none of them flags Rc<RefCell<T>>; rc_mutex even recommends Rc<RefCell<T>>. No clone-named lint counts .clone() calls in general. The inference holds. Caveat: the configurable disallowed_types lint (style, active only when configured in clippy.toml) can flag all uses of std::cell::RefCell, though not only inside Rc. I found no evidence on whether disallowed_methods can ban Clone::clone, so a Clippy-native partial route may exist before writing ast-grep rules.

verdict.corrected_claim: ast-grep (0.51.1, 2026-11-02; about 16.5k GitHub stars) runs YAML structural rules through `ast-grep scan`. It outputs JSON (pretty, stream or compact) or, with --format, GitHub annotations or SARIF, and --error/--warning override per-rule severity. Inference, qualified: it is the cheapest engine for syntactic team rules, such as banned patterns or counts of Rc<RefCell<>> or .clone() call sites. It has no type information, scope analysis or data-flow analysis, so it cannot express rules that depend on types or name resolution, for example which type .clone() is called on or semantic ECS invariants. areas.title: Pluggable custom rules and architecture conformance (hard gates), with Rust focus
areas.summary_before_verification: Ford et al. define an architectural fitness function as "an objective integrity assessment of some architectural characteristic(s)". Their examples include both pass/fail structure checks (cyclic dependencies) and metric thresholds (cyclomatic complexity < 50), so Geiger's hard gates and soft measurements are both fitness functions. They differ in whether the result is binary (static) or depends on context. In Rust, the Cargo crate graph is already a compile-time layer gate: a workspace crate can only use crates its Cargo.toml declares. A hexagonal workspace with one crate per layer therefore gets the most important gate, "domain must not depend on infrastructure", by checking forbidden edges in `cargo metadata` output or with cargo-deny `deny` + `wrappers`. Visibility (`pub(crate)`, `pub(in path)`) and cargo-modules `--acyclic` cover module-level structure inside a crate. Rust-native ArchUnit equivalents exist but are young: bylaw 0.1.0 (Aug 2026) and layered-crate, which has documented limitations. Without writing any compiler code, Clippy's `disallowed-methods/types/macros` lints in a per-crate clippy.toml can ban specific APIs per layer on stable Rust; the threshold lints (cognitive complexity, function length) yield soft signals. Custom semantic rules, such as ECS conventions, need type information. Today that means rustc_private lints on a pinned nightly: dylint is active (v6.3.2, 2026-10-30), and bevy_lint is built the same way. Marker, the attempt at a stable lint API, has had no commits since December 2023. bevy_lint shows what ECS lints look like: schedule restrictions per module, naming conventions for Plugin and SystemSet, unit-in-bundle and ZST-query checks. Syntax-only tools (ast-grep YAML, tree-sitter queries) are cheap to write and scope by file glob, but they have no type information. Semgrep (Rust GA, cross-function dataflow) and CodeQL (Rust GA since CLI 2.23.3, Oct 2025) are oriented to security analysis. Baselines and ratchets come in two designs: identity-based (ArchUnit FreezingArchRule ignores line numbers and shrinks automatically) and count-per-file-per-rule (ESLint bulk suppressions). SonarQube's "new code" quality gate, with a 20-line fudge factor, is the closest existing model for Geiger's locality requirement.

findings.claim: Ford's own workshop slides define an architectural fitness function as an objective integrity assessment of architectural characteristics. They categorize fitness functions as atomic (singular context, one aspect) vs holistic (shared context, combined aspects) and triggered (unit test, pipeline, timed task) vs continuous. The second edition (2023) reportedly adds further dimensions such as temporal and intentional/emergent; I could not open the book text (O'Reilly returned 403), so that list is unverified.

sources.title: Building Evolutionary Architectures Workshop (Neal Ford; slides credit Ford, Parsons, Kua)
sources.quote: An architectural fitness function provides an objective integrity assessment of some architectural characteristic(s).

sources.title: Building Evolutionary Architectures Workshop (Neal Ford)
sources.quote: run against a singular context and exercise one particular aspect of the architecture.

findings.relevance: Gives Geiger established vocabulary. Each Geiger rule is an atomic, triggered fitness function run per pull request. The aggregate score is a holistic one.

verdict.corrected_claim: Ford's workshop slides (PDF metadata: created 2018-09-13, so it reflects the 1st-edition material) define an architectural fitness function as 'an objective integrity assessment of some architectural characteristic(s)'. They list atomic vs holistic, triggered vs continuous, and also static vs dynamic, automated vs manual, temporal, domain-specific, and intentional vs emergent. So temporal and intentional/emergent are not 2nd-edition additions: the same slides already include them. The 2nd-edition (2023) chapter 2 is still unverified (O'Reilly returns 403). Calling Geiger's aggregate score 'holistic' stretches the term: in the slides, holistic means a check run 'against a shared context' that exercises combined aspects such as security and scalability. It does not mean a weighted sum of atomic results.
verdict.evidence: I downloaded https://nealford.com/downloads/Evolutionary_Architectures_workshop_by_Neal_Ford.pdf (131 pages; pdfinfo CreationDate 2018-09-13, title 'Building Evolutionary Architectures Workshop—1 day.key'), extracted the text and found both quotes verbatim (slides 48/73/74). The same 'Categories of Fitness Functions' sequence (slides 79-91) also contains 'temporal: architects may want to build a time component into assessing fitness', 'intentional ... emergent: …some fitness functions will emerge during development of the system', 'static: have a fixed result, such as the binary pass/fail of a unit test', 'dynamic', 'automated', 'manual' and 'domain-specific'. Holistic: 'run against a shared context and exercise a combination of architectural aspects such as security and scalability'. The O'Reilly ch02 page returned 403 to both WebFetch and curl.

findings.claim: The same slides treat metric thresholds and structural checks as fitness functions alike. Examples include a 'Cyclic Dependency Function' built on JDepend and 'Cyclomatic complexity < 50 for all projects' as a maintainability check. Unit tests, metrics, monitors and chaos engineering are all presented as kinds of fitness function.

findings.claim: In a Cargo workspace, a crate can use another workspace crate only if its Cargo.toml declares the dependency. A hexagonal layout with one crate per layer (domain, application, adapters, infrastructure) therefore has layering enforced by the compiler at crate granularity. The remaining gate is to forbid adding the wrong edge to Cargo.toml. Inference: rests on the Rust Book statement and the Rust Reference rule that external crates enter scope via --extern.

sources.title: The Rust Programming Language, ch. 14.3 Cargo Workspaces
sources.quote: Cargo doesn't assume that crates in a workspace will depend on each other, so we need to be explicit about the dependency relationships.

sources.title: The Rust Reference: Preludes
sources.quote: provided to the compiler (as with the `--extern` flag with `rustc`) are added to the _extern prelude_.

findings.relevance: The most important hard gate for Malte's layered workspaces needs no source analysis, only a check on the manifest graph.

verdict.corrected_claim: The core inference holds. A workspace crate cannot name another workspace crate unless its Cargo.toml declares it. The Book: 'we can't use it in other crates in the workspace unless we add `rand` to their Cargo.toml files as well'. So per-layer crates give compiler-enforced layering at crate granularity. Two caveats are missing. (a) An allowed dependency can `pub use` re-export a forbidden crate, so the manifest gate must check the transitive closure, not only direct edges. (b) Source inclusion bypasses the crate boundary entirely: `#[path = "..."] mod x;` or `include!` can pull another crate's files into domain. The Reference places no limit on the path, but I did not test this. The Reference also notes that sysroot crates (`alloc`, `test`) can be added with `extern crate`, which is harmless for layering.
verdict.evidence: https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch14-03-cargo-workspaces.html: the quoted sentence is verbatim; also 'even though `rand` is used somewhere in the workspace, we can't use it in other crates in the workspace unless we add `rand` to their Cargo.toml files as well.' https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/names/preludes.html: the quote is verbatim ('External crates imported with `extern crate` in the root module or provided to the compiler (as with the `--extern` flag with `rustc`) are added to the _extern prelude_'). https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/modules.html: 'the file path is relative to the directory the source file is located', with no restriction stated, so #[path] can reach files outside the crate (inference, not tested).

findings.claim: `cargo metadata --format-version=1` outputs the resolved workspace dependency graph as JSON. The output includes workspace_members and resolve.nodes[].deps[].dep_kinds, which distinguish dev, build and normal dependencies. Cargo keeps compatibility within a format version, apart from additions such as new fields. A forbidden-edge check, such as 'domain may depend only on these crates', is a small script over this JSON.

sources.title: cargo metadata (The Cargo Book)
sources.quote: The resolved dependency graph for the entire workspace.

sources.title: cargo metadata (The Cargo Book)
sources.quote: "dev", "build", or null for a normal dependency.

findings.relevance: A cheap, stable, deterministic input for Geiger's layer gates. The dev-dependency distinction lets test-only edges, such as test fixtures in domain, be allowed.

verdict.evidence: https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-metadata.html: 'The resolved dependency graph for the entire workspace.' and '"dev", "build", or null for a normal dependency.' are verbatim. workspace_members is described as 'Array of members of the workspace.' On compatibility: 'Within the same output format version, the compatibility is maintained, except some scenarios', and new fields are listed as not incompatible. Caveat: `resolve` 'is null if --no-deps is specified', so the check must run without --no-deps.

findings.claim: cargo-deny's `bans.deny` entries accept `wrappers`, which let only the listed crates depend directly on a banned crate and deny every other dependent. The documented use case is phasing out a crate. Inference (not tested): the same setting can express 'only the infrastructure crate may depend on sqlx/godot'. The docs imply workspace members can be denied, because `allow-workspace` (default false) exists to exempt them.

sources.title: cargo-deny: bans config
sources.quote: This field allows specific crates to have a direct dependency on the banned crate but denies all transitive dependencies on it.

sources.title: cargo-deny: bans config
sources.quote: Workspace members take precedence over explicit deny entries

findings.relevance: An off-the-shelf, config-only hard gate for which framework or I/O crates each layer may use, suited to a pluggable rule pack.

verdict.corrected_claim: The `wrappers` quote is verbatim, and the untested inference ('only infrastructure may depend directly on sqlx/godot') is plausible. Two details are overstated. (1) The docs do not describe phasing out a crate as the use case. That idea appears only as the example reason string 'we want to get rid of this crate but there is still one user of it'. (2) The quote 'Workspace members take precedence over explicit deny entries' applies only when `allow-workspace = true`, which targets deny-by-default policies (`deny = [{ name = "*" }]`). It suggests, but does not state, that workspace members can otherwise be denied. Also, `wrappers` limits only direct dependents of the banned crate. It does not stop domain from depending on infrastructure itself.
verdict.evidence: I fetched https://embarkstudios.github.io/cargo-deny/checks/bans/cfg.html with curl. It contains 'This field allows specific crates to have a direct dependency on the banned crate but denies all transitive dependencies on it.' and the example `{ name = "all-versionsd", wrappers = [...], reason = "we want to get rid of this crate but there is still one user of it" }`. allow-workspace: 'If true, automatically allows all workspace members even when using a deny-by-default policy (i.e., when deny = [{ name = "*" }] is specified)', with default false. cargo-deny is current at 0.20.2 (crates.io, 2026-07-09).

findings.claim: Inside a crate, Rust visibility restricts access at module granularity: `pub(crate)`, `pub(super)` and `pub(in path)`, where path must be an ancestor module. cargo-modules `dependencies --acyclic` fails when the internal module dependency graph contains a cycle. Together these cover module-level hard gates without custom lints.

sources.title: The Rust Reference: Visibility and privacy
sources.quote: `pub(in path)` makes an item visible within the provided `path`.

sources.title: cargo-modules README
sources.quote: If found it will search for cycles in the directed graph and return an error for any cycles it found.

findings.relevance: Covers intra-crate structure, for example in the Godot game crate, where layers may be modules rather than crates.

verdict.corrected_claim: The facts are right, but 'together these cover module-level hard gates' is overstated. Rust visibility is ancestor-based: `pub(in path)` requires that `path` 'resolves to an ancestor module'. So it cannot express directional rules between sibling layer modules. An item that adapters need via `pub(super)`/`pub(crate)` is equally visible to a sibling domain module. `cargo modules dependencies --acyclic` detects only cycles, not wrong-direction edges. Directional module-layer rules still need a dependency-rule tool (cargo-bylaw, layered-crate, cargo-pup, rust_arkitect) or a custom lint. cargo-modules is active (0.28.0, 2026-10-18).
verdict.evidence: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/visibility-and-privacy.html: '`pub(in path)` makes an item visible within the provided `path`.' and '`path` must be a simple path which resolves to an ancestor module of the item whose visibility is being declared.' The cargo-modules README (raw from github.com/regexident/cargo-modules main) has the verbatim quote 'If found it will search for cycles in the directed graph and return an error for any cycles it found.' The crates.io API gives cargo-modules 0.28.0 on 2026-10-18.

findings.claim: Clippy's `disallowed-methods`, `disallowed-types` and `disallowed-macros` options ban fully qualified paths, with optional `reason` and `replacement`, without writing lint code. Clippy looks for clippy.toml starting from CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR, so each workspace crate can have its own ban list, for example a domain crate banning godot types or std::time. Clippy marks the configuration file itself as unstable.

sources.title: Configuring Clippy
sources.quote: Note: The configuration file is unstable and may be deprecated in the future.

findings.relevance: The cheapest type-aware user-defined hard gate on stable Rust. It suits team rule packs such as 'domain must not call X'.

verdict.evidence: https://doc.rust-lang.org/clippy/lint_configuration.html: 'The list of disallowed types, written as fully qualified paths.' The same structure applies to methods and macros, with fields path, reason (optional), replacement (optional) and allow-invalid. https://doc.rust-lang.org/clippy/configuration.html: 'Note: The configuration file is unstable and may be deprecated in the future.' Search order: CLIPPY_CONF_DIR, then CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR, then the current directory, walking up to parents. So per-crate files work, and a crate without its own file uses the nearest parent file. Note that CLIPPY_CONF_DIR, if set, overrides per-crate lookup.

findings.claim: Clippy's configurable thresholds provide soft, per-function measurements out of the box: cognitive-complexity-threshold (default 25), too-many-lines-threshold (default 100) and too-many-arguments-threshold (default 7). They emit pass/fail lints at a threshold rather than continuous values. Inference: a score needs the raw value, so Geiger would have to compute the metric itself or parse lint output at varied thresholds.

verdict.corrected_claim: The thresholds and defaults are right (cognitive-complexity 25, too-many-lines 100, too-many-arguments 7), but two points are wrong or missing. (1) The lints do report the raw value: the messages read 'the function has a cognitive complexity of ({cc}/{threshold})', 'this function has too many lines ({line_count}/{threshold})' and 'too many arguments ({args}/{threshold})'. Setting a very low threshold and parsing one run yields per-function values, so no sweep over thresholds is needed. Geiger still parses diagnostics, and values below the threshold are never reported. (2) Clippy itself disowns cognitive_complexity as a metric. It sits in the off-by-default `restriction` group 'so as to not mislead users into using this lint as a measurement tool', and its docs say 'We used to think it measured how hard a method is to understand.' Geiger should not use it as a complexity measure.

Examples are ArchUnit (Java; layeredArchitecture, onionArchitecture), import-linter (Python; forbidden, protected, layers, independence and acyclic-siblings contracts, plus custom contract types), Deptrac (PHP), Konsist (Kotlin; assertArchitecture) and jQAssistant (rules as Cypher queries over a Neo4j graph of the code).

findings.claim: Baselines use two matching designs. ArchUnit's FreezingArchRule stores known violations, reports only new ones, ignores line numbers when matching, and automatically shrinks the store when violations are fixed. ESLint bulk suppressions (announced 2025-04-04) store a count per file per rule in eslint-suppressions.json. When the count grows, ESLint reports all violations of that rule in that file, and leftover unused suppressions cause a non-zero exit.

findings.relevance: Geiger's gates must tolerate legacy violations but block new ones. These are the two proven matching strategies: violation identity vs count per file and rule. Both ratchet down automatically.

verdict.corrected_claim: ArchUnit's FreezingArchRule stores known violations, reports only new ones, ignores line numbers by default, and automatically shrinks the store when violations are fixed. ESLint bulk suppressions (announced 2025-04-04) store a count per file per rule in eslint-suppressions.json. When the count grows, ESLint reports all violations of that rule in that file. Per the current ESLint docs (not the 2025 blog, which calls it a warning), leftover unused suppressions cause exit code 2 unless --pass-on-unpruned-suppressions is used. ESLint does not shrink the file automatically; the user must run --prune-suppressions. Only ArchUnit ratchets down automatically.
verdict.evidence: ArchUnit guide 8.6: "If violations are fixed, FreezingArchRule will automatically reduce the known stored violations to prevent any regression." and "By default FreezingArchRule will ignore line numbers". ESLint blog (Published 04 Apr, 2025): "if more violations are found for the same rule in the same file, ESLint will report all of them." The blog describes unused suppressions only as a warning: "ESLint outputs a warning when it finds suppressed violations that no longer occur". https://eslint.org/docs/latest/use/command-line-interface: "By default, ESLint exits with exit code 2 and displays an error message if there are unused suppressions in the suppressions file." https://eslint.org/docs/latest/use/suppressions: "To remove the suppressions that are no longer needed, you can use the --prune-suppressions flag." findings.claim: Inference on fit by mechanism. (a) Hard gates: the Cargo dependency graph checked via cargo metadata or cargo-deny wrappers, Clippy disallowed_* lints and cargo-modules --acyclic. These are deterministic and stable-toolchain, with few false positives. (b) Soft scored rules: tools that produce counts or continuous values, such as metric extractors, Clippy threshold lints and ast-grep match counts, combined with a ratchet (Betterer or Sonar new-code style). (c) User-defined domain rules such as ECS conventions: dylint/rustc_private lints when they need types; ast-grep or tree-sitter when syntax is enough. A rule with known false positives, like zst_query, should start as soft or nursery before becoming a gate. This rests on findings rust-1 to rust-11, syn-1, base-1 and base-3.

The cargo-modules README documents `--acyclic` ("Require graph to be acyclic"; the `dependencies` command "will search for cycles ... and return an error"). The cargo-deny bans docs document `wrappers` ("allows specific crates to have a direct dependency on the banned crate but denies all transitive dependencies on it"). The Clippy CHANGELOG lists disallowed_methods, disallowed_types, disallowed_macros and disallowed_names. The tier split follows from these facts. Caveats that do not overturn the claim: cargo-modules --acyclic finds module-level cycles inside one crate; Cargo already forbids cycles between crates. Layer rules between workspace crates therefore need a cargo metadata check or cargo-deny bans. Betterer is a JS/TS tool, so for Rust it serves as a pattern, not a drop-in. 'Few false positives' is a reasonable inference for path-based checks, not a measured result. I did not re-verify the underlying findings rust-1 to rust-11, syn-1, base-1 and base-3.
