open_questions: Does any static quality score (CodeHealth, SonarQube ratings, etc.) predict maintainer merge decisions on agent PRs? METR's merge data (aiq-9) could serve as a validation set for Geiger.

Under the Cursor DiD design, are warning and complexity increases still significant when expressed as density per KLOC rather than totals? The paper's GMM suggests warnings largely track size, while complexity does not.
How often do agents game static-analysis rules (suppressions, splitting functions to dodge length limits, threshold edits) compared with test gaming? No quantitative study was found.
Do results from Java, Python and TypeScript (Sonar, CodeScene, Cursor sample) transfer to Rust, where the compiler and clippy already enforce much of what these smells measure?
GitClear's full 2025 and 2026 methods (how AI-assisted lines are identified, churn definitions) are gated; the exact churn figures for 2024 and 2025 were not verified from primary text.
Will the METR productivity redesign (2026) produce usable estimates for agentic, multi-agent workflows?

areas.title: Dagger as the measurement framework, and collisions for the name "Geiger"
areas.summary_before_verification: Dagger is now in a 1.0 beta. The changelog dates it 2026-10-22 and the blog post 2026-10-23. Dagger calls itself "third-generation CI" built for coding agents. The engine and SDKs are Apache-2.0. Dagger Cloud (Cloud Engines and Cloud Checks) is a paid, usage-billed service. Its architecture fits Geiger's gate/score split partly. A Check is a function marked @check that only passes or fails, so it suits hard gates. The Check API also has an optional `report: Directory` output, and the dagger CLI exits non-zero when a check fails. The API has no numeric score field, so Geiger would have to compute and aggregate soft scores itself. Notable 2025-2026 changes: `dagger check` (v0.19.7, 2025-11-20), BuildKit replaced by Dagger's own engine (v0.21, 2026-05-22), workspaces configured by dagger.toml, official modules, per-test reporting, and Cloud Checks with native GitHub and Entire integrations. "Smart checks" that run only the checks a change affects are listed only as "Coming soon", so Geiger cannot rely on them for locality today. LLM is a native core type: it uses tools, can attach MCP servers and has skills, and its agent APIs are marked experimental. container-use is a separate experimental MCP server whose last release was 2025-08-19. Rust is a weak spot. Rust has only an experimental client library, not a module SDK, and the official module catalog has no Rust or Cargo module. Daggerverse has community Rust modules. On the name: cargo-geiger is an active, popular Rust tool. It has 270k downloads, v0.14.0 from 2026-10-12, and about 1.66k stars. It already uses the radiation metaphor for "how much unsafe code is in your crate". It also holds the crates.io names `geiger` and `cargo-geiger`, and `geiger` on npm is taken. Several other dev tools named geiger exist: react-geiger (about 1.1k stars), go-geiger, puck-security/geiger (credential triage) and Atomburstofficial/geiger, published on npm as `geiger-scan` (an AI-agent inventory scanner from 2026). For a Rust-first product called "Geiger", the cargo-geiger collision is the obvious conflict.

findings.claim: Dagger 1.0 is in beta. The changelog dates it 2026-10-22 and the blog post 2026-10-23. After five years of 0.x, Dagger calls it a stable architecture but asks users to test it before the stable release. The latest GitHub release tags are v0.21.11 (2026-10-21). The Rust crate dagger-sdk is at 1.0.0-beta.25.

findings.claim: Dagger architecture as of 1.0 beta: the engine serves the Dagger API and runs pipelines locally, on a server, or as a Cloud Engine. Modules are typed APIs of functions, objects, Checks, services and Generators. Function results are cached by their inputs, and Dagger evaluates artifacts lazily as a DAG of sandboxed functions.

sources.title: Dagger glossary (1.0-beta docs)
sources.quote: Dagger also caches function results, keyed by inputs (arguments, parent state, module source). A function cache hit skips the function entirely.

sources.title: Dagger Introduction
sources.quote: Dagger computes artifacts lazily, as an incremental DAG of sandboxed functions, on your machine or on a shared remote engine.

findings.relevance: Input-keyed caching means unchanged crates or files need not be re-measured, which helps compute per-PR deltas cheaply.

verdict.evidence: Glossary https://docs.dagger.io/reference/glossary (1.0-beta): Engine "serves the Dagger API and runs pipelines." "It runs on a local machine, on a server, or as a Cloud Engine, and it stores the cache." Module: "A reusable, typed API for automation: functions, objects, Checks, services, and Generators". Cache: "Dagger also caches function results, keyed by inputs (arguments, parent state, module source)." "A function cache hit skips the function entirely." Introduction https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/introduction (1.0-beta): "Dagger computes artifacts lazily, as an incremental DAG of sandboxed functions, on your machine or on a shared remote engine."

findings.claim: A Dagger Check is a function marked @check (or the SDK's equivalent) that passes or fails. `dagger check` runs every check in the workspace locally, in CI, or as Cloud Checks, and exits non-zero if any check fails. The command was introduced in v0.19.7 (2025-11-20).

sources.title: Dagger glossary
sources.quote: A Check passes or fails, so it can be used as a gate. A module marks it with @check or its SDK's equivalent.

findings.relevance: Fits Geiger's hard gates (e.g. layer violations) directly. Soft score deltas need logic on top, such as a check that fails when the score drops by more than 0.2.

verdict.evidence: Glossary: "A Check passes or fails, so it can be used as a gate." "A module marks it with `@check` or its SDK's equivalent." (In the source these two sentences appear in the reverse order of the quote.) https://docs.dagger.io/using/checking (1.0-beta): "Runs all checks in your workspace in parallel. Exits non-zero if any check fails." and "Results are identical on your laptop, in CI, and in the cloud." The glossary's Cloud Checks entry: "Runs a repository's Checks on Cloud Engines on each push to GitHub or pull request". Changelog v0.19.7, Nov 20, 2025, 'Dagger Checks': "`dagger check` gives module developers one command to run validation anywhere: local dev, CI, and agents."

findings.claim: The core Check API type has only six fields (assertion, id, pass, error, report, sync). `report` is an optional Directory, and no field holds a numeric score or metric.

findings.relevance: A per-check report directory can carry Geiger's offending-areas report. Score aggregation and weighting must be built by Geiger, for example in a module that reads the measurement outputs.

verdict.evidence: https://docs.dagger.io/reference/api/check (1.0-beta) lists exactly 6 fields: assertion (String), id (ID!), pass (Boolean!), error (Error), report (Directory) "An optional report produced by the check.", sync (Check!). None holds a numeric score or metric. The `dagger check` CLI reference also has no score or metric output.

findings.claim: Dagger lists 'Smart checks' (running only the checks a change affects, based on recorded file reads) and 'Test splitting' under 'Coming soon', not as shipped features.

sources.quote: Dagger will run only the checks that a change affects. It records which workspace files each artifact reads, so you do not maintain your own filter scripts.

findings.relevance: Bears on Geiger's locality requirement. Diff-scoped measurement has to come from Geiger's own logic (e.g. git diff to crates or functions) until this ships.

verdict.evidence: Changelog https://dagger.io/changelog/ 'Coming soon' section (retrieved 2026-11-07). Smart checks: "Dagger will run only the checks that a change affects." "It records which workspace files each artifact reads, so you do not maintain your own filter scripts." Test splitting: "Dagger will split large test suites across engines." Neither has a version or date, so neither has shipped.

findings.claim: Dagger 1.0 adds per-test reporting. Official modules report each test separately. Since v0.20.8 (2026-05-06), Dagger Cloud shows each test from any framework that emits OpenTelemetry test attributes.

findings.relevance: Shows the reporting shape Dagger favors: OpenTelemetry traces and test trees, not code-quality metrics. Geiger's measurements could be emitted the same way.

areas.title: What is defensible in a code-quality scoring product when the measurements are cheap to build
areas.summary_before_verification:
The measurement layer is a commodity, and licences now fence it off. Qlty bundles 60+ open-source linters (over 20,000 rules) in its CLI. Sonar's Rust support wraps 85 Clippy rules. Both incumbents have closed off reuse of their engines by competitors. Qlty's BSL forbids using its CLI for a "Code Quality Service" or an "AI Coding Service". Sonar moved its analyzers from LGPLv3 to SSALv1 in November 2024, and SSALv1 excludes competing products and outside AI that ingests analyzer output.

The vendors' moats sit in assets that are hard to copy:
- **SIG:** a benchmark that grew from about 500 evaluations (2010) to more than 30,000 systems and 400 billion lines of code (2026). It is recalibrated every year to a fixed 5/30/30/30/5 distribution and tied to a TÜViT "Trusted Product Maintainability" certificate. SIG's lab licence runs to 2027-05-18; TIOBE's lapsed in 2025.
- **CodeScene:** peer-reviewed validation of its Code Health metric, though the papers are written by its own staff.
- **Sonar:** distribution and an open-core rule library. It had $175M ARR in 2022 and claims more than 7M developers. Pricing is per line of code, and some languages are Enterprise-only.

Money is moving into AI code verification and review:
- Sonar bought Tidelift (Dec 2024), AutoCodeRover (Feb 2025) and Gitar (May 2026).
- CodeRabbit raised $60M at a $550M valuation (Sep 2025).
- Qodo raised $70M (Mar 2026).
- Cursor bought Graphite (Dec 2025).
- Code Climate spun its quality product out as Qlty (Nov 2024). Its founder was named CEO of another company in July 2026.

Incumbents already ship the "agent plus quality gate" loop. Sonar's default gate covers new code only, and its hosted MCP server (Mar 2026) lets agents check their output against quality gates. CodeScene ships an MCP server with Code Health checks before commit and push. Budget framings are established practice: Google SRE error-budget release freezes, web performance budgets, and Betterer's ratchet. A per-PR score budget is therefore a known pattern, not a moat. Domain rule packs exist only as fragmented community or vendor linters (bevy_lint: unofficial, nightly-only; Microsoft.Unity.Analyzers: 46 analyzers and 23 suppressors; Redpoint's clang rules for Unreal) and are not tied to scores or budgets. My inference: Geiger's defensible ground is a pluggable domain/architecture rule format, stable and explainable score-delta semantics for agent PR budgets, and over time a calibration dataset. Generic metrics are not defensible.

verdict.evidence: Fetched raw LICENSE.md (qltysh/qlty, main). It says: 'Licensor: Qlty Software Inc.', 'The Licensed Work is (c) 2025 Qlty Software Inc.' The Additional Use Grant reads: 'You may make use of the Licensed Work, provided that you do not use the Licensed Work for a Code Quality Service or to produce (by integration, ingestion, analysis, training, or otherwise) an Artificial Intelligence Coding Service.' It also gives 'Change Date: 2028-12-10' and 'Change License: GNU General Public License, Version 3'. Two nuances. First, under the BSL terms each version converts on the Change Date 'or the fourth anniversary of the first publicly available distribution of a specific version ... whichever comes first', and 'the Change Date may vary for each version'. Second, both restricted services are defined as commercial offerings to third parties other than your employees and contractors, so internal use is allowed. The relevance note goes further than the licence: an internal or non-AI scoring use is not barred, and Geiger can still call the underlying OSS linters directly.

findings.claim: SonarQube's maintainability rating is a density measure. The technical debt ratio is the sum of rule-assigned remediation minutes divided by (cost to develop one line, 30 minutes by default, times LOC). Default grades: A ≤5%, B 5-<10%, C 10-<20%, D 20-<50%, E ≥50%.

sources.title: SonarQube Server docs: Metric definitions
sources.quote: The maintainability rating reflects the density of technical debt relative to the size of the code.

findings.relevance: A widely used aggregation precedent. Because it divides by total LOC, it suffers the dilution Malte describes in requirement (4): one bad PR barely moves the rating of a large repository.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://docs.sonarsource.com/sonarqube-server/latest/user-guide/code-metrics/metrics-definition/ (accessed 2026-11-07). Quotes: 'The maintainability rating reflects the density of technical debt relative to the size of the code.'; 'sqale_debt_ratio = technical debt /(cost to develop one line of code * number of lines of code)'; 'by default, 30 minutes, can be changed'; grid 'A ≤ 5% to 0%', 'B ≥ 5% to <10%', 'C ≥ 10% to <20%', 'D ≥ 20% to < 50%', 'E ≥ 50%'. Debt is the sum of remediation costs, each 'taken over from the effort assigned to the rule that raised the issue'. Caveat for the relevance note: Sonar also rates new code separately (about-new-code page), which partly addresses dilution.

findings.claim:
SIG's moat is a growing benchmark repository used to calibrate relative thresholds:
- In February 2010 it held results of over 500 evaluations.
- It is recalibrated at least once a year so that systems fall into a 5/30/30/30/5 percent distribution across 1-5 stars (3 stars is the market average).
- In 2024 SIG reported more than 18,000 systems and over 200 billion LOC.
- The State of Software 2026 report reports more than 30,000 systems and over 400 billion LOC.

sources.title: Baggen, Schill, Visser et al., Standardized Code Quality Benchmarking for Improving Software Maintainability (SQM 2010)
sources.quote: Such calibration is performed with an updated set of systems at least once per year.

sources.title: SIG: Maintainability Model 2024 update
sources.quote: over 200 billion lines of code across more than 18,000 systems and over 300 technologies

sources.title: SIG State of Software 2026
sources.quote: SIG’s benchmark spans more than 30,000 systems and over 400 billion lines of code; this year’s findings draw on the systems analyzed over the past year.

findings.relevance: Benchmark data accumulates over years and cannot be copied. But a score relative to the benchmark drifts when thresholds are recalibrated, which conflicts with a fixed per-PR point budget such as 0.2 points.

verdict.evidence: SQM 2010 PDF (downloaded, read): 'Currently (February 2010), the benchmark repository holds results for over 500 evaluations'; 'calibrated such that systems have a <5, 30, 30, 30, 5> percentage-wise distribution over 5 levels of quality'; 'Such calibration is performed with an updated set of systems at least once per year.' SIG 2024 update page (dated 26.08.2024): 'over 200 billion lines of code across more than 18,000 systems', model 'is updated annually', '3 stars is the market average'. State of Software 2026 PDF: 'SIG's benchmark spans more than 30,000 systems and over 400 billion lines of code'. Caveat: the 5/30/30/30/5 target is stated in the 2010 paper (per lowest-level attribute); the 2024 page does not restate it. The 2010 paper also says the benchmark's size helps 'prevent abupt model changes due to re-calibration'.

findings.claim: 'Trusted Product Maintainability' is a TÜViT certification scheme. Labs are licensed (ISO/IEC 17025:2017 competence) to evaluate against vendor-specific criteria. SIG Software Lab holds a licence for the SIG/TÜViT criteria valid 2024-05-07 to 2027-05-18 (earlier licence 2021-2024). TIOBE's lab held a licence for TIOBE/TÜViT criteria based on ISO/IEC 25010, valid 2023-02-09 to 2025-01-14.

findings.relevance: Third-party certification is a moat that sells to procurement and auditors, not to developers. It took SIG years of standardised evaluations to earn, and it is not open to a new entrant soon.

verdict.corrected_claim: ISO/IEC 25010:2023 (published November 2023) replaced ISO/IEC 25010:2011. Its product quality model has nine characteristics, including maintainability, flexibility and safety. findings.claim: CodeScene's research is its credibility asset. 'Code Red' (Tornhill & Borg, 2022): across 39 proprietary codebases (30,737 files), low Code Health code had 15x more defects and took 124% more time to resolve issues. A follow-up (arXiv 2601.02200, 2026-01-05) on 5,000 Python files found Code Health associated with semantics-preserving AI refactoring. Both papers are written by CodeScene staff.

findings.relevance: Evidence that a score predicts outcomes (defects, time, agent success) is what makes customers trust one score over another. Geiger would need comparable validation, and should note the vendor authorship.

verdict.corrected_claim: 'Code Red' (Tornhill & Borg, accepted at TechDebt 2022) studied 39 proprietary codebases (30,737 files). A follow-up (arXiv 2601.02200, 2026-01-05; Borg, Hagatulah, Tornhill, Söderberg) had LLMs refactor 5,000 Python files from competitive programming. It found Code Health associated with semantic preservation after refactoring. Tornhill and Borg work at CodeScene; Borg is also at Lund University. Hagatulah and Söderberg are at Lund University only. So the follow-up is not written by CodeScene staff alone.

It warns that SonarQube's Maintainability Rating produces many false positives and questions studies that use SonarQube output as ground truth. Its authors are affiliated with competitor CodeScene.

sources.quote: caution is advised with SonarQube due to its tendency to generate many false positives.

verdict.corrected_claim: The study 'Ghost Echoes Revealed' (Borg, Ezzouhri, Tornhill; arXiv 2408.10754, 2024-08-20) was accepted at ICSME 2024, the 40th edition. findings.claim:
Budget and ratchet policies are established practice:
- Google's SRE error-budget policy (2018) halts all changes except P0 and security fixes once the four-week error budget is exhausted.
- web.dev defines performance budgets as limits on site-performance metrics, enforceable in CI with tools such as Lighthouse CI.
- Betterer (MIT) snapshots a metric in a results file and fails the build if it gets worse.

sources.title: Google SRE Workbook: Example Error Budget Policy
sources.quote: If the service has exceeded its error budget for the preceding four-week window, we will halt all changes

sources.title: web.dev: Performance budgets 101
sources.quote: A performance budget is a set of limits imposed on metrics that affect site performance.

sources.title: Betterer docs: Introduction
sources.quote: makes sure that the value changes how you want it to change

findings.relevance: Geiger's 'no PR may lower the score by more than 0.2' is a direct analogue of these practices. Teams already understand it, but it is not novel enough to defend.

verdict.evidence: SRE workbook page: 'four-week window', 'we will halt all changes and releases other than P0 issues or security fixes until the service is back within its SLO'; Date 2018-02-19, author Steven Thurgood. web.dev: 'A performance budget is a set of limits imposed on metrics that affect site performance.'; section 'Add performance budgets to your build process' lists Lighthouse CI (page undated). Betterer intro: 'makes sure that the value changes how you want it to change!', results in a '.betterer.results' file, an idea 'popularised by snapshot testing'. The test fails when the result gets worse, and CI mode fails on any difference from the expected results. github.com/phenomnomnominal/betterer shows 'MIT license'.

findings.claim:
Engine-specific rule packs exist but are fragmented and not tied to scores:
- bevy_lint (v0.6.0, Bevy 0.18) is an unofficial, Clippy-like community linter. It requires a pinned nightly Rust toolchain and has lint groups such as correctness, suspicious and performance.
- Microsoft.Unity.Analyzers (MIT) ships 46 Unity-specific Roslyn analyzers (UNT IDs, including retired ones) and 23 suppressors (USP IDs).
- Redpoint's Clang fork for Unreal Engine supports custom .clang-rules that match UCLASS metadata.

findings.claim: Inference: Geiger should build its measurement backend on permissively licensed tools such as Clippy, rustc lints, bevy_lint (MIT/Apache) and custom rustc or AST rules, not on Sonar analyzers or the Qlty CLI. Both incumbents' licences exclude competing services and AI-agent use, so either dependency would be a legal risk. This rests on fact-1 (Qlty BSL use grant) and fact-2 (SSALv1 non-competitive purpose).

sources.quote: (c) employing, using, or engaging artificial intelligence technology that is not part of the Program to ingest, interpret, analyze, train on, or interact with the data provided by the Program

findings.relevance: Determines which measurement tools Geiger can legally use. Interpreting the licences needs legal review.

verdict.corrected_claim: Geiger should build its measurement backend on permissively licensed tools (Clippy, rustc lints, bevy_lint under MIT/Apache-2.0, custom rustc or AST rules), not on Sonar analyzers or the Qlty CLI. The two licences restrict different things. Sonar's SSALv1 allows only a 'Non-competitive Purpose'. That excludes offering SonarQube-like functionality, competing with SonarQube, and using any outside AI technology to ingest or interact with the program's data. So agent use is excluded broadly. Qlty's BSL 1.1 use grant excludes using the CLI for a commercial 'Code Quality Service' for third parties, or to produce a commercial 'Artificial Intelligence Coding Service'. It does not exclude internal AI-agent use, and the code becomes GPLv3 on 2028-12-10. A hosted Geiger would plausibly fall under both exclusions, so either dependency is a legal risk. This needs legal review.
verdict.evidence: qltysh/qlty LICENSE.md: 'provided that you do not use the Licensed Work for a Code Quality Service or to produce (by integration, ingestion, analysis, training, or otherwise) an Artificial Intelligence Coding Service'. Both terms are defined as a 'commercial offering that allows third parties (other than your employees and contractors)'; 'Change Date: 2028-12-10'; 'Change License: GNU General Public License, Version 3'. sonar-java LICENSE.txt ('Last Updated November 13, 2024'): '"Non-competitive Purpose" means any purpose except for (a) providing to others any product or service that includes or offers the same or substantially similar functionality as SonarQube, (b) Competing with SonarQube, and/or (c) employing, using, or engaging artificial intelligence technology'. bevy_lint README: licensed under Apache-2.0 or MIT.

findings.relevance: Strategic framing for Malte: where Geiger could compete and where it would duplicate incumbents.

verdict.corrected_claim: New-code-only gates are already shipped by incumbents (Sonar way quality gate), so they are not defensible. Calibration data (SIG), third-party certification (TÜViT-licensed labs) and vendor outcome research (CodeScene) are assets that incumbents built over years. The domain-specific rule-pack gap appears open. Plausible bets for Geiger: (1) a pluggable rule-pack format with hard architectural gates; (2) a per-PR delta that is stable and explainable; (3) over time, outcome-validation data. On (2), benchmark calibration does not by itself break per-PR stability. SIG recalibrates about once a year and uses a large benchmark to prevent abrupt changes. The real requirement is pinning or versioning thresholds for the duration of a budget. The claims about agent MCP hooks (tool-2, tool-3) and distribution (mkt-2) were not verified in this check. Market sizing is unverified.
verdict.evidence: Sonar about-new-code page: 'Likewise, the built-in Sonar way quality gate defines conditions applying to new code only.' SQM 2010 PDF: 'Such calibration is performed with an updated set of systems at least once per year' and the benchmark's heterogeneity helps 'to prevent abupt model changes due to re-calibration'. SIG 2024 page: model 'is updated annually'. Certification and vendor research are supported by the fact-4 and emp-1 checks above. tool-2, tool-3 and mkt-2 were not in this batch and are unchecked.

areas.title: How much do Geiger's candidate measurements vary when the relevant code is unchanged (reruns, CI runners, toolchain upgrades), and what error levels does industrial practice accept before a check may block a merge? Find published figures, or measure: line/region coverage (cargo-llvm-cov vs tarpaulin engines), cargo-mutants outcomes (timeouts, unviable mutants, --in-diff), nextest flaky tests, Clippy finding counts across consecutive stable Rust releases, and LLM-judged scores (Qlty SlopOne, desloppify). Is a 0.2-point per-PR budget on a 0-100 score above the resulting noise floor?
areas.summary_before_verification: Industrial practice sets two error levels. A check that blocks a merge must have essentially zero effective false positives (Google compiler checks). An advisory check shown in code review may have under 10%, and Google shows most of those results only on changed lines. At Microsoft, 90% of surveyed developers accept at most 5% false positives. No published source states a noise tolerance for a numeric score like Geiger's. Published variance figures exist only for other ecosystems. Whether a line counts as covered flips between runs in all 47 projects Hilton et al. studied. PIT mutation scores vary by 4 percentage points on average between repeated runs (Shi et al., Java). Google sees about 1.5% of test runs flaky. Projects that gate on coverage set Codecov thresholds of 0.15–1 percentage points to absorb noise; AnkiDroid observed 0.12 pp at most. Every Clippy release adds lints and changes existing ones. LLM judges are not repeatable even at temperature 0. SlopOne and desloppify publish no run-to-run stability figures; SlopOne offers a cache and an offline mode. My conclusion (an inference): the 0.2-point budget sits above the noise floor for deterministic, workspace-wide metrics only if base and head are measured as a pair in the same container with the same toolchain. It is likely below the noise floor for mutation scores, file-level or crate-level local scores on timing-dependent code, uncached LLM judgments, and any comparison across a toolchain upgrade.

findings.claim: Google's Tricorder (ICSE 2015) requires analyses that break the build to have essentially zero effective false positives. Code-review analyses may have an effective false-positive rate below 10%, and most analyses show results only on changed lines by default.

sources.title: Sadowski et al., Tricorder: Building a Program Analysis Ecosystem, ICSE 2015
sources.quote: These analyses break the build when they find an issue, so the effective false positive rate must be essentially zero.

sources.title: Sadowski et al., Tricorder: Building a Program Analysis Ecosystem, ICSE 2015
sources.quote: We still enforce a very low effective false positive rate here (< 10%). Additionally, we only display results for most analyses on changed lines by default

findings.relevance: Direct evidence for Q4: a hard gate needs zero false positives, a soft signal may have up to 10%. It also supports scoring changed lines rather than the whole codebase.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://research.google.com/pubs/archive/43322.pdf (Sadowski et al., ICSE 2015), saved locally as .local/geiger-research/sources/noise-factcheck/tricorder.pdf. Both quotes appear verbatim: 'These analyses break the build when they find an issue, so the effective false positive rate must be essentially zero.' and 'We still enforce a very low effective false positive rate here (< 10%). Additionally, we only display results for most analyses on changed lines by default'. Context: the same paper defines the not-useful rate as NOT USEFUL/(NOT USEFUL + PLEASE FIX + APPLY FIX). A rate of 10% or more puts an analyzer 'on probation', and above 25% Google 'may decide to turn the analyzer off immediately'. This is the 2015 policy.

findings.claim: Google's criteria (CACM, April 2018): a compiler check must 'produce no effective false positives'. A code-review check may have up to 10%. Tricorder disables an analyzer whose not-useful/please-fix click ratio exceeds 10% until its authors improve it.

sources.title: Sadowski et al., Lessons from Building Static Analysis Tools at Google, CACM 61(4), 2018
sources.quote: produce no effective false positives (the analysis should never stop the build for correct code)

sources.title: Sadowski et al., Lessons from Building Static Analysis Tools at Google, CACM 61(4), 2018
sources.quote: If the ratio for an analyzer goes above 10%, the Tricorder team disables the analyzer until the author(s) improve it.

findings.relevance: Gives Geiger a precedent for the gate/score split and for putting a noisy rule on probation instead of letting it block merges.

verdict.evidence: Opened the MIT-hosted PDF https://6826.csail.mit.edu/2020/papers/google-analysis-cacm.pdf (CACM, DOI 10.1145/3188720). Verbatim: 'produce no effective false positives (the analysis should never stop the build for correct code)'; code-review results 'are allowed to include up to 10% effective false positives'; 'If the ratio for an analyzer goes above 10%, the Tricorder team disables the analyzer until the author(s) improve it.' The CACM text calls this 'the ratio of "Please fix" vs. "Not useful" clicks', so the claim's not-useful reading is right in substance but the paper's wording is loose. The ICSE 2015 paper differs: it uses probation at 10% or more and possible immediate disabling above 25%, so the policy changed between the two papers. The cacm.acm.org copy still returns 403.

findings.claim: Microsoft developer survey (Christakis & Bird, ASE 2016): 90% of developers accept a false-positive rate up to 5%, 47% accept up to 15%, and only 24% accept up to 20%.

sources.title: Christakis & Bird, What Developers Want and Need from Program Analysis, ASE 2016
sources.quote: 90% of developers are willing to accept up to a 5% false positive rate, 47% of developers are willing to accept a false positive rate up to 15%

findings.relevance: Sets a human-acceptance level for wrong verdicts: if more than about 5% of PRs fail the 0.2-point budget from noise alone, most developers would find the check unacceptable. This is an inference from false-positive tolerance to flaky-gate tolerance.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/07/ase-2016.pdf. Verbatim: 'From the graph, 90% of developers are willing to accept up to a 5% false positive rate, 47% of developers are willing to accept a false positive rate up to 15%, and only 24% percent of developers can handle a false positive rate as high as 20%.' The numbers match. The step from tolerance of false positives to tolerance of a flaky budget gate is the researcher's own inference, and the finding labels it as one. The survey asked about program-analysis warnings, not about failing merge checks.

findings.claim: Google (2016) saw about 1.5% of all test runs report a flaky result, and about 84% of observed pass-to-fail transitions involved a flaky test. Lam et al. (OOPSLA 2020, 55 Java projects) found that 75% of flaky tests are already flaky when added, and 85% are caught if detectors run on new or modified tests.

sources.title: Micco, Flaky Tests at Google and How We Mitigate Them, Google Testing Blog
sources.quote: we see a continual rate of about 1.5% of all test runs reporting a "flaky" result.

sources.title: Lam et al., A Large-Scale Longitudinal Study of Flaky Tests, OOPSLA 2020, doi:10.1145/3428270
sources.quote: We find that 75% of flaky tests (184 out of 245) are flaky when added

findings.relevance: Flaky tests are the main source of noise in pass/fail-based measurements. Lam's result supports running flakiness detection (e.g., nextest stress or retries) on the tests a PR adds or changes.

verdict.evidence: Fetched https://testing.googleblog.com/2016/05/flaky-tests-at-google-and-how-we.html with curl (John Micco, Friday, May 27, 2016). Verbatim: 'we see a continual rate of about 1.5% of all test runs reporting a "flaky" result' and 'about 84% of the transitions we observe from pass to fail involve a flaky test!' Opened http://mir.cs.illinois.edu/winglam/publications/2020/LamETAL20OOPSLA.pdf. Verbatim: 'We find that 75% of flaky tests (184 out of 245) are flaky when added' and 'The percentage of flaky tests that can be detected does increase to 85% when detectors are run on newly added or directly modified tests.' Scope: the 245 tests are flaky tests from 55 Java projects that iDFlakies or NonDex detected and that compile at the commit that added them. They are not all flaky tests.

findings.claim: Hilton, Bell & Marinov (ASE 2018; 7,816 builds of 47 projects) found that every project had at least one commit where the set of covered lines changed although total coverage moved less than 0.01 pp. One unchanged line flipped between covered and uncovered 128 times. The causes included timers and network-socket state.

sources.title: Hilton, Bell, Marinov, A Large-Scale Study of Test Coverage Evolution, ASE 2018
sources.quote: every project had at least one commit where there were occluded changes, indicating that “steady” coverage does not imply “no change” to code covered.

sources.title: Hilton, Bell, Marinov, A Large-Scale Study of Test Coverage Evolution, ASE 2018
sources.quote: We see lines which only flip once, all the way up to a single line which flips coverage 128 times.

findings.relevance: Line-level and file-level coverage noise matters most for Geiger's local scoring. A PR touching a file with nondeterministically covered lines can lose score without any real change.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://mir.cs.illinois.edu/marinov/publications/HiltonETAL18TestCoverageEvolution.pdf (ASE '18). Verbatim: '7,816 builds of 47 projects'; occluded changes are defined as commits 'where the difference in coverage was less than 0.01 percentage points'; 'every project had at least one commit where there were occluded changes'; 'a single line which flips coverage 128 times'. The causes are a periodic database health check (timing) and code 'dependent on a network socket's state'. Caveat: these commits changed code, so not every occluded change is noise. The paper says one project (P25) had occluded changes from generated code that changed between commits. Only the flip analysis tracks unmodified lines.

findings.claim: Shi, Bell & Marinov (ISSTA 2019; PIT on 30 Java projects) found that mutation scores vary by 4 percentage points on average between repeated runs, and 9% of mutant-test pairs have an unknown status because of nondeterministic coverage.

sources.title: Shi, Bell, Marinov, Mitigating the Effects of Flaky Tests on Mutation Testing, ISSTA 2019
sources.quote: mutation scores vary by four percentage points on average between repeated executions, and 9% of mutant-test pairs have an unknown status.

findings.relevance: If mutation score enters the 0-100 score with weight w, run-to-run noise of about 4w points exceeds 0.2 for any w above 0.05, unless runs are deterministic, as they were in my Rust experiment (mut-local).

verdict.corrected_claim: Shi, Bell & Marinov (ISSTA 2019) ran PIT on 30 Java projects that were chosen from projects already studied for flaky tests. They found that about 4% of mutants have an unknown status because coverage is nondeterministic, so the overall mutation score can lie anywhere from 77.7% to 82.0%. That is a bound of about 4 percentage points: the lowest value assumes every unknown mutant survived, the highest that every one was killed. It is not a measured average difference between reruns. 9% of mutant-test pairs had an unknown status. The submitted abstract on the ISSTA program page gives 5 points instead.
verdict.evidence: The abstract of https://mir.cs.illinois.edu/marinov/publications/ShiETAL19FlakyMutation.pdf contains the quoted sentence verbatim. The body shows how the number was derived: 'The lowest possible mutation score is if all the unknown mutants actually survived, and the highest possible mutation score is if all the unknown mutants are actually killed. As such, the overall mutation score ranges from 77.7% to 82.0%.' The conclusion says these factors 'can account for (on average) a four percentage point variation'. On sample selection: '30 open-source projects selected from projects recently studied in the context of flaky tests'. The ISSTA 2019 program page (conf.researchr.org) has a different abstract: 'mutation scores vary by 5 percentage points on average'. So the 4w-points noise estimate in the relevance note is a worst-case bound on a flaky-test-heavy sample, not a typical spread between reruns.

findings.claim: Google's production mutation testing (Petrović et al., 2021) runs only on changed lines and shows surviving mutants in code review. It does not block merges. Developers initially classified 85% of reported mutants as unproductive. Suppression heuristics raised the productive share from 15% to 89%.

sources.title: Petrović, Ivanković, Fraser, Just, Practical Mutation Testing at Scale: A view from Google, arXiv 2102.11378v2
sources.quote: developers at Google initially classified 85% of reported mutants as unproductive.

sources.title: Petrović, Ivanković, Fraser, Just, Practical Mutation Testing at Scale: A view from Google, arXiv 2102.11378v2
sources.quote: considering only changed lines of code (Section 2, based on our prior work [12]), and surfacing mutants during code review.

findings.relevance: The largest industrial mutation deployment treats surviving mutants as review comments on the diff, not as a blocking numeric gate. Unproductive mutants are noise of a different kind, separate from run-to-run variance.

verdict.corrected_claim: Google's production mutation testing (Petrović et al., arXiv 2102.11378v2, 2021) creates mutants only on changed lines and shows surviving mutants in code review as findings. Like other analyzer findings, they do not need to be resolved before submission 'unless a human reviewer marks them as mandatory'. Developers initially classified 85% of reported mutants as unproductive. Suppression heuristics based on developer feedback raised the productive share from 15% to 89%.
verdict.evidence: Opened https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.11378 (v2, 26 Feb 2021). The quotes appear verbatim, including 'improved the ratio of productive mutants from 15% to 89%'. On blocking, Section 'Surfacing Mutants in the Code Review Process' says: 'findings do not need to be resolved by the author before submission, unless a human reviewer marks them as mandatory.' So 'does not block merges' is the default, but a reviewer can make a finding blocking.

findings.claim: Projects that gate merges on coverage deltas add tolerances to absorb noise. AnkiDroid uses a Codecov project threshold of 0.15 because 0.12 was the largest variability it observed, and still sets the status to informational. CorfuDB added a 0.2% threshold 'to account for flaky tests' (2023). Codecov's 'threshold' setting lets coverage drop by that amount while still passing.

sources.title: AnkiDroid .codecov.yml (main branch, read 2026-11-07)
sources.quote: .12 was observed as the largest variability owing to timing forcing different test branch choice

sources.title: CorfuDB commit: Codecov allow 0.2% coverage threshold (#3553)
sources.quote: Add 0.2% code coverage threshold to account for flaky tests.

sources.title: Codecov docs: Commit Status
sources.quote: Allow the coverage to drop by <number>% , and posting a success status.

findings.relevance: Practitioners already allow about 0.1–0.2 pp of coverage drop for noise alone, which equals Geiger's entire per-PR budget. Evidence comes from two projects, not a survey.

verdict.corrected_claim: Projects add Codecov tolerances to absorb coverage noise. AnkiDroid uses a project threshold of 0.15 because 0.12 was the largest variability it observed. It still makes both the project and patch statuses informational, so its coverage check does not block merges. CorfuDB added a 0.2% threshold 'to account for flaky tests' (2023-03-20). Other projects use larger tolerances: PostgREST 1% for 'random coverage fluctuations' (2021), and kanonproxy 2% after dependency-only upgrades moved coverage by 0.15 to 1.02 points (2026-03-15). Codecov's recipe page suggests a 10% threshold 'based on how flaky your tests are'. Observed tolerances therefore range from about 0.15 to 2 points or more, and the cited evidence does not show a typical value of 0.1 to 0.2.
verdict.evidence: Opened the raw AnkiDroid .codecov.yml: '.12 was observed as the largest variability owing to timing forcing different test branch choice', 'threshold: 0.15', 'informational: true' on both project and patch. Opened the CorfuDB patch, dated Mon, 20 Mar 2023: 'Add 0.2% code coverage threshold to account for flaky tests.' https://docs.codecov.com/docs/commit-status: 'Allow the coverage to drop by <number>%, and posting a success status.' https://docs.codecov.com/docs/common-recipe-list: '# adjust accordingly based on how flaky your tests are # this allows a 10% drop from the previous base commit coverage threshold: 10%'. https://github.com/PostgREST/postgrest/issues/1800: 'We introduced a 1% threshold to silence the random coverage fluctuations'. https://github.com/compscidr/kanonproxy/pull/227: 'failing codecov/project due to minor coverage fluctuations (0.15-1.02%) caused by dependency version changes, not source code changes'.

findings.claim: SonarQube's default 'fudge factor' ignores quality-gate conditions on coverage and duplication until new code has at least 20 lines. Sonar says the aim is to avoid overly strict enforcement on small changes.

sources.title: SonarQube Server docs: Introduction to quality gates
sources.quote: The conditions on coverage are ignored until the number of new lines to cover is at least 20.

findings.relevance: Precedent for a minimum sample size in Geiger's local, changed-code scores: below about 20 lines a percentage is too coarse to gate on.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://docs.sonarsource.com/sonarqube-server/latest/quality-standards-administration/managing-quality-gates/introduction-to-quality-gates/ (latest, read 2026-11-07). Verbatim: 'a fudge factor is used by default during quality gate calculation'; 'The conditions on duplication are ignored until the number of new lines is at least 20. The conditions on coverage are ignored until the number of new lines to cover is at least 20.' Rationale: 'This is used to avoid overly strict enforcement when dealing with small changes'. Note the different denominators: new lines for duplication, new lines to cover for coverage.

findings.claim: The tarpaulin README warns that ptrace and LLVM engines can give very different coverage results. It says LLVM coverage returns no data when a test exits non-zero and that fork-like syscalls overwrite profraw files.

sources.title: cargo-tarpaulin README (read 2026-11-07)
sources.quote: In these cases coverage results may differ a lot between ptrace and llvm and llvm coverage may be a worse choice.

findings.relevance: Changing the coverage engine shifts the score in steps. Geiger must pin one engine, one tool version and one toolchain for both base and head.

verdict.evidence: Opened the raw README on the default develop branch of https://github.com/xd009642/tarpaulin. Under 'Nuances with LLVM Coverage': '1. If a test has a non-zero exit code coverage data isn't returned', '3. Unable to handle fork and similar syscalls (one process will overwrite another's profraw file)', 'In these cases coverage results may differ a lot between ptrace and llvm and llvm coverage may be a worse choice.' Scope: the large difference is stated only for these cases, and the same README says LLVM is 'generally being far more accurate'. It also notes that ptrace is the Linux default and works only on x86_64; on Mac and Windows, LLVM is the default.

findings.claim: cargo-mutants sets test timeouts relative to the baseline: by default 5× baseline test time, minimum 20 s. Build timeouts are off by default because build time varies and timeouts would make builds flaky. Unviable mutants are 'inconclusive'. Exit code 3 reports timeouts. The docs warn that --in-diff can miss regressions in code outside the diff and ignores test-only diffs.

sources.title: cargo-mutants book: Hangs and timeouts
sources.quote: The default test timeout is 5 times the baseline test time, with a minimum of 20 seconds.

sources.title: cargo-mutants book: Hangs and timeouts
sources.quote: because build time can be quite variable there’s some risk of this causing builds to be flaky, and so it’s off by default.

sources.title: cargo-mutants book: Testing code changed in a diff
sources.quote: it’s certainly possible that edits in one region cause code in a different region or a different file to no longer be well tested.

findings.relevance: Load can push a test past the timeout, which turns a mutant outcome into 'timeout'. The baseline-relative timeout limits this. Geiger has to decide how timeouts and unviable mutants count in the score.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://mutants.rs/timeouts.html: "The default test timeout is 5 times the baseline test time, with a minimum of 20 seconds." and "because build time can be quite variable there’s some risk of this causing builds to be flaky, and so it’s off by default." Opened https://mutants.rs/using-results.html: "unviable — The attempted mutation doesn’t compile. This is inconclusive about test coverage". Opened https://mutants.rs/exit-codes.html: "3 : Some tests timed out: possibly the mutations caused an infinite loop, or the timeout is too low." Opened https://mutants.rs/in-diff.html: both the cited quote and "a diff that only deletes or changes test code won’t cause any mutants to run". cargo-mutants NEWS.md confirms build timeouts were removed by default because they "would sometimes make builds flaky". Latest release is v27.1.0 (2026-06-02), the version used locally.

findings.claim: cargo-nextest marks a test that passes on retry as flaky and by default treats it as successful. Since nextest 0.9.131 it can fail the run on flaky tests with --flaky-result fail or flaky-result = "fail".

sources.title: cargo-nextest docs: Retries and flaky tests
sources.quote: By default, flaky tests are treated as ultimately successful.

sources.title: cargo-nextest docs: Retries and flaky tests
sources.quote: To fail a test run on flaky tests, pass in --flaky-result fail or set NEXTEST_FLAKY_RESULT=fail in the environment.

findings.relevance: Geiger can detect flakiness with retries and either exclude flaky tests from coverage and mutation or report them as a separate rule, instead of letting them move the score. The locally installed nextest is 0.9.124, older than 0.9.131.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://nexte.st/docs/features/retries/: "By default, flaky tests are treated as ultimately successful." and "To fail a test run on flaky tests, pass in --flaky-result fail or set NEXTEST_FLAKY_RESULT=fail in the environment." The section is marked 0.9.131, and the page also documents flaky-result = "fail" in config. The cargo-nextest-0.9.131 release notes (2026-03-18) say "tests that pass on retry are marked as failures. The default remains \"pass\"." The local `cargo nextest --version` is 0.9.124. The latest release is 0.9.151 (2026-11-03). The docs say --flaky-result does not enable retries by itself, so --retries is also needed.

findings.claim: Every 6-week stable Rust release changes Clippy. Rust 1.92–1.99 added 1–8 new lints each, with 11–25 enhancements and 4–11 false-positive fixes per release; Rust 1.90 alone had 43 false-positive fixes. Rust 1.99 has been the current stable since 2026-10-01.

sources.title: rust-clippy CHANGELOG.md (read 2026-11-07)
sources.quote: Current stable, released 2026-10-01

sources.title: rust-clippy CHANGELOG.md, Rust 1.95 section
sources.quote: Added [`unnecessary_trailing_comma`] to `pedantic`

findings.relevance: A Clippy-count metric shifts with each toolchain upgrade even when the code does not change. Upgrades need a separate rebaseline step, or base and head must be compared on the same toolchain.

verdict.evidence: Downloaded raw CHANGELOG.md from rust-lang/rust-clippy master and counted the bullets per section. New Lints for 1.92–1.99: 5,1,5,5,3,1,7,8, a range of 1–8. Enhancements: 11,12,18,22,16,18,25,12, a range of 11–25. False Positive Fixes: 9,4,10,11,7,11,7,4, a range of 4–11. Rust 1.90 has 43 False Positive Fixes. The Rust 1.99 section reads "Current stable, released 2026-10-01". Every section carries a "Current stable" line, but 1.99 is the newest, and the next release, about 2026-11-12, is after today. The Rust 1.95 section contains "Added [`unnecessary_trailing_comma`] to `pedantic`".

findings.claim: In Li et al.'s 2023 survey of 31 Rust developers, 42% complained that Clippy produces many and frequent false positives. 68% configure lints as 'warn' and 16% as 'deny'.

sources.title: Li et al., Unleashing the Power of Clippy in Real-World Rust Projects, arXiv 2310.11738
sources.quote: a lot of (42%) participants complained that Clippy produce relatively many and frequent false positives.

findings.relevance: With a sample of 31 developers this is weak evidence. It still suggests that broad Clippy groups (pedantic, nursery) suit a soft score better than a hard gate.

verdict.evidence: Downloaded the https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.11738 PDF, v1 submitted 18 Oct 2023, by Chunmiao Li, Yijun Yu et al. Text: "Surprisingly, a lot of (42%) participants complained that Clippy produce relatively many and frequent false positives." Also: "Most participants (68%) preferred 'warn' when configuring Clippy, while only 16% chose 'deny'." Also: "we gathered a total of 31 responses". The paper says "preferred" rather than "configure", which is a negligible difference.

findings.claim: LLM outputs are not repeatable. Ouyang et al. found that ChatGPT gave no two requests with equal test output on 75.76%, 51.00% and 47.56% of tasks in three benchmarks, and that temperature 0 does not guarantee determinism. Haldar & Hockenmaier (EMNLP Findings 2025) found that LLM judges have low intra-rater reliability across runs. That study covered natural-language generation, not code.

sources.title: Ouyang, Zhang, Harman, Wang, An Empirical Study of the Non-determinism of ChatGPT in Code Generation, arXiv 2308.02828v2
sources.quote: setting the temperature to 0 does not guarantee determinism in code generation

sources.title: Haldar & Hockenmaier, Rating Roulette: Self-Inconsistency in LLM-As-A-Judge Frameworks, Findings of EMNLP 2025
sources.quote: we show that LLM judges have low intra-rater reliability in their assigned scores across different runs.

findings.relevance: An LLM-judged component re-run on each PR adds noise of unknown size. It should be cached by content hash, sampled several times, or kept out of the blocking delta.

verdict.evidence: Downloaded the arXiv 2308.02828v2 PDF (17 Oct 2024): "the ratio of coding tasks with zero equal test output across different requests is 75.76%, 51.00%, and 47.56%" for CodeContests, APPS and HumanEval. It also says "setting the temperature to 0 does not guarantee determinism in code generation". OER is the mean pairwise output-equivalence over 5 candidates, so OER=0 means no pair matched. The data is ChatGPT at default temperature 1. Downloaded the https://aclanthology.org/2025.findings-emnlp.1361.pdf PDF, Haldar & Hockenmaier, UIUC, on NLG: "we show that LLM judges have low intra-rater reliability in their assigned scores across different runs." Independent newer code-specific support: arXiv 2502.20747 (Klishevich et al., 28 Feb 2025) on LLM code review at temperature 0, five repeats: "even with temperature minimized, LLM responses varied to different degrees."

findings.claim: Qlty SlopOne (research preview, announced 2026-09-27) combines static-analysis signals with decisions from the Jev model. Its CLI can reuse cached analyses offline. Qlty publishes no run-to-run stability figures and says its methodology is unpublished. Issue #2863 records SlopOne outputs that differ in the last bit across platforms (libm exp). desloppify scores subjective dimensions with an LLM, and its CI profile skips those phases.

sources.title: Qlty blog: SlopOne: Winning the code quality fight with Jev
sources.quote: combines signals from traditional static analysis with decisions from Jev.

sources.title: Qlty docs: slop-one command
sources.quote: Use existing cached analyses; make no API calls

sources.title: qlty issue #2863: explanation parity test fails on musl and x86_64 macOS
sources.quote: The platform's libm returns a different last bit for `exp`

sources.title: desloppify README (read 2026-11-07)
sources.quote: uses an LLM to assess subjective quality dimensions

findings.relevance: Neither LLM-judged tool documents its stability. Caching (SlopOne) and excluding subjective phases from CI (desloppify) are the available ways to keep LLM noise out of a per-PR gate.

verdict.corrected_claim: Qlty SlopOne (free research preview, blog post 2026-09-27) combines static-analysis signals with decisions from Jev. Its CLI has --offline ("Use existing cached analyses; make no API calls") and also a built-in per-file gate, --max-drop, default 1 point. Qlty publishes no run-to-run stability figures and says it will publish its methodology and measurements "soon". Issue #2863, closed 2026-09-25 by PR #2865, is about a test that compared SlopOne trend-report explanation values bit-exactly against a Python fixture. Two values differed in about the 17th significant digit on x86_64 macOS and musl targets. The libm `exp` cause was suspected but not reproduced. The fix loosened the test to a 1e-12 tolerance, so cross-platform last-bit differences can remain, but they are far too small to matter for a 0.2-point budget. desloppify scores subjective dimensions with an LLM, and its `--profile ci` skips slow and subjective phases to collect a mechanical snapshot.

areas.title: Which existing products already deliver per-change quality scores, regression gates or bundled agent-loop checks that overlap Geiger, and how far does each go? Cover at least aislop, DRS-OSS, GitHub Copilot cloud agent's built-in validation, Cursor Bugbot, Claude Code Code Review and OpenAI Codex review. For each: deterministic or LLM-judged; whether teams can add architecture or domain rules; Rust depth; whether a non-zero per-PR budget on an aggregate score can be set; pricing; adoption.
areas.summary_before_verification: land-21's claim that no tool combines a repository score, a per-PR budget, team-written deterministic gates and change-scoped Rust scoring holds only in a narrow form. aislop (MIT CLI v0.20.0, 2026-11-01; 731 stars; about 82k npm downloads in the last 30 days) already combines a deterministic 0-100 score with configurable weights, PR scoping (`--changes --base`), a CI threshold, a findings baseline, an agent Stop-hook that blocks regressions, and opt-in architecture rules. It has three gaps that matter for Geiger. (1) There is no non-zero budget: the hook blocks on any drop (`delta < 0`), and CI gates on an absolute `failBelow` or on any new finding. (2) Its import-ban and layering rules extract imports only from JS/TS, Python and Go files, so they never fire on Rust. Its shipped example rules also use YAML keys the loader ignores. (3) Its Rust support is shallow: cargo fmt, clippy, brace-counted function length (an open issue documents wrong lengths on Rust code), comment rules and audit. A hosted tier ($29-$249/month) adds PR gates with score thresholds. DRS-OSS is a research prototype (3 stars): an LLM classifier (Llama 3.1 8B) trained on 14 Apache projects that posts a risky/safe label with a confidence. It accepts no team rules and has no score budget. The agent platforms all review with LLMs and do not gate by default. Copilot cloud agent runs CodeQL, advisory-database checks, secret scanning and Copilot code review before it completes a PR, with no score and no team-rule gate. Its repository hooks can deny individual tool calls. Bugbot (about $1.00-$1.50 per run) reads BUGBOT.md, team rules and learned rules. Its check is neutral unless fail-on-unresolved is enabled, where that option is available to the organization. Claude Code Code Review never blocks a PR. Codex review flags only P0 and P1 issues and tells teams to keep deterministic checks in CI. The likeliest platform entrant on the score side is GitHub Code Quality (GA 2026-07-20, $10 per active committer per month). It offers repository reliability and maintainability scores and ruleset gates, but its scores are four categorical levels set by the worst finding, it accepts no budget on an aggregate, and its Code Quality query lists do not include Rust. Pomona (Bloomberg) is in-house only: it validates agent PRs with the team's own test and lint commands and a deterministic 100-line size limit. Q7 defensibility should therefore rest on three gaps: Rust-native depth, architecture gates that work on Cargo crates and modules, and a configurable non-zero per-PR budget with change-scoped deltas. It should not rest on the claim that no tool scores changes deterministically.

findings.claim: Copilot cloud agent runs repository-defined hooks from `.github/hooks/*.json`. A `preToolUse` hook can approve or deny tool executions. The page does not say any hook can block task completion, and cloud agent supports only a subset of events.

sources.title: About hooks (GitHub Copilot cloud agent)
sources.quote: Hooks are a way of executing custom shell commands at strategic points in an agent's workflow

findings.relevance: This is an integration point: Geiger could run inside Copilot's loop as a hook. Whether it can block completion the way aislop does with the Claude Stop hook is unverified.

verdict.corrected_claim: Copilot cloud agent runs repository-defined hooks from `.github/hooks/*.json` and supports a subset of events, including sessionStart, preToolUse, postToolUse, agentStop and subagentStop. A `preToolUse` hook can approve or deny tool executions. Per the hooks reference, an `agentStop` hook under cloud agent can return `decision: "block"`, which forces another agent turn using `reason` as the prompt. The extra turn counts against the job timeout, and after 8 consecutive blocks the runtime ends the turn anyway. Geiger could therefore block completion inside Copilot's loop, the way aislop does with the Claude Stop hook.
verdict.evidence: The cited about-hooks URL redirects (301) to /en/copilot/concepts/customizations/hooks, which contains the quote and lists agentStop in the cloud-agent subset. https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/hooks-reference : 'agentStop The main agent finishes a turn. Yes — can block and force continuation. Fires. decision: "block" forces another turn, which still counts against the job's timeout.' Also: 'After 8 consecutive block continuations, the CLI overrides the hook and ends the turn anyway'. The claim's open question is answered: blocking is supported.

verdict.evidence: I opened all three cited pages. The quotes are present. Blog: '$10 per active committer, per month.' and 'Quality gates through GitHub rulesets, including coverage thresholds, with an evaluate mode for gradual rollout.' Metrics page: 'Codebase has high-severity issues, including bugs or major maintainability risks. ≥1 "Error" level finding'. Thresholds page: 'Code Quality AI findings cannot be set as a threshold.' The error is in the coverage gate. areas.title: What do 2026 studies of real autonomous-agent pull requests (AIDev dataset, MSR 2026 Mining Challenge) show about (a) how agent PRs change static-quality metrics once normalized for size or churn, (b) which quality signals agents degrade or game in practice (lint suppressions, threshold or config edits, function splitting, duplication, over-mocked or deleted tests), and (c) how quality decays across a sequence of agent tasks on one codebase?
areas.summary_before_verification: (a) Size or churn normalization changes the result. At repository level, a staggered difference-in-differences (DiD) study finds that warnings rise about 18% and cognitive complexity about 39% after agent adoption, persistently (2601.13597, which controls for LOC). It also reports some pre-trend coefficients. Per PR, studies that normalize for size find little difference. Agent-to-agent SonarQube differences mostly disappear once issues are counted per KLOC of churn, but that study has no human baseline (2601.20109). Kraishan (2609.17598) finds that no agent carries a higher per-line maintenance burden than humans in the same repositories, though its quality measures are regex-based. Signals that do separate agents from humans are less conventional ones: semantic redundancy (1.87x, one repository), and Maintainability Index and complexity getting worse in 'readability' commits, alongside LOC growth. (b) No peer-reviewed study counts lint suppressions or threshold and config edits in agent PRs. My own count on AIDev v3 has no human baseline. It finds that 8.7% of agent PRs with code patches add at least one suppression marker and 6.6% end net-positive; added markers outnumber removed ones about 2:1; Claude Code is highest at 20.1% (n=333). Edits to threshold keys in lint or coverage configs are rare (0.08%). Test 'gaming' looks like weak tests rather than deleted tests: agents add mocks more often (36% vs 26% of commits), 80.2% of agent test patches have weak or no oracles, and Python agent tests often miss the agent's own changed lines. Java agent PRs that add no coverage delete 2.6 tests for every test they add. The largest size-controlled within-repo study (114k Java PRs), however, finds that agent-supported PRs delete tests less often than human-authored ones. I found no study of function splitting to game complexity metrics. (c) Every multi-step benchmark finds decay. In SlopCodeBench, erosion rises in 77% of trajectories and verbosity in 75.5%, and quality prompts lower the starting level but not the rate of decay. CodeClash codebases become 'messy and redundant'. In CodeThread, agents resolve up to 13.1% fewer tasks when building on agent code, and traditional maintainability metrics do not explain the gap. In NITR, agents pass dependency-control probes in 4.3% of cases. In real repositories, 22.7% of AI-introduced static-analysis issues survive to HEAD, clones introduced in agent PRs mostly get merged, and human review of agent PRs is becoming more lenient. For Geiger this means: normalize per changed line and compare against a human baseline in the same repository; treat suppressions, config edits and oracle-free tests as tamper signals; and do not assume classic metrics capture the maintainability that hurts later agents.

findings.claim: Repository-level staggered DiD on AIDev v3 (401 'agent-first' repos vs 606 matched controls; 117 'IDE-first' repos vs 73 controls; SonarQube monthly) finds agent adoption followed by persistent rises of ~18% in static-analysis warnings and ~39% in cognitive complexity. Outcomes are repository totals with LOC as a time-varying covariate, not per-PR per-line rates. The authors flag isolated significant pre-treatment coefficients as a limitation.
