verdict.corrected_claim: Kraishan (single-author arXiv preprint v1, 2026-09-12) studies 37,623 PRs: 33,596 from five agents across 2,807 repositories, and 4,027 human PRs restricted to the 810 repositories that also contain agent PRs (Dec 2024 to Jul 2025). After normalizing by PR size, no agent has higher 90-day churn per changed line than humans. Churn is measured only on each PR's most-changed file. Revert rates (detected from commit messages) differ by vendor: Codex 6.1%, Devin 14.5%, human 11.5%. The structural measures are regex counts on added diff lines, and static coverage reaches only 23.7% of PRs. Agents and tasks self-select. Claude Code PRs are about 8x larger, which confounds its results.
verdict.evidence: Opened https://arxiv.org/html/2609.17598. Abstract: 'drawn from 2,807 GitHub repositories'. Corpus section: 'we kept human PRs only from repositories that also contain agent PRs (810 repositories)'. Threats: 'Churn on the most-changed file is a proxy for whole-PR churn'. 'Static coverage (23.7% of PRs)'. 'Agents are not randomly assigned to tasks.' The cited quote ('none of the five agents imposes a measurably higher per-line maintenance burden...') matches exactly. The claim wrongly implies that all PRs come from the same 810 repositories.

findings.claim: In 403 readability-motivated agent commits (Python, AIDev), radon's Maintainability Index fell in 56.1% and cyclomatic complexity rose in 42.7%, while LOC rose in 71.5% (large effect sizes for LOC and cyclomatic complexity). The paper does not normalize for size, and MI is partly size-driven, so part of the decline may be volume.

sources.title: Horikawa et al.: Do AI Agents Really Improve Code Readability? (MSR 2026 Mining Challenge)
sources.quote: Maintainability Index deteriorated in 56.1% of the commits, indicating a tendency toward reduced maintainability. Similarly, Lines of Code increased in 71.5% of the cases

findings.relevance: Agents that state a quality goal still worsen classic metrics, which argues for measuring outcomes rather than trusting intent. Small Python-only sample.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://arxiv.org/html/2603.13723 (MSR '26). The quote matches exactly. Abstract: 'the Maintainability Index decreased in 56.1% of commits, while Cyclomatic Complexity increased in 42.7%'. 403 of 577 commits are analyzed with radon. Effect sizes: 'Cyclomatic Complexity (0.63), Lines of Code (0.64), and Source Lines of Code (0.60) exhibit large effect sizes'. Threats: 'our analysis focuses on Python projects'. There is no size normalization. The median change in cyclomatic complexity is 0.00, so the mean increase comes from a subset of commits.

findings.claim: On 617 PRs from one repository (crewAI), agent PRs show about 1.87x higher semantic redundancy (embedding-based Average Max Redundancy 0.2867 vs 0.1532 for humans), while LOC and cyclomatic complexity differ little. Reviewers were more neutral or positive toward the agent PRs.

sources.title: Huang et al.: More Code, Less Reuse (MSR 2026 Mining Challenge)
sources.quote: While traditional metrics show minimal differences between agentic-PRs and human-PRs, redundancy metric analysis shows code in agentic-PRs contain significantly more redundancy

findings.relevance: Suggests duplication-of-logic (Type-4 clones) is a stronger agent-specific signal than complexity. Text-based duplication tools (like Uncle Bob's dryer) would miss it. Evidence comes from a single repository.

verdict.corrected_claim: Only the semantic-redundancy analysis is limited to 617 PRs from crewAI. Agent PRs there show Average Max Redundancy of 0.2867 vs 0.1532 for humans (about 1.87x, Mann-Whitney significant). The radon LOC and cyclomatic-complexity comparison (small differences) and the reviewer-sentiment analysis (more neutral or positive toward agent PRs) use a broader dataset of 3,858 Python PRs. The redundancy result still rests on a single repository.
verdict.evidence: Opened https://arxiv.org/html/2601.21276. 'Dataset A (Full Python Dataset): This dataset comprises 3,858 PRs across all filtered Python repositories. We use this broad dataset to analyze traditional code metrics (RQ1) and reviewer sentiment (RQ2).' 'Dataset B (Core Case Study): This dataset consists of 617 PRs from the crewAI repository'. 'the Average Max Redundancy (AMR) for AI agents is 0.2867, compared to only 0.1532 for humans'. Threats: 'we only analyzed the crewAI repository for RQ1 due to computational costs'. The cited quote matches.

findings.claim: NiCad found 28,425 clones in 497 of 7,851 agent PRs (AIDev). In 320 of those PRs the clones recur across several commits, and they usually survive review and are merged. A companion genealogy study (350 lineages, 6 projects) attributes 85.71% of clones to humans and 14.29% to agents, with similar survival rates (80% vs 76%).

sources.title: Uchoa et al.: A Study on Code Clone Lifecycles in Pull Requests Created by AI Agents (MSR '26)
sources.quote: the findings indicate that clones tend to persist once introduced, progressing through the PR lifecycle and ultimately being merged into the codebase.

sources.title: Sousa et al.: An Empirical Study of Code Clone Genealogies in Human-AI Collaborative Development (MSR '26)
sources.quote: humans introduce 85.71% of code clones, whereas agents contribute only 14.29%. Despite similar clone survival rates for both humans (80%) and agents (76%)

findings.relevance: Review does not remove duplication, so a duplication measurement needs to run before merge. Whether agents duplicate more than humans per changed line is still open.

verdict.corrected_claim: NiCad found 28,425 clone instances (about 94% precision) in 497 of 7,851 merged agent PRs that add code (Python, C#, Java, Ruby only; AIDev). In 320 PRs clones recur across commits. The sample was filtered to merged PRs, so 'merged' is partly by construction. The clone merge rate depends on the lifecycle: 11 to 42.5% when clones appear in a single commit, and 63.8 to 81.4% when they recur. The authors say agent clone lifecycles resemble those reported for humans. The genealogy study (350 lineages in 6 projects, 516 human vs 473 agent merged PRs) attributes 85.71% of lineages to human-merged PRs and 14.29% to agent-merged PRs, with survival of 80% vs 76%. In that small sample, agents originated fewer clone lineages per PR than humans.
verdict.evidence: Opened https://mhepaixao.github.io/homepage/files/msr26lifecycle.pdf. 'Filter only merged PRs that add code'. 'when PRs are classified as Single, the merge rates of clones are 42.5% for Python, 39.5% for C#, and only 11.0% for Ruby'. Recurring: '77.8% of Python PRs, 81.4% of C# PRs, and 63.8% of Ruby PRs'. 'AI-generated clones show lifecycle and type distributions comparable to those reported for human developers'. Opened https://mhepaixao.github.io/homepage/files/msr26genealogy.pdf; the quote matches. Method: '989 merged PRs in total, of which 516 (54%) were merged by humans, and 473 (46%) were merged by agents'.

findings.claim: I counted suppression markers in AIDev v3 pr_commit_details (33,580 agent PRs; 24,196 with code-file patches; agent-only, because AIDev ships no human patches). 8.7% of these PRs add at least one marker (#[allow/#[expect, noqa, type: ignore, eslint-disable, @ts-ignore, nolint, @SuppressWarnings and similar) and 6.6% are net-positive; merged PRs are at 6.1%. Totals: 16,112 markers added vs 8,457 removed, 1.68 per 1k added code lines. By agent: Claude Code 20.1% (n=333), Devin 12.6%, Copilot 12.1%, Cursor 10.8%, Codex 6.7%. Rust #[allow/#[expect: 904 added vs 494 removed, in 143 PRs. 2.6% of PRs touch a lint or coverage config file, and 0.08% add lines with threshold keys (max-complexity, fail_under, coverageThreshold and similar). Without a human baseline these rates cannot show gaming. Large patches are missing from the data.

sources.title: AIDev dataset card (v5; v3 tag used for the count), CC-BY-4.0
sources.quote: Note that the `patch` data does not include large patches since the GitHub API does not provide them.

findings.relevance: Fills the gap that no study counts suppressions. Suppressions are common enough (roughly 1 in 11 agent PRs, 1 in 5 for Claude Code) that Geiger needs a rule covering them, such as a net-new-suppression hard gate or a penalty. Threshold and config edits are rare but cheap to block. Script and counts: .local/geiger-research/sources/gap-agent-pr-quality-and-gaming/aidev_v3_suppression_counts.py and aidev_v3_suppression_counts.json.

verdict.corrected_claim: I re-ran the counts on AIDev v3 pr_commit_details. The arithmetic in the JSON reproduces: 8.7% add, 6.6% net-positive, 6.1% net-positive among merged PRs, 1.68 markers per 1k added lines. But the method inflates these numbers. pr_commit_details holds one row per commit and file (12,026 of 33,580 PRs have several commits). About 41% of added markers (6,545 of about 16,055) come from commits whose message starts with 'Merge ', which most likely bring in base-branch code written by others. Excluding those commits gives: 6.7% of 24,196 code PRs add at least one marker; 5.1% are net-positive; 9,510 markers added vs 5,777 removed. By agent: Claude Code 17.4% (net 14.7%, n=333), Devin 8.4%, Copilot 8.0%, Cursor 7.5%, Codex 5.8%. Rust #[allow/#[expect: 419 added vs 308 removed, in 109 PRs. Further limits: v3 truncates commits at 30 per PR, and large patches are missing. The lint-config regex skips pyproject.toml, setup.cfg, Cargo.toml, package.json and tox.ini, so the 2.6% config and 0.08% threshold rates are lower bounds; the threshold regex also matches line-length. Totals are concentrated in a few PRs (for example, Claude Code's 1,470 eslint-disable additions come from 17 PRs). There is no human baseline, so the counts cannot show gaming. The practical conclusion still holds: roughly 1 in 15 to 20 agent PRs, and 1 in 6 to 7 Claude Code PRs, adds suppressions.
verdict.evidence: Read .local/geiger-research/sources/gap-agent-pr-quality-and-gaming/aidev_v3_suppression_counts.py and .json and recomputed the ratios. Ran scratchpad/insp2.py and insp3.py: 'Counter({'normal': 9510, 'merge': 6545})'; 'ALL 24196 add% 6.7 net% 5.1 A 9510 D 5777 rustA 419 rustD 308 rustPRs 109'. Dataset card https://huggingface.co/datasets/hao-li/AIDev (raw README): the large-patch quote matches, and 'file-level `pr_commit_details` may be missing for commits beyond the first 30 of very large PRs.' v3 is listed as having the 30-item truncation issue.

findings.claim: Across 1.2M commits in 2,168 TS/JS/Python repositories (2025), coding-agent commits touch tests more often than non-agent commits (23% vs 13%) and add mocks more often (36% vs 26%).

sources.title: Hora, Robbes: Are Coding Agents Generating Over-Mocked Tests? An Empirical Study (MSR 2026 technical track)
sources.quote: 36% of commits made by coding agents add mocks to tests, compared with 26% by non-agents

findings.relevance: Mock-heavy tests raise coverage without checking real interactions, so Geiger's coverage component can be satisfied this way. Supports weighting mutation or oracle signals over line coverage.

verdict.corrected_claim: Across about 1.25M commits from 2025 in 2,168 TS/JS/Python repositories that contain agent config files (not AIDev), 23% of coding-agent commits add or change test files, vs 13% of non-agent commits. Among test commits, 36% of agent test commits add mocks, vs 26% of non-agent test commits. The 36% vs 26% comparison is not over all commits. The study measures how often mocks are added, not whether tests are over-mocked.
verdict.evidence: Opened https://arxiv.org/html/2602.00409 (v1 30 Jan 2026, MSR '26). The abstract wording matches the cited quote, but Observation 3 in the body says: '36% of test commits made by coding agents add mocks to test code, compared with 26% of test commits made by non-agents.' Arithmetic check: there are 11,035 agent test commits among 48,563 agent commits, so 36% of all agent commits (about 17.5k) cannot be mock-adding test commits. Test share: '23% of commits made by coding agents involve the addition or modification of test files, compared with 13%'.

findings.claim: Of 86,156 test-file patches in 33,596 agent PRs (AIDev-pop), 80.2% have weak or no explicit oracle signal (assertion). After adjusting for size and agent, strong-oracle PRs are more likely to be merged (OR 1.28). The paper reports no human baseline.

sources.title: Banik, Chowdhury, Shamim: All Smoke, No Alarm: Oracle Signals in Agent-Authored Test Code
sources.quote: 80.2% of test patches contain weak or no explicit oracle signals.

findings.relevance: Shows that test-file presence or count would be easy for agents to satisfy without real testing. Geiger should measure test strength, for example with mutation testing or assertion density.

verdict.corrected_claim: Of 86,156 cumulative test-file patches (per PR and file) from AIDev-pop agent PRs, 80.2% have weak or no explicit oracle signal in their added lines. This includes edits to existing test files. On newly created test files, strong-oracle rates range from 18% (Codex) to 67% (Claude Code). Raw merge rates are lower for strong-oracle PRs. After adjusting for agent, size, popularity, task type and language, the multi-signal strong-oracle group (S3) has higher merge odds (OR 1.28). This odds ratio does not apply to all strong-oracle PRs. The paper has no human baseline.
verdict.evidence: Opened https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18168 and https://arxiv.org/html/2606.18168. The quote matches. 'While raw merge rates are lower for strong-oracle PRs, a regression analysis...'. 'S3 oracles associate with significantly higher merge rates after adjustment (OR = 1.28'. 'has_multi_strong (best patch is S3)'. 'On newly added test files, strong-oracle rates range from 18% to 67% across agents.' 'we concatenate all patches for each unique (PR, filename) pair in commit order'.

findings.claim: In 4,882 agent PRs (532 Java, 4,350 Python), existing tests cover 61.5% (Java) and 27.0% (Python) of changed executable lines. Agent tests add coverage in only 35.9% and 22.5% of Code+Tests PRs. In Java PRs where coverage does not improve, agents deleted 82 tests and added 31.

sources.title: Dipongkor et al.: Test Coverage Analysis of Agentic Pull Requests
sources.quote: Java agents sometimes delete more tests than they add (a 2.6 deletion-to-addition ratio in non-improving Java PRs), while Python agents add tests that exercise some other code

findings.relevance: Supports diff-coverage of the agent's own changed lines (locality, Q-locality) as a measure, and a deleted-test signal. The deletion figure covers a small subset of PRs.

verdict.corrected_claim: Of 4,882 agent PRs (532 Java, 4,350 Python), coverage could be measured only for 213 Java and 1,664 Python merged PRs in 10 Java and 34 Python buildable repositories. In those PRs, existing tests cover 61.5% (Java) and 27.0% (Python) of changed executable lines. Agent tests add coverage in 35.9% (23/64) of Java and 22.5% (136/605) of Python Code+Tests PRs. Among non-improving Java PRs that did not already reach 100% diff coverage (a few dozen PRs), agents deleted 82 tests and added 31.
verdict.evidence: Opened https://arxiv.org/html/2607.18057 (v1, July 2026). The quote matches. 'yielding coverage results for 213 of the 532 Java PRs and 1664 of the 4350 Python PRs'. 'Only 35.9% of Java (23/64) and 22.5% of Python (136/605) Code + Tests PRs actually show any improvement.' 'In Java, 42.2% already reach 100% diff coverage from the existing tests. Among the rest, agents delete more tests than they add (82 deleted vs. 31 added, a 2.6 ratio)'.

findings.claim: Conflicting evidence on test deletion. In 114,134 merged Java PRs (391 repos, Jan 2025-Apr 2026), within-repository mixed-effects models that control for change size find that agent-supported PRs add tests more often and modify or delete tests less often than human-authored PRs. Coverage of production changes did not differ in the 95 repos the authors could build, and test-smell differences were borderline.

sources.title: Milanese et al.: Testing with Coding Agents: A Large-Scale Comparison of Agent-Supported and Human-Authored Pull Requests
sources.quote: Agent-supported pull requests add tests more often (odds ratios 1.50-1.58) and modify (0.70-0.76) and delete (0.51-0.77) them less often.

findings.relevance: Real-world agent PRs do not systematically delete tests, so Geiger's tamper protection should focus on weak tests and suppressions rather than test deletion alone. The paper also warns that pooled comparisons across projects can reverse within-repo effects.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35297 (v1, 26 Oct 2026, Milanese et al.). Abstract matches the quote exactly and states: "We analyze 114,134 pull requests merged between January 2025 and April 2026 in 391 Java repositories", "mixed-effects models that control for change size", "in the 95 repositories we could build, in the coverage of their production changes" (no difference), "Differences in test smells are borderline and not reproduced for individual test methods", and pooled comparisons "can hide or reverse". Scope notes: Java only, not AIDev; 'agent-supported' means developer-agent collaboration, not fully autonomous PRs; in test-only PRs agent tests cover less of the code they exercise; authors say relationship with test quality "remains uncertain". Independent search for contradicting evidence could not run (session web-search budget exhausted).

findings.claim: A practitioner audit (self-published, exploratory) labeled 358 public 2026 PRs that touched tests, using an LLM plus manual checks. Unexplained test weakening was near zero for both agents and humans. 19-39% of PRs changed checks deliberately. In a small experiment, Codex changed production code to satisfy a wrong test (3 of 3 runs without a guard) instead of weakening the test.

sources.title: 358 pull requests that changed tests: agents rarely weakened them. They bent the code instead. (DEV Community)
sources.quote: No meaningful agent-vs-human difference

findings.relevance: A second practitioner report next to Böckeler, and it partly contradicts the gaming premise. Gaming may appear as bending code toward a wrong check rather than tampering with the check itself.

verdict.evidence: Opened the DEV post (datetime attribute 2026-10-04T22:02:51Z, author Mykyta/'cherven'). Corpus 198+98+62 = 358 PRs. Quotes: "No meaningful agent-vs-human difference."; "19-39% of PRs changed or removed a check on purpose, usually because the behavior under test changed."; "It changed the code to satisfy the wrong test in 3 of 3 runs without the guard and 2 of 3 with it"; "Treat the numbers as exploratory". LLM (Claude) first-pass labels; author checked only the 6 'weakened' verdicts and reversed 3. Caveats: one model, one run per task; author promotes his own tool (repopilot), and the same model helped build the detectors. Low confidence is appropriate.

findings.claim: In agentic Python refactoring PRs (AIDev), 24.17% of modified files gain new Pylint issues (mostly convention-level) and 4.7% gain new Bandit findings, yet 73.5% of PRs merge, including some that add findings. In 3,907 Java agentic refactoring commits, changes in design and implementation smells are statistically significant but practically negligible.

sources.title: Almukhtar, Ghammam, Ming: Quality and Security Signals in AI-Generated Python Refactoring Pull Requests
sources.quote: 73.5% of the analyzed PRs are merged, including cases that introduce new lint or security findings, often alongside the removal of existing issues.

sources.title: Horikawa et al.: Agentic Refactoring: An Empirical Study of AI Coding Agents
sources.quote: Changes in design and implementation smell counts are statistically significant but practically negligible.

findings.relevance: Lint regressions get through human review, so a score with hard gates adds information that merge decisions miss. Removals offsetting additions in the same PR argue for showing both sides rather than only the net delta.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21453 (20 May 2026): AIDev Python refactoring PRs; "24.17% of modified files introduce new Pylint issues predominantly convention level violations such as long lines-while 4.7% introduce new Bandit findings"; quote on 73.5% merged appears verbatim. Opened https://arxiv.org/html/2511.04824 (v2 26 Oct 2026, TOSEM): "yields 3907 Agentic Refactoring Commits" from AIDev Java; Finding #8 heading matches quote exactly. Note: the same paper's RQ4 frames this as "statistically significant but generally small structural improvements", i.e. the smell change direction is slight improvement, not regression.

findings.claim: Among 400 repeat reviewers of agent PRs (11,429 reviews, seven months, AIDev), approval rose from 30.1% to 36.8% while inline comments fell 22%. Human-PR approval fell over the same period, and median PR size was flat.

sources.title: Yu et al.: Habituation at the Gate: Rising Approval and Declining Scrutiny in Human Review of AI Agent Code
sources.quote: inline comment volume decreases (-22%, p=0.0014), suggesting reviewers spend more time in queue but less time actively inspecting code.

findings.relevance: Human review becomes a weaker gate over time, which supports Q7's premise that an automated, non-habituating score or gate is needed.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22721 (21 Jun 2026, Yu et al.). Abstract: "400 repeat reviewers who collectively submitted 11,429 reviews over a seven-month observation period"; "approval rate from 30.1% to 36.8%"; "human PR approval rates decline over the same period"; "median PR size is flat"; quote with "-22%, p=0.0014" matches exactly. Also reports review latency +3.5x. Single preprint; no replication found (web-search budget exhausted).

findings.claim: In SlopCodeBench, 15 agents extend their own code across 36 problems and 196 checkpoints. Structural erosion rises in 77% of trajectories and verbosity in 75.5%. Agent code is 2.3x more verbose and 2.0x more eroded than code in 473 human Python repos. Explicit quality prompts lower starting levels by up to a third but do not change the rate of decay.

sources.title: Orlanski et al.: SlopCodeBench: Benchmarking How Coding Agents Degrade Over Long-Horizon Iterative Tasks
sources.quote: Explicit quality guidance reduces initial verbosity and erosion by up to a third, without affecting degradation rates.

findings.relevance: Closest benchmark to Malte's 50-PR scenario. Decay continues even with quality prompts, so a per-PR budget must be enforced by measurement, not by instruction.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.24755 (v1 25 Mar 2026, v2 7 May 2026). Abstract: "36 problems and 196 checkpoints", "Evaluating 15 coding agents", "structural erosion rising in 77% of trajectories and verbosity in 75.5%", "Compared to 473 open-source Python repositories, agent code is 2.3x more verbose and 2.0x more eroded"; quote on quality guidance matches exactly. Context: best agent passes only 14.8% of checkpoints; benchmark is synthetic and agents extend their own code, not real PRs. Replication search not possible (search budget exhausted).

findings.claim: In CodeClash (1,680 tournaments, 25,200 rounds, 8 models), agent-managed codebases keep growing in file count and filename redundancy (59% for Qwen3 Coder, 35% for Claude Sonnet models), where human codebases plateau.

sources.title: Yang et al.: CodeClash: Benchmarking Goal-Oriented Software Engineering
sources.quote: Models also struggle with long-term codebase maintenance, as repositories become progressively messy and redundant.

findings.relevance: File sprawl and redundant modules are a form of decay that function-level metrics miss. Supports adding structure-level measurements such as duplication across files and module count.

verdict.corrected_claim: In CodeClash (1,680 tournaments, 25,200 rounds, 8 LMs, 6 arenas), the number of agent-created files grows almost linearly with rounds, and filename redundancy (fraction of files sharing name prefixes) is high for Qwen3 Coder (59%) and Claude Sonnet models (35%); most agent-created files are never reused. The paper contrasts this with human codebases only qualitatively (file creation 'quickly plateaus'); it does not measure human codebases.
verdict.evidence: Opened https://arxiv.org/html/2511.00839 (v2 12 May 2026). Quote matches exactly. "We run 1680 tournaments ( 25 , 200 rounds total) to evaluate 8 LMs across 6 arenas." "the filename redundancy metric (the fraction of files sharing name prefixes with other files) which is particularly high for Qwen3 Coder (59%) and Claude Sonnet models (35%)". Human side: "In most human-managed codebases, the rate of file creation quickly plateaus once the overall structure has been established" — an unmeasured general statement. Redundancy is reported as a level, not shown to keep growing. Arenas are competitive game bots, not product repos.

findings.claim: CodeThread (four frontier agents, four benchmarks) finds that agents resolve up to 13.1% fewer tasks when building on agent-written code than on human code. Many traditional maintainability metrics do not explain the gap. Input validation, error handling and code size explain it better.

sources.title: Patel et al.: Is Agent Code Less Maintainable Than Human Code?
sources.quote: Regression analysis reveals that many traditional software engineering maintainability metrics do not explain this difference.

findings.relevance: Challenges Q7's premise directly: a score built on classic metrics may not predict how hard the next agent task will be. Geiger's weights should be checked against downstream task success.

verdict.corrected_claim: CodeThread (four models via the SWE-Agent scaffold: Claude 4.5 Sonnet, GPT-5, GLM 4.7, MiniMax M2.5; four benchmarks) finds downstream resolve rates are usually lower on agent-written code, with a maximum gap of 13.1 percentage points (GLM on SWE-Bench Pro, 45.2% vs 32.0%); most gaps are 3-8 points and some pairs favour agent code. Of four static metrics tested (cyclomatic complexity, cognitive complexity, Halstead volume, LLOC), only downstream LLOC change was significant; an input/error-contract indicator and task difficulty were also significant, but model fit is modest (McFadden R2 = 0.069).
verdict.evidence: Opened https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.21804 (v2 29 Sep 2026) and the HTML version. Abstract quote matches exactly; "task resolve rate drops of up to 13.1%". Table 2: "SWE-Bench Pro ... 45.2 32.0 − 13.1" for GLM, and positive deltas such as "+ 6.2" and "+ 3.1" for some pairs. Text: "GLM shows the largest and most consistent effect ... dropping by 13.1% on SWE-Bench Pro. Claude and MiniMax also drop by around 3 - 8 %". "Most static maintainability metrics have similar distributions, except Δ LLOC at PR 2". 'Up to 13.1% fewer tasks' overstates scope: it is a single worst case in percentage points.

findings.claim: The NITR benchmark (23 configurations) finds that agents solve 36.2% of maintainability probes on average. Dependency-control probes are solved in 4.3% and responsibility decomposition in 15.2%. 13.3% of outcomes pass all functional tests but fail the structural oracle.

sources.title: Zhu et al.: Needle in the Repo: A Benchmark for Maintainability in AI-Generated Repository Edits
sources.quote: The hardest pressures are architectural rather than local edits, especially dependency control (4.3%) and responsibility decomposition (15.2%).

findings.relevance: Shows that architecture rules, such as a layer gate (domain must not import infrastructure), are where agents fail most and tests catch least. This supports hard gates for hexagonal-layer rules in Malte's Rust workspace.

verdict.corrected_claim: NITR evaluates 23 configurations (GPT, Claude, Gemini, Qwen families, in both direct-inference and agent mode). Averaged over all configurations, 36.2% of probes are solved (best 57.1%); agent mode raises the average from 28.2% to 45.0% but does not remove architectural failures. Dependency control is solved in 4.3% and responsibility decomposition in 15.2%; 64/483 outcomes (13.3%) pass all functional tests but fail the structural oracle. The abstract does not break the 13.3% down by dimension.
verdict.evidence: Opened https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.27745 (29 Mar 2026). Quote matches exactly. "we evaluate 23 coding configurations across GPT, Claude, Gemini, and Qwen families in both direct-inference and agent-based settings"; "agent-mode configurations improve average performance from 28.2% to 45.0%, but do not eliminate these architectural failures". So '36.2%' is not an agent-only figure. The relevance note's 'tests catch least' for architecture rules is not shown by the abstract. Probes are small synthetic codebases.

findings.claim: Across 302.6k verified AI-authored commits (Copilot, Claude, Cursor, Gemini, Devin; 6,299 repos; attributed by bot logins and Co-authored-by trailers), 7.5-14.8% of commits introduce at least one static-analysis issue, 89.3% of the issues are code smells, and 22.7% survive to the latest revision.

sources.title: Liu et al.: Debt Behind the AI Boom: A Large-Scale Empirical Study of AI-Generated Code in the Wild
sources.quote: More importantly, 22.7% of tracked AI-introduced issues still survive at the latest version of the repository.

findings.relevance: Evidence from real repositories that issues from AI changes accumulate over later commits. It mixes autonomous agents with assistant commits and has no human survival baseline in the abstract.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.28592 (v3 13 Oct 2026) and the HTML. Abstract: "302.6k verified AI-authored commits from 6,299 GitHub repositories", "code smells ... accounting for 89.3% of all issues", "Between 7.5% and 14.8% of each assistant's commits introduce at least one issue"; quote on 22.7% matches exactly. HTML: the five assistants are GitHub Copilot, Claude, Cursor, Gemini, Devin; attribution uses actor logins, author emails, author names and Co-authored-by trailers (claim lists only two of four, a minor omission). No human survival baseline; tools ESLint, Pylint, Semgrep (JS/TS/Python only); autonomous and assisted commits are not separated, as the relevance note says.

findings.claim: Inference from a-1 to a-3, b-1 to b-6 and c-1 to c-3: (1) Geiger's per-PR budget should be normalized per changed line and calibrated against a same-repository human baseline. Raw deltas mostly track size (a-2), and normalized comparisons with humans are mixed (a-3 vs a-1). (2) The behaviours with real-world evidence that need gates or tamper protection are net-new suppressions (b-1), mock-heavy or oracle-free tests (b-2, b-3), uncovered changed lines (b-4), duplication (a-5, a-6, c-2) and architectural dependency violations (c-4). Test deletion and threshold or config edits are rare or not over-represented in agent PRs (b-1, b-5), and function splitting is unmeasured. (3) Classic complexity and MI metrics may not predict downstream agent difficulty (c-3), so the score's weights need validation.

sources.title: Beyond Bug Fixes
sources.quote: higher issue counts are primarily driven by larger PRs.

sources.title: Is Agent Code Less Maintainable Than Human Code?
sources.quote: many traditional software engineering maintainability metrics do not explain this difference.

findings.relevance: Bears directly on Q4 (which agent behaviours need gates or tamper protection), Q5/Q6 (size normalization) and the premise of Q7.

verdict.corrected_claim: From the findings verified here: (1) Normalize per-PR deltas by churn and compare against a same-repository human baseline. Beyond Bug Fixes shows cross-agent differences in raw issue counts mostly vanish after churn normalization, and b-5 shows pooled cross-project comparisons can hide or reverse within-repo effects. (2) Unexplained test deletion or weakening is rare in real PRs (b-5, b-6). Deliberate check changes are common (19-39% of test-touching PRs in b-6), so surface them for review instead of treating them as rare. b-6 also shows a gaming mode the list omits: agents bending production code to satisfy a wrong test, or adding silent fallbacks. Architectural dependency control is the weakest maintainability dimension in NITR (c-4). (3) In CodeThread, cyclomatic complexity, cognitive complexity and Halstead volume did not explain downstream agent difficulty; LLOC change did, and the model fit was weak. The study did not test the Maintainability Index, so the score's weights need validation against downstream outcomes. Parts that rest on a-1 to a-6 and b-1 to b-4 were not checked here.
verdict.evidence: Opened https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.20109 (27 Jan 2026): "apparent differences in raw issue counts across agents largely disappear after normalizing by code churn, indicating that higher issue counts are primarily driven by larger PRs". This compares agents with each other, not agents with humans. Opened https://arxiv.org/html/2606.21804: the static features are "four static proxies for maintenance cost" (CC, CogC, Halstead Volume, LLOC), and "Most static maintainability metrics have similar distributions, except Δ LLOC at PR 2". No MI was tested. DEV post (b-6): "19-39% of PRs changed or removed a check on purpose"; "It changed the code to satisfy the wrong test in 3 of 3 runs without the guard". Not verifiable here: a-1 to a-6 and b-1 to b-4, the claim that 'function splitting is unmeasured', and whether threshold or config edits are rare. A web search for counter-evidence could not run because the session's search budget was exhausted.

Does the 18%/39% repo-level rise in warnings and complexity (2601.13597) survive per-LOC or per-churn normalization, given the pre-trend coefficients the authors report?
