areas.title: What outcome evidence supports scoring a change instead of the whole codebase? Which change-level features predict defect-inducing changes in just-in-time (JIT) defect prediction, how stable are those models over time, do simple models match deep ones, can risk be localized to lines for a report, do diff-time findings get fixed more often than batch reports, and what did Google and Meta observe when they deployed change-risk scores?
areas.summary_before_verification: The evidence supports scoring changes, but for prediction and workflow reasons. No study I read shows that a change-scoped maintainability score prevents later defects. Just-in-time (JIT) defect prediction works at a modest level. Kamei et al. (TSE 2013, 11 projects, more than 250k changes) report 68% accuracy and 64% recall, and inspecting the riskiest changes that make up 20% of changed lines finds 35% of defect-inducing changes. Size and diffusion features predict best: number of files, churn and added lines. The Size family stays the top contributor over time and is robust to noise in SZZ labels. Models drift, though. AUC drops by up to 22 points (Qt) and 34 points (OpenStack) one year after training, so the authors recommend retraining on the last three months of data. Simple models match or beat deep models on open benchmarks: logistic regression on added lines alone outperforms CC2Vec and DeepJIT, and JITLine is both simpler and finer-grained. Meta's own results conflict. A fine-tuned LLM caught 1.05 to 1.52 times as many SEVs as logistic regression, but a BERT model did worse than logistic regression. Risk can be localized for a report: Meta's attention highlighting finds the outage-causing hunk 54% of the time when it shows 26% of the changed lines. That result rests on a small expert set, and early users rated it 7 positive and 48 negative. Delivery matters more than model quality. Google's file-level bug-prediction flags in code review produced no measurable behavior change because developers could not clear them. Facebook's Infer had a near-zero fix rate as a batch tool and over 70% at diff time, with the same analysis. At Meta, the Diff Risk Score lets low-risk diffs land during code freezes. RADAR reports revert rates of 1/3 and production-incident rates of 1/50 of non-RADAR diffs, but its authors say the comparison is not causal. For agent PRs, size and rework signals (commits per PR, churn) still predict follow-up fixes. Author-experience features have no evidence base for agents.

findings.claim: Kamei et al. (TSE 2013; 6 open-source and 5 commercial projects, more than 250,000 changes, C/C++ and Java) predicted defect-inducing changes with 68% accuracy and 64% recall. Ranking by risk per changed line, 20% of inspection effort (measured as modified LOC) finds 35% of defect-inducing changes. In open-source projects, the number of files (NF), relative churn (LA/LT, LT/NF) and fix commits (FIX) increase risk, and the time since a file's last change (AGE) decreases it. In commercial projects, NF, relative churn and the past number of developers on a file (NDEV) increase risk.

sources.title: Kamei et al., A Large-Scale Empirical Study of Just-in-Time Quality Assurance, TSE 39(6) (local copy kamei.pdf)
sources.quote: using only 20 percent of the effort it would take to inspect all changes, we can identify 35 percent of all defect-inducing changes

sources.title: Kamei et al., TSE 2013, Section on RQ3
sources.quote: the number of files and whether or not the change fixes a defect are riskincreasing factors, whereas the average time interval since the previous change is a risk-decreasing factor

findings.relevance: This is the baseline evidence that a change-scoped score predicts later defects, and it names which change features carry the signal: size and diffusion, not code-style metrics. It also shows the accuracy is modest, so a per-PR gate built on these features alone would produce many false alarms.

verdict.evidence: Opened the local copy of Kamei et al., TSE 39(6), June 2013 (sources/test-quality/kamei.pdf; IEEE header 'VOL. 39, NO. 6, JUNE 2013'). Abstract: 'average accuracy of 68 percent and an average recall of 64 percent' and 'using only 20 percent of the effort it would take to inspect all changes, we can identify 35 percent of all defect-inducing changes'. Effort = 'the number of modified lines'; EALR ranks by 'Rd(x) = Y(x)/Effort(x)', i.e. risk per changed line. Dataset: 'six open source projects and five commercial projects, containing more than 250,000 changes... (C/C++ and Java)'. RQ3: 'for the open source projects, the number of files (NF), the relative churn metrics (LA/LT and LT/NF), and whether or not the change was to fix a defect (FIX) are the most important, risk-increasing factors'; AGE 'is risk decreasing'; commercial: 'the number of developers that touched a file (NDEV) in the past is also risk increasing'. Minor points: the second quote comes from the Introduction's RQ3 summary, not the RQ3 section. The paper also reports precision of only 34-37%, which supports the 'many false alarms' relevance. In commercial projects AGE was risk-increasing; the claim does not mention this.

findings.claim: JIT models drift. On 37,524 Qt and OpenStack changes, models trained on short periods lost 3-22 (Qt) and 3-34 (OpenStack) AUC points one year after training. The authors recommend retraining on data from the last three months and, for quality-improvement plans, training on at least six months of history.

sources.title: McIntosh & Kamei, Are Fix-Inducing Changes a Moving Target? TSE 44(5), doi:10.1109/TSE.2017.2693980 (preprint)
sources.quote: JIT models should be retrained using recently recorded data (within three months).

sources.title: McIntosh & Kamei, TSE 2018, RQ1 results
sources.quote: our short-period models lose 3–22 and 3–34 AUC percentage points one year after being trained

findings.relevance: Any learned weighting in Geiger that predicts defects needs scheduled retraining, so a fixed score threshold, such as -0.2 points per PR, cannot rest on a frozen defect model.

verdict.evidence: Downloaded https://rebels.cs.uwaterloo.ca/papers/tse2017_mcintosh.pdf. Abstract: '37,524 changes from the rapidly evolving QT and OPENSTACK systems' and 'JIT models should be retrained using recently recorded data (within three months)... trained using six months (or more) of historical data'. RQ1: 'our short-period models lose 3–22 and 3–34 AUC percentage points one year after being trained ... in QT and OPENSTACK, respectively.' The paper adds that long-period Qt models trained on periods 5 and later lost only 1-9 AUC points, so drift is smaller with more training data.

findings.claim: In McIntosh & Kamei, the Size family of change properties was the most stable predictor. It was the top contributor in every period of the long-period Qt models and statistically significant in all Qt periods. In some OpenStack periods, the Review family outweighed it.

sources.title: McIntosh & Kamei, TSE 2018, RQ2 results
sources.quote: consistency of the importance of Size suggests that advice about limiting change size is sound.

findings.relevance: Change size is a stable, agent-independent feature that Geiger could weight in a per-PR risk component.

verdict.corrected_claim: In McIntosh & Kamei, Size was the most consistent top contributor, but its importance fluctuated (10%-43% of explanatory power in Qt three-month short-period models). In Qt, Size was the top contributor in all long-period periods, in 8 of 11 three-month and 5 of 6 six-month short-period periods, and statistically significant in all periods. Even in Qt, the Review family outranked Size in short-period periods 5, 6 and 9, and History outranked it in period 6. In OpenStack, Review outranked Size in many periods, including all six-month long-period models, and Size was non-significant in 2 of 9 three-month short-period models.
verdict.evidence: https://rebels.cs.uwaterloo.ca/papers/tse2017_mcintosh.pdf RQ2: 'the Size family is the top contributor in 8 of the 11 three-month periods and 5 of the 6 six-month periods of our short-period JIT models, and all of the three- and six-month periods for our long-period JIT models.' Also: 'in QT, the Review family achieves a larger importance score than the Size family in periods 5, 6, and 9 of the three-month short-term models'. OpenStack: Review is larger in '(d) all periods of the six-month long-term models'. The quote 'consistency of the importance of Size suggests that advice about limiting change size is sound' is present. The abstract says the magnitude 'fluctuates considerably'. The claim's wording 'some OpenStack periods' understates the Review effect and omits the Qt exceptions.

findings.claim: The number of files modified, the top JIT feature, is robust to mislabeling by SZZ variants. Fan et al. studied 126,526 changes from 10 Apache projects. Mislabeling by AG-SZZ reduced performance by 1-5%, and mislabeling by B-SZZ wasted 9-10% more inspection effort. The second- and third-ranked metrics were less robust.

sources.title: Fan et al., The Impact of Mislabeled Changes by SZZ on Just-in-Time Defect Prediction, IEEE TSE (author page abstract)
sources.quote: the top-most important metric for identifying bug-introducing changes (i.e., number of files modified in a change) is robust to the mislabeling noise generated by SZZ

findings.relevance: Labels from SZZ (linking fixes back to the changes that introduced the bugs) are noisy. The diffusion feature survives that noise, which supports using it in Geiger even with imperfect defect labels.

verdict.corrected_claim: Fan et al. (IEEE TSE, published online July 2019; 126,526 changes, 10 Apache projects) found that the top-ranked metric, number of files modified, is robust to SZZ mislabeling. AG-SZZ labels reduced performance by 1%-5% on average (statistically significant). B-SZZ and MA-SZZ caused no considerable performance drop. B-SZZ and AG-SZZ mislabels wasted 9%-10% and 1%-15% more inspection effort, respectively, and only the B-SZZ effect was significant. The second- and third-ranked metrics were more affected by noise, unless random forest was the classifier.
verdict.evidence: https://yuanrui-fan.github.io/publication/tse2019 (abstract, fetched with curl): 'the changes mislabeled B-SZZ and AG-SZZ lead to 9%–10% and 1%–15% more wasted inspection effort, respectively'; 'But the second- and third-most important metrics are more likely to be impacted by the mislabeling noise, unless random forest is used as the underlying classifier.' The quoted 'top-most important metric... is robust' sentence is present. The claim's core holds but omits the random-forest exception and the AG-SZZ effort figure. Only the abstract was readable; the full text was blocked (core.ac.uk 403).

findings.claim: Cabral et al. (ICSE 2019, 10 GitHub projects) show that the share of defect-inducing changes shifts over time. Labels also arrive late (verification latency), because a change is known to be defect-inducing only after its fix lands. Existing JIT approaches scored up to 97.2% lower g-mean than methods designed for this shift.

sources.title: Cabral, Minku, Shihab, Mujahid, Class Imbalance Evolution and Verification Latency in JIT Software Defect Prediction, ICSE 2019, doi:10.1109/ICSE.2019.00076 (abstract page)
sources.quote: Based on 10 GitHub projects, we show that JIT-SDP suffers from class imbalance evolution, significantly hindering the predictive performance of existing JIT-SDP approaches.

findings.relevance: For agent PRs, a defect label arrives weeks or months after the PR. Any defect-calibrated score for a fast agent loop will train on stale labels.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://research.birmingham.ac.uk/en/publications/class-imbalance-evolution-and-verification-latency-in-just-in-tim. Abstract: 'Based on 10 GitHub projects, we show that JIT-SDP suffers from class imbalance evolution, significantly hindering the predictive performance of existing JIT-SDP approaches.' It also says: 'Compared to state-of-the-art class imbalance evolution learning approaches, the predictive performance of JIT-SDP approaches was up to 97.2% lower in terms of g-mean.' On verification latency: 'labeled training examples arrive with a delay'. Published 25 May 2019, ICSE 2019, pp. 666-676, doi 10.1109/ICSE.2019.00076. The explanation 'only after its fix lands' is a fair gloss, not a quote.

findings.claim: Simple models match or beat deep models on open benchmarks. Zeng et al. (ISSTA 2021, 310,370 changes from 6 projects) found that neither CC2Vec nor DeepJIT consistently beat traditional JIT models. Logistic regression on the added-lines count alone (LApredict) outperformed both and was 81k and 120k times faster in training and testing.

sources.title: Zeng, Zhang, Zhang, Zhang, Deep Just-in-Time Defect Prediction: How Far Are We? ISSTA 2021, doi:10.1145/3460319.3464819
sources.quote: such a simplistic approach can outperform CC2Vec and DeepJIT in defect prediction, and can be 81k X/120k X faster in training/testing.

findings.relevance: A cheap size-based risk term is a credible baseline for Geiger. Deep models need a benchmark against it before they earn a place.

verdict.corrected_claim: On Zeng et al.'s data (ISSTA 2021; 310,370 changes from 6 projects), neither CC2Vec nor DeepJIT consistently beat traditional JIT models. LApredict (logistic regression on added-lines count) outperformed both 'for most cases' and was 81k/120k times faster in training/testing than CC2Vec. The result does not generalize to all open benchmarks: on JIT-Defects4J (Ni et al., FSE 2022), LApredict had the lowest AUC of the baselines (0.694), below DeepJIT (0.775), CC2Vec (0.791), JITLine (0.802) and JIT-Fine (0.881).
verdict.evidence: Downloaded https://zhangyuqun.github.io/publications/issta2021.pdf. Abstract quote verified. Intro: 'LApredict can outperform CC2Vec and all other existing approaches for most cases in JIT defect prediction, and can be 81k X/120k X faster than CC2Vec in training/testing.' Contradicting evidence: https://kui-liu.github.io/papers/2022-ni-best.pdf Table 4 shows AUC 'LApredict 0.694', 'DeepJIT 0.775', 'CC2Vec 0.791', 'JIT-Fine 0.881'. Text: 'building a simple supervised model cannot better capture the characteristics of defect-inducing commits.'

findings.claim: JITLine (MSR 2021) uses bag-of-tokens features with a random forest and explains predictions with LIME (local model explanations). On 37,524 OpenStack and Qt commits, it was 26-38% more accurate (F-measure) and 70-100 times faster than CC2Vec and DeepJIT. Its line-level predictions were 133-150% more accurate (Top-10 Accuracy) than a baseline NLP approach. The same study shows that CC2Vec's F-measure falls by 38.5% (OpenStack) and 45.7% (Qt) once the test data is excluded from training.

sources.title: Pornprasit & Tantithamthavorn, JITLine: A Simpler, Better, Faster, Finer-grained Just-In-Time Defect Prediction, MSR 2021, doi:10.1109/MSR52588.2021.00049
sources.quote: the fine-grained predictions at the line level by our approach are 133%-150% more accurate (Top-10 Accuracy) than the baseline NLP approach

findings.relevance: Line-level risk localization, which Geiger's report needs, is achievable with a light model, not only an LLM.

verdict.evidence: Downloaded https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.07068 (v2, 16 Mar 2021). Abstract: 'the F-measure of CC2Vec is decreased by 38.5% for OpenStack and 45.7% for Qt'; '37,524 commits from OpenStack and Qt'; 'at least 26%-38% more accurate (F-measure), 17%-51% more cost-effective (PCI@20%LOC), 70-100 times faster than the state-of-the-art approaches (i.e., CC2Vec and DeepJIT)'. The quoted 133%-150% Top-10 Accuracy line is present. LIME is used for line-level ranking (Sec. on 'Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME)'). Independent support: on JIT-Defects4J, Ni et al. FSE 2022 Table 4 gives JITLine AUC 0.802, above DeepJIT and CC2Vec.

findings.claim: ReDef evaluates code language models (CodeBERT, CodeT5+, UniXcoder, Qwen2.5) on 3,164 defective and 10,268 clean function-level changes from 22 C/C++ projects. Defective changes are identified by revert commits. Performance barely moved when the diffs were deliberately distorted, for example by swapping added and deleted blocks. The authors conclude the models rely on superficial cues, not on the meaning of the change.

sources.title: Nam, Kim, Ryu, Baik, ReDef: Do Code Language Models Truly Understand Code Changes for JIT Software Defect Prediction? arXiv 2509.09192v2
sources.quote: under counterfactual tests, performance remains effectively stable, revealing that what appears to be robustness in fact reflects a reliance on superficial cues rather than true semantic understanding

findings.relevance: This is a critique of LLM-based risk scores. A model that ignores what the change does gives little reason to trust its line highlights or its gate decisions on agent code.

verdict.evidence: Downloaded https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.09192v2 (stamp 'arXiv:2509.09192v2 [cs.SE] 2 Apr 2026'). Abstract: 'curated from 22 large-scale C/C++ projects. Defective cases are anchored by revert commits'; '3,164 defective and 10,268 clean modifications'; 'CodeBERT, CodeT5+, UniXcoder, and Qwen2.5'; perturbations such as 'swapping added/deleted blocks, inverting diff polarity'. The quoted sentence about superficial cues is present. Caveats: this is an arXiv preprint; ambiguous cases were filtered by GPT-assisted triage; the study covers function-level changes only.

findings.claim: Meta's diff risk models (Abreu et al., 2024) predict SEVs (production incidents). The logistic regression baseline catches 18.7%, 27.9% and 84.6% of SEVs while gating 5%, 10% and 50% of diffs. A BERT model (StarBERT) caught only 0.61-0.85 times as many SEVs as the logistic regression. Risk-aligned generative LLMs (iCodeLlama-34B, iDiffLlama-13B) caught 1.40, 1.52 and 1.05 times as many. The logistic regression uses size, diffusion, author experience, file history and service criticality.

sources.title: Abreu et al., Moving Faster and Reducing Risk: Using LLMs in Release Deployment, arXiv 2410.06351
sources.quote: Our baseline regression model captures 18.7%, 27.9%, and 84.6% of SEVs while respectively gating the top 5% (weekend), 10% (yellow), and 50% (red) of risky diffs.

sources.title: Abreu et al., arXiv 2410.06351, abstract
sources.quote: The generative LLMs, iCodeLlama-34B and iDiffLlama-13B, when risk-aligned, capture more SEVs than the logistic regression model in production: 1.40×, 1.52×, 1.05×, respectively.

findings.relevance: This is the only industrial head-to-head comparison found. A fine-tuned LLM beats logistic regression at Meta's scale with Meta's data, which conflicts with the open-benchmark result in jit-6. Geiger would lack both the data and the scale.

verdict.corrected_claim: Meta's logistic regression DRS baseline captures 18.7%, 27.9% and 84.6% of SEVs when gating the top 5%, 10% and 50% of diffs. StarBERT captures 0.61x, 0.85x and 0.81x as many SEVs. Risk-aligned iCodeLlama-34B captures 1.26x, 1.28x and 0.98x, and risk-aligned iDiffLlama-13B (diff-pretrained) captures 1.40x, 1.52x and 1.05x. Without risk alignment, both LLMs were worse than the logistic regression (0.58x-0.90x). Results come from replay on historical diffs. The logistic regression uses diff size relative to file, diffusion (files, authors), criticality (prior SEVs in file or folder, high-criticality service), file complexity and language, and author expertise.
verdict.evidence: Downloaded https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.06351 (v1, 8 Oct 2024). Results summary: 'When iCodeLlama-34B is risk aligned, captures 1.26×, 1.28×, and 0.98× as many SEVs as the logistic regression... The corresponding number for iDiffLlama-13B are 1.40×, 1.52×, 1.05×.' The abstract's '1.40×, 1.52×, 1.05×' therefore belongs to iDiffLlama-13B only. 'Without aligning for diff risk... iCodeLlama-34B model only captures 0.58×, 0.65×, and 0.82×'. Evaluation: 'We mine historical data to determine how well the model would have done'. Table I lists features including 'Previous SEV in the file', 'Is file involved in high-criticality service', 'Total logical complexity of files touched'.

findings.claim: Meta Engineering (2025-08-06) says DRS, a fine-tuned Llama model, let Meta land more than 10,000 diffs during a 2024 partner-event freeze 'with minimal production impact' and eliminate major code freezes. The post gives no SEV-rate numbers and calls LLM explainability an open problem.

sources.title: Meta Engineering, Diff Risk Score: AI-driven risk-aware software development
sources.quote: we landed 10,000+ code changes (that previously could not have landed during a freeze) with minimal production impact

findings.relevance: The reported benefit is throughput (letting low-risk changes through), not defect prevention. It suggests Geiger's per-change score is more useful for routing work than for pass/fail gating.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://engineering.fb.com/2025/08/06/developer-tools/diff-risk-score-drs-ai-risk-aware-software-development-meta/ (posted August 6, 2025). It says: 'Built on a fine-tuned Llama LLM'; 'DRS has helped us eliminate major code freezes'; 'During one such period, a major partner event in 2024, we landed 10,000+ code changes (that previously could not have landed during a freeze) with minimal production impact'; 'LLM explainability remains an open area of research'. The post gives no SEV-rate numbers. Caveat for the relevance note: the companion paper the post cites, Mockus et al., TOSEM 34(7), 2025, doi 10.1145/3722216 (https://mockus.us/papers/UnfreezeMeta.pdf), does report an outcome. Quote: 'Compared to the prior year, despite 42% more diffs landed, there was a reduction in SEVs of 52%.' That comparison is for the winter 2023 freeze, with 16% of diffs gated, and is an uncontrolled year-over-year comparison. So the claim that the reported benefit is throughput, not defect prevention, is too strong.

findings.claim: Meta's RADAR paper (Adams et al., 2026) reports that significant LOC per human-landed diff grew 105.9% year over year and per-developer diff volume grew 51%, with agentic AI responsible for over 80% of that growth. DRS gates automated review and landing. Its default threshold for human diffs is P5, meaning only the lowest-risk 5% qualify. RADAR reviewed 535K+ diffs and landed 331K+. Its revert rate is 1/3 and its production-incident rate 1/50 of non-RADAR diffs. The authors state this is not a causal estimate, because diffs are pre-selected as low risk.

sources.title: Adams et al., Automating Low-Risk Code Review at Meta: RADAR, Risk Calibration, and Review Efficiency, arXiv 2605.30208v2
sources.quote: significant lines of code per human-landed diff grew by 105.9% year over year and per-developer diff volume rose 51%, with agentic AI responsible for over 80% of that growth

sources.title: Adams et al., arXiv 2605.30208, Section 6.3 Internal Validity
sources.quote: Because diffs are not randomly assigned to RADAR, unobserved confounding can influence observed changes.

findings.relevance: This is the closest deployment to Geiger's agent-PR scenario. A per-change risk score routes agent diffs. The safety outcomes are observational and confounded by selection, so they do not show that the score prevents defects.

verdict.evidence: Opened arXiv 2605.30208 (abstract page shows v2, 12 Jun 2026; PDF text read). Abstract quote matches exactly. 535K+ reviewed / 331K+ landed, revert 1/3 and PI 1/50 of non-RADAR diffs (Table 5) confirmed. Sec 2.3: 'For human-authored diffs, the default DRS threshold is P5, meaning only the lowest-risk 5% of diffs qualify'; AI/bot diffs use P50 (allowlisted RACER runbooks) or P20. Sec 6.3 quote matches. Detail to fix: the 'not a causal estimate' sentence sits in the RQ2 results ('While this is not a causal estimate, it is an important operational indicator that widening the approval envelope has not been associated with safety degradation at scale'). The reason the authors give, in 6.3, is non-random assignment and confounding: rollout, evolving eligibility, shifting diff complexity and test coverage. They do not say 'because diffs are pre-selected as low risk'; that is the checker's paraphrase. The abstract also makes a stronger claim: 'without compromising production safety'.
verdict.corrected_claim: RADAR (Adams et al., arXiv 2605.30208v2, June 2026) reports 105.9% YoY growth in significant LOC per human-landed diff and 51% growth in per-developer diff volume, with agentic AI responsible for over 80% of that growth. DRS gates automated review and landing: P5 by default for human diffs, P20 for non-allowlisted AI/bot sources, P50 for allowlisted runbooks. RADAR reviewed 535K+ diffs and landed 331K+. Revert rate is 1/3 and production-incident rate 1/50 of non-RADAR diffs. The authors call this 'not a causal estimate' and note under internal validity that diffs are not randomly assigned to RADAR, so unobserved confounding can influence the results. Their abstract nonetheless claims the system works 'without compromising production safety'.

findings.claim: Meta's highlighting of risky diff regions (Liu et al., AIware 2026) aggregates DRS attention weights to lines, hunks and files. On a set of outages whose root-cause lines experts labeled, the top-2 hunks covered the root-cause lines 53.85% of the time, with developers reviewing 26.28% of changed lines on average. The top-10 lines gave 30.76% coverage at 7.6% of lines. The coverage figures are consistent with a few dozen diffs, but the paper does not state the count. Early in-tool feedback was 7 positive and 48 negative. Downstream outcomes were not measured.

sources.title: Liu et al., A Preliminary Study on Explaining Risk of Code Changes using LLM-Based Prediction Models, AIware '26, arXiv 2607.02782
sources.quote: the highlighted snippets cover expert-labeled outage-causing change lines 53.85% of the time when highlighting the top-2 hunks, while requiring developers to review 26.28% of the changed lines on average

sources.title: Liu et al., arXiv 2607.02782, Section 4.4 User Feedback
sources.quote: We received 55 pieces of feedback: 7 positive and 48 negative.

findings.relevance: Localizing risk to hunks for a report is feasible, but early developer reception was poor. The reported causes: highlighted test or generated code, boilerplate, and highlights that may point toward lower risk instead of higher.

verdict.evidence: Opened arXiv 2607.02782v1 (2 Jul 2026, AIware '26, DOI 10.1145/3805760.3814916; all authors at Meta, but the paper calls the company 'FAANGCompany'). Abstract quote matches. Table 1 shows hunk top-2 at 53.85% with 26.28% review; line top-10 at 30.76% with 7.60%. Sec 4.4: 'We received 55 pieces of feedback: 7 positive and 48 negative.' Of the 48 negative responses, 17 had text, citing test/auto-generated code, boilerplate, and 'directional ambiguity'. Limitations: 'we have not yet measured downstream outcomes such as reduced time-to-resolution or reduced post-landing incident rates.' The O-RC dataset size is never stated. The percentages fit 13 or 26 diffs (7/13, 4/13, 11/26), except 64.38%, which fits neither. Nuances: coverage is binary per diff at hunk level (at least one top-N hunk contains a root-cause line), and Table 1 labels the column 'Precision'. The authors call the feedback a 'small, uncontrolled, and self-selected' debugging signal.

findings.claim: DRS-OSS (Sayedsalehi, Rigby, Mockus) is an open-source diff risk scorer for CI built on a Llama 3.1 8B classifier, with a GitHub App. On ApacheJIT it reports ROC-AUC 0.895, and the riskiest 30% of commits contain 86.4% of risky commits. The authors warn that Llama may have seen Apache code during pretraining, which could inflate these results.

sources.title: Sayedsalehi, Rigby, Mockus, DRS-OSS: A Diff-Risk Scoring Tool for Continuous Integration Workflows, arXiv 2511.21964v3
sources.quote: sending only the riskiest 30% of commits for extra scrutiny captures 86.4% of risky commits in the test set

findings.relevance: This is an existing open tool Geiger could wrap as a Dagger step. It has no Rust-specific validation, and its benchmark results may be inflated by contamination.

verdict.evidence: Opened arXiv 2511.21964 (v3, 7 Jun 2026). Abstract: 'The default packaged backend uses a Llama 3.1 8B sequence classifier ... on ApacheJIT, where it reaches an ROC-AUC of 0.895'. The system includes 'a GitHub App'. Sec V.B quote matches: 'sending only the riskiest 30% of commits for extra scrutiny captures 86.4% of risky commits in the test set' (Table IV recall@30% = 0.864). Sec VI: 'Llama may have seen Apache code during pretraining ... not a contamination-free estimate of generalization.' Caveat: baselines in Table III are compared 'at their reported operating points', not rerun. ApacheJIT is Java, and the paper does not evaluate Rust.

findings.claim: Google deployed file-level bug prediction (TWR) as a line-1 comment in code review in September 2011, flagging the top 0.5% of files. Three months later, mean review time (2.01 to 1.94 days) and comments per review (5.97 to 6.38) did not change significantly. Developers ignored the flags because nothing they did could clear them. This was file-level, history-based prediction, not JIT change-level prediction.

sources.title: Lewis, Lin, Sadowski, Zhu, Ou, Whitehead, Does Bug Prediction Support Human Developers? Findings From a Google Case Study, ICSE 2013, doi:10.1109/ICSE.2013.6606583
sources.quote: We deployed a bug prediction algorithm across Google, and found no identifiable change in developer behavior.

sources.title: Lewis et al., ICSE 2013, Section V.C.3 Interpretation
sources.quote: unless there was an actionable means of removing the flag and “fixing” the file, developers did not find value in the bug prediction, and ignored it

findings.relevance: An accurate risk flag shown at review time still changed nothing when it was not actionable. Geiger's score must tell the author or agent which edit moves it.

verdict.evidence: Opened static.googleusercontent.com .../41145.pdf. Both quotes match. Deployed September 2011 (launch 16 Sep), comment on line 1, 'set to flag the top 0.5% of the Google code base'. Table II: time to review 2.01 to 1.94 days, comments 5.97 to 6.38. 'Student's t-tests show that neither change was significant'. TWR is file-level and based on bug-fix history. Omitted confound: 'After four weeks, the comments were given the same priority as a high-level lint warning: developers could see it if warnings were enabled, but otherwise the comment was not visible ... [this] reduced visibility of our comments.' Measurement compared reviews from three months on either side of launch, with 5th/95th-percentile outliers removed. Non-actionability is the authors' interpretation of qualitative feedback, not a measured cause. The paper does not establish the flag's accuracy in deployment, so the relevance phrase 'an accurate risk flag' overstates.
verdict.corrected_claim: Google deployed file-level, history-based bug prediction (TWR) in September 2011 as a line-1 comment in code review (Mondrian), flagging the top 0.5% of files company-wide. After four weeks the comment was demoted to a hidden-by-default lint warning, which reduced its visibility. Comparing reviews from three months before and after launch, mean review time (2.01 to 1.94 days) and comments per review (5.97 to 6.38) did not change significantly. The authors attribute the null result mainly to non-actionability: developers had no way to clear the flag. This was file-level prediction, not JIT change-level prediction.

findings.claim: At Facebook, Infer run as a nightly batch job, with 20-30 issues hand-assigned to developers, got a fix rate near zero. The same analysis, with the same false-positive rate, reached over 70% fixes when its findings were posted as comments on the diff during code review. The batch sample was small.

sources.title: Distefano, Fähndrich, Logozzo, O'Hearn, Scaling Static Analyses at Facebook, CACM 62(8), doi:10.1145/3338112 (UCL author-accepted manuscript)
sources.quote: the fix rate rocketed to over 70%. The same program analysis, with same false positive rate, had much greater impact when deployed at diff time.

sources.title: Distefano et al., CACM 2019, Human Factors
sources.quote: We assigned 20-30 issues to developers, and almost none of them were acted on.

findings.relevance: This is direct evidence that findings scoped to the diff and delivered in its review get fixed far more often than batch reports about the whole codebase. It supports reporting Geiger results on the PR.

verdict.evidence: Opened UCL AAM PDF (Distefano et al., CACM 2019). Sec 4: Infer was 'run once per night on the entire Facebook Android codebase' and issues were manually assigned. 'We assigned 20-30 issues to developers, and almost none of them were acted on. ... the fix rate ... was near zero.' Then: 'the fix rate rocketed to over 70%. The same program analysis, with same false positive rate, had much greater impact when deployed at diff time.' Intro also gives 70% vs 0%. Caveats: this is a first-party anecdote, a sequential before/after rather than a controlled comparison, and the false-positive rate was what the team 'thought was less than 20%'.

findings.claim: Google's FindBugs history shows that diff-time delivery is not enough on its own. The 2006 nightly dashboard 'saw little use'. In a 2009 Fixit week, engineers reviewed 3,954 warnings and fixed only 16% (640). A later code-review integration was discontinued because false positives cost developer trust. Tricorder now disables any analyzer whose 'Not useful' clicks exceed 10%.

sources.title: Sadowski, Aftandilian, Eagle, Miller-Cushon, Jaspan, Lessons from Building Static Analysis Tools at Google, CACM 61(4), doi:10.1145/3188720
sources.quote: the dashboard saw little use because a bug dashboard was outside the developers’ usual workflow, and distinguishing between new and existing static-analysis issues was distracting.

sources.title: Sadowski et al., CACM 2018, Attempt 3
sources.quote: the presence of effective false positives caused developers to lose confidence in the tool

findings.relevance: Diff-time reporting helps only with low noise and a reliable split between new and existing findings. Both are design requirements for Geiger's delta score.

verdict.evidence: Opened storage.googleapis.com .../4365.pdf (CACM 61(4), 2018; text via pdftotext). Confirmed: 2006 nightly dashboard 'saw little use'. May 2009 Fixit: 'reviewed a total of 3,954 such warnings (42% of 9,473 total), but only 16% (640) were actually fixed'. Two errors. First, the code-review integration 'was discontinued when the code-review tool was replaced in 2011 for two main reasons: the presence of effective false positives caused developers to lose confidence in the tool, and developer customization resulted in an inconsistent view of analysis results.' False positives were one of two reasons, alongside the tool replacement. Second, Tricorder: 'computing the ratio of "Please fix" vs. "Not useful" clicks. If the ratio for an analyzer goes above 10%, the Tricorder team disables the analyzer until the author(s) improve it.' The disable is temporary, the metric is a ratio, and it was described as of 2018. Code-review checks may include 'up to 10% effective false positives'.
verdict.corrected_claim: Google's FindBugs history shows that diff-time delivery is not enough on its own. The 2006 nightly dashboard 'saw little use', partly because new and existing issues were hard to tell apart. In the May 2009 Fixit, engineers reviewed 3,954 warnings and only 16% (640) were fixed. A later code-review integration was discontinued in 2011, when the review tool was replaced, for two reasons: effective false positives cost developer trust, and per-developer customization made results inconsistent. As described in 2018, Tricorder temporarily disables an analyzer when its 'Not useful' vs 'Please fix' click ratio exceeds 10%, until the authors improve it.

findings.claim: Hilton et al. (ASE 2018; 7,816 builds of 47 projects) show that whole-project coverage hides per-change effects. In a 1-million-line project, a 100-line coverage change moves the total by one hundredth of a percentage point. Patch coverage did not correlate with overall coverage (Kendall tau r = -0.01). Patches often changed the coverage of unchanged code.

sources.title: Hilton, Bell, Marinov, A Large-Scale Study of Test Coverage Evolution, ASE 2018, doi:10.1145/3238147.3238183
sources.quote: a change in coverage of even 100 lines would only impact coverage by one hundredth of one percentage point

sources.title: Hilton et al., ASE 2018, RQ2 finding
sources.quote: Patches often impact coverage of existing (nonpatch) code, and high patch coverage does not correlate with increasing non-patch coverage.

findings.relevance: This directly supports Malte's locality concern (a bad change barely moves a global average). It also shows that a change score needs both a patch component and an impact-on-unchanged-code component.

verdict.evidence: Opened jonbell.net/publications/coverage (PDF, ASE 2018). '7,816 builds of 47 projects'. 'for a project with 1 million lines of code, a change in coverage of even 100 lines would only impact coverage by one hundredth of one percentage point'. Kendall tau between patch and overall coverage: 'no correlation between the two variables [r=-0.01,p<0.01]'. 'Finding: Patches often impact coverage of existing (nonpatch) code, and high patch coverage does not correlate with increasing non-patch coverage.' Nuance: the 1M-line figure is illustrative arithmetic, not a measured result. The paper also notes small changes 'can add up over time'.

findings.claim: In open-source repositories with at least 500 stars, merged agent PRs got verified follow-up fixes at 1.62 times the odds of merged human PRs (6,774 agent PRs, 5,044 human PRs). Holding repository and PR size fixed, a PR with ten times the commits had 6.1 times the odds of a fix, and ten times the churn had 1.3 times the odds. Separately, in 1,210 merged agent bug-fix PRs, differences in SonarQube issue counts between agents largely disappeared after normalizing by churn.

sources.title: Takerngsaksiri, Duong, Barnett, Who Finishes the Job? A Study of Follow-Up Fixes and Commit Authorship on AI Coding Agent Pull Requests, arXiv 2609.26847v2
sources.quote: a merge with ten times the commits carries 6.1 times the odds of a verified fix

sources.title: Cynthia, Muttakin, Roy, Beyond Bug Fixes: Post-Merge Code Quality Issues in Agent-Generated Pull Requests, MSR '26, arXiv 2601.20109
sources.quote: apparent differences in raw issue counts across agents largely disappear after normalizing by code churn, indicating that higher issue counts are primarily driven by larger PRs

findings.relevance: Size and rework features still carry signal for agent-authored PRs. These are preprint and MSR short-paper results on GitHub data.

verdict.evidence: Opened arXiv 2609.26847 (v2, 24 Sep 2026). The study follows 6,774 agent and 5,044 human PRs. The 1.62 odds ratio, however, comes from a within-repository comparison on the shared observation window: 'AI agents 2,012 ... Humans 4,063 ... Odds ratio, within repositories (218 strata) ... 1.62 [1.10-2.39]', with a 30-day fix window. RQ4 models agent merges only, with repository and 'number of non-boilerplate files shipped' held fixed: 'ten times the commits ... 6.1 times the odds ... churn carry 1.3 times (p < 0.001)'. The churn signal is 'post-first-push churn', i.e. rework after the first push, not total PR churn. Review items gave 2.4x. Pooled distributions were 'nearly identical (all effects negligible to small)'. Opened arXiv 2601.20109 (MSR '26; replication repo named MSR-Mining-2026). Quote matches, and the sample is '1,210 merged agent-generated bug-fix PRs from Python repositories'.
verdict.corrected_claim: In open-source repositories with at least 500 stars (AIDev-pop), within the same repositories and a shared window, merged agent PRs got verified follow-up fixes within 30 days at 1.62 times the odds of merged human PRs (95% CI 1.10-2.39; 2,012 agent vs 4,063 human PRs, drawn from 6,774 agent and 5,044 human PRs overall). Among agent PRs, with repository and number of non-boilerplate files fixed, ten times the commits gave 6.1 times the odds of a fix, and ten times the post-first-push churn (rework) gave 1.3 times. Separately, in 1,210 merged agent bug-fix PRs from Python repositories (MSR '26 mining-challenge paper), differences in SonarQube issue counts between agents largely disappeared after normalizing by churn.

findings.claim: Inference: for agent-authored PRs, Geiger can still use change size, diffusion (files, subsystems, entropy), file history (age, past fixes, past developers) and PR rework (commits per PR). Author-experience and ownership features lose their meaning when the author is an agent. This rests on Kamei (jit-1) and McIntosh (jit-3) on stable features, Fan (jit-4) on NF robustness, and agent-1 on size and rework predicting fixes. Meta's logistic regression includes author experience (meta-1), and no study I found tests JIT experience features on agent authors.

sources.title: McIntosh & Kamei, TSE 2018
sources.quote: the role that code change properties (e.g., Size, Experience) play within JIT models fluctuates over time

sources.title: Abreu et al., arXiv 2410.06351
sources.quote: how much experience author had modifying the changed code previously

findings.relevance: This decides which features a Geiger change-risk term can use for agent PRs.

verdict.evidence: McIntosh & Kamei TSE (rebels.cs.uwaterloo.ca PDF) quote matches. The paper says 'The Size family is a consistent top-contributor' but that the magnitude of family importance fluctuates, and recommends retraining within three months. So it supports Size as consistently important, not 'stable features' in general. The Abreu et al. arXiv 2410.06351 quote matches: it describes predictor clusters in Meta's LR model, including author experience. Agent-1 (2609.26847) supports rework signals (commits per PR, post-first-push churn) with file count held fixed. It does not show raw change size predicting fixes, and pooled signal differences were negligible to small. An extended search found no JIT study testing experience features on agent authors; the closest work (e.g. arXiv 2601.00753) predicts review effort, not defects. That experience features 'lose their meaning' for agents is an untested hypothesis. The operator's or agent's own history could stand in for them. jit-1 and jit-4 were not provided, so I could not check them.
verdict.corrected_claim: Inference: for agent-authored PRs, Geiger can reasonably use change size and diffusion, file history, and PR rework (commits per PR, post-first-push churn). Size is the most consistent JIT contributor (McIntosh & Kamei), though feature importance drifts and models need recent retraining. For agent PRs, the evidence is for rework signals, not raw size. Author-experience and ownership features are untested on agent authors and may need redefining, e.g. as agent or operator history, rather than being dropped outright. Meta's LR model includes author experience.

findings.claim: Inference: the outcome evidence supports a change-scoped score that is delivered at diff time, actionable and clearable, and low-noise. It does not show that scoring changes, rather than the whole codebase, reduces later defects. JIT models predict defect-inducing changes moderately well (jit-1, jit-6). Delivery mode decides whether anyone acts: compare fb-1 and goog-2 with goog-1. Meta's deployments report throughput gains, with safety outcomes that are only observational (meta-2, meta-3). I found no controlled study in which per-change quality budgets, like Geiger's -0.2 points per PR, reduced defects.

sources.title: Adams et al., arXiv 2605.30208, Section 6.2 Construct Validity
sources.quote: Time to close and diff review wall time capture responsiveness and queueing effects but do not directly measure defect prevention or long-term maintainability.

sources.title: Liu et al., arXiv 2607.02782, Limitations
sources.quote: we have not yet measured downstream outcomes such as reduced time-to-resolution or reduced post-landing incident rates

findings.relevance: This sets what Geiger can claim: change-level scoring is well motivated, but that it prevents defects is unproven and would need Geiger's own evaluation.

verdict.evidence: Both quotes verified: 2605.30208 Sec 6.2 ('do not directly measure defect prevention or long-term maintainability') and 2607.02782 Sec 6 ('we have not yet measured downstream outcomes...'). The core conclusion follows: no evidence that change-scoped scoring reduces defects; a search for controlled studies of new-code quality gates found only vendor docs (SonarSource 'Clean as You Code'). One sentence overreaches: 'Delivery mode decides whether anyone acts: compare fb-1 and goog-2 with goog-1.' In goog-1 the flag was already delivered at review time and still failed; the authors blame non-actionability. In goog-2 a diff-time integration was also discontinued, over false positives and customization. Diff-time delivery is therefore necessary but not sufficient, and all three are observational first-party anecdotes. meta-2, jit-1 and jit-6 were not provided, so I could not check them.
verdict.corrected_claim: Inference: the outcome evidence, all observational and mostly first-party anecdotes, supports a change-scoped score that is delivered at diff time, actionable and clearable, and low-noise. Diff-time delivery helped Infer (fb-1). The goog-1 and goog-2 failures show it is not sufficient without actionability and low false positives. None of this shows that scoring changes, rather than the whole codebase, reduces later defects. Meta's deployments report throughput gains, with safety outcomes that are observational and confounded by selection. No controlled study was found in which per-change quality budgets, like Geiger's -0.2 points per PR, reduced defects.
