open_questions: Do JIT features such as size, diffusion and file history keep their predictive power on Rust Cargo workspaces and Godot game code? No Rust JIT dataset was found.

Does a code-quality delta, such as complexity or architecture violations added by a PR, add predictive power beyond size and diffusion in JIT models? None of the sources tests maintainability metrics as JIT predictors.
How should Geiger handle verification latency (labels arriving weeks after an agent PR) and model drift (retrain within three months) if it calibrates weights against defects?
Is Meta's 1/50 production-incident rate for RADAR diffs explained by selecting low-risk diffs? The paper provides no causal estimate.
Exact size of Liu et al.'s expert-labeled outage set: the percentages imply a few dozen diffs, but the paper does not state the count.
Would hunk-level risk highlights help agents, as opposed to human reviewers, fix code? No study tests this.

areas.title: Has any repository- or system-level aggregate score (SIG star rating, Quamoco grade, SonarQube debt ratio, CodeScene average Code Health) been validated against maintenance outcomes at project level? Which aggregation from function to file to repository (sum, mean, max or percentile, inequality indices, risk profiles, several combined) preserves predictive signal, and how sensitive are the resulting rankings to the weights?
areas.summary_before_verification: Short answer: almost none of this has been validated, and what exists is small. Only four repository-level outcome validations were found, and each covers 4 to 10 systems. SIG's maintainability rating correlated with defect resolution speed across 10 open-source projects and 107 snapshots (Spearman 0.62 in 2010, 0.64 in the 2012 journal version). A 2019 replication with SIG's recalibrated 2018 model cut that correlation to 0.33, even though the base metrics kept their correlations. So the aggregation layer, not the measurements, decided most of the outcome signal. Quamoco's grade ranked 5 Java systems close to a 9-expert ranking (rho = 0.9, p = 0.05), and Bakota et al. fit an exponential maintainability-cost relation on 5 systems. In the one controlled study (4 functionally equivalent systems, 6 developers), Sjøberg et al. found the maintainability surrogates mutually inconsistent, and only size and low cohesion tracked effort. Different aggregate models also disagree with each other: Quamoco and SQALE showed zero agreement (Cohen's kappa = 0.0) on 20 C# projects. No validation of CodeScene average Code Health or SonarQube debt ratio at project level was found. The CodeScene evidence is file-level and vendor-authored, and it names project-level extrapolation as future work. At file level, SonarQube's size-normalised TD Ratio did much worse (AUC 0.60) than its absolute TD Time (0.86) and a plain line-count baseline (0.95). No study compares mean, max, percentile, Theil and risk-profile aggregation against project-level outcomes. The file-level studies disagree: Zhang et al. (255 projects) favour using several aggregators together, or the mean/median for effort-aware ranking, while a smaller preprint favours the sum. Inequality indices largely carry the same information as one another (Vasilescu 2011), and the max correlates with defects about as well as the sum (Zimmermann 2007). On weights, Dawes (1979) shows that validity against an outcome is robust to weight changes as long as each weight keeps its sign. Composite-indicator research shows that rankings and threshold decisions near the top still move with weights and aggregation method. Inference for Geiger: treat the repository score as a convention, not a validated health measure. Expect user weights to keep overall validity but flip marginal PR pass/fail decisions near a 0.2-point budget, and validate locally.

findings.claim: Luijten and Visser (SQM 2010) found that SIG's aggregate maintainability rating had Spearman rho = 0.62 with a defect-resolution-speed rating. The data covered 10 open-source projects, 107 snapshots and about 9,000 closed defects. Sub-characteristics (0.41-0.64) and maintainability correlated more strongly than most base properties (volume 0.29, duplication 0.31, unit size/complexity/coupling 0.51). Team size and popularity were not measured, and snapshots of the same system were treated as independent.

sources.title: Luijten, Visser: Faster Defect Resolution with Higher Technical Quality of Software (SQM 2010)
sources.quote: Maintainability is correlated to defect resolution time with one of the highest factors of all (0.62), showing again the reinforcing effect of aggregation in the model.

sources.title: Luijten, Visser: Faster Defect Resolution with Higher Technical Quality of Software (SQM 2010)
sources.quote: We did not measure some aspects of software projects that could have an influence on the issue handling process, such as team size or project popularity.

findings.relevance: This is the strongest repository-level outcome validation of a star-style aggregate. It is still observational, rank-based, on 10 Java-heavy OSS projects, and not adjusted for confounders.

verdict.evidence: Opened the SQM 2010 PDF (saved at .local/geiger-research/sources/aggregation-check/sqm2010.pdf). Both quotes are present verbatim. Table II gives volume 0.29, duplication 0.31, unit size, unit complexity and module coupling 0.51 each, unit interfacing -0.14 (p=0.897, not significant), analysability 0.51, changeability 0.64, stability 0.41, testability 0.53, maintainability 0.62. Table I lists '107' total snapshots and '89' selected, and '9,192' selected defects. The threats section says 'multiple snapshots of the same system might be regarded as independent data points since they are separated in time'. It also says 'Most projects in our study have Java as the main programming language.' Corrections: (a) the correlations used 89 of the 107 snapshots; (b) maintainability (0.62) is not the top value, since changeability is 0.64; (c) stability (0.41) is lower than the unit-level properties (0.51), so 'sub-characteristics correlated more strongly than most base properties' holds only against volume and duplication; (d) unit interfacing was -0.14 and not significant, and the claim leaves it out. Independent check: SIG's 2026 model-changes doc (raw.githubusercontent.com/Software-Improvement-Group/sigridci/main/docs/reference/quality-model-documents/2026-model-changes.md) says 'The Volume system property has been removed from the maintainability model.' The validated 2010 model therefore no longer matches the current Sigrid model.
verdict.corrected_claim: Luijten and Visser (SQM 2010) report Spearman rho = 0.62 (one-sided, p<0.001) between SIG's aggregate maintainability rating and a defect-resolution-speed rating. The data covered 10 mostly-Java OSS projects, 89 selected snapshots (of 107 collected) and 9,192 closed or resolved defects. Sub-characteristics ranged from 0.41 (stability) to 0.64 (changeability), so maintainability was not the highest value. Base properties were volume 0.29, duplication 0.31, and unit size/complexity/module coupling 0.51; unit interfacing was -0.14 and not significant. Team size and popularity were not measured, and snapshots of the same system were treated as independent data points.

findings.claim: A 2019 replication (Wijnmaalen, Chen, Bijlsma, Oprescu; SIG co-authors) re-scored the Bijlsma et al. 2012 systems with SIG's 2018 model. The maintainability-to-defect-resolution correlation fell from 0.64 to 0.33, and for enhancements from 0.53 to 0.47. The base system properties kept similar correlations. The authors blame the new modularity properties: component balance correlated -0.34 with defect resolution. The aggregation and weighting layer therefore changed most of the outcome signal, while the measurements kept theirs.

sources.title: Wijnmaalen et al.: The Relation between Software Maintainability and Issue Resolution Time: A Replication Study (SATToSE 2019)
sources.quote: The overall maintainability correlation with defect resolution time decreased significantly while the original system properties correlate similar with defect resolution time

sources.title: Wijnmaalen et al.: The Relation between Software Maintainability and Issue Resolution Time: A Replication Study (SATToSE 2019)
sources.quote: The other surprising result is the large drop of maintainability from 0.64 to 0.33.

findings.relevance: This is direct evidence that changing how components are combined, which is what user-tuned weights do, can halve the outcome validity of a repository score.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-2510/sattose2019_paper_11.pdf. Both quotes are verbatim. Table 5 gives defect maintainability 0.64 -> 0.33 and component balance -0.34 (p=0.001); Table 6 gives enhancement maintainability 0.53 -> 0.47. Co-authors Chen and Bijlsma are listed as SIG. Problems with the claim: (1) Not all base properties kept similar correlations. The authors write 'except for module coupling which shows a significant drop from 0.55 to 0.36', and unit interfacing went from 0.19 (p=0.042) to 0.05 (p=0.640). (2) The 2018 model did more than reweight. It added new measurements (component balance, component independence) and new sub-characteristics (modularity, reusability), and it used stricter yearly-recalibrated thresholds. The paper says 'the added maintainability sub-characteristic modularity with its system properties component balance and component independence are the biggest causing factor'. So 'aggregation/weighting changed the signal while the measurements kept theirs' is overstated: new measures with negative correlations entered the aggregate. (3) Snapshots were 'reacquired (with small deviations)'; Webkit had about 500 KLOC less. The component-depth setting followed 'our own interpretation'. The venue is a SATToSE seminar paper.
verdict.corrected_claim: A 2019 SATToSE replication (Wijnmaalen, Chen, Bijlsma, Oprescu; Chen and Bijlsma at SIG) re-scored reacquired snapshots of the Bijlsma et al. 2012 systems with SIG's 2018 model. The maintainability-to-defect-resolution correlation fell from 0.64 to 0.33, and for enhancements from 0.53 to 0.47. Most original system properties kept similar correlations, but module coupling fell from 0.55 to 0.36 and unit interfacing became non-significant. The authors attribute the drop mainly to the newly added modularity sub-characteristic and its new system properties: component balance correlated -0.34 and modularity -0.30 with defect resolution. A model revision that adds new measures to the aggregate and recalibrates thresholds can therefore halve the outcome correlation of the composite. This is not evidence about reweighting fixed measures.

findings.claim: SIG ratings are benchmark-relative and recalibrated every year. The 4-star unit-complexity threshold moved from 24.3% (2017) to 21.1% (2018) of code in units with McCabe above 5, so unchanged code receives a lower rating.

sources.title: Wijnmaalen et al.: replication study (SATToSE 2019)
sources.quote: SIG calibrates the thresholds for all ratings (both systemproperties and characteristics) yearly.

findings.relevance: A benchmark-relative score drifts without any code change. Geiger's 0.2-point-per-PR budget requires frozen thresholds and weights per baseline.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-2510/sattose2019_paper_11.pdf. The quote 'SIG calibrates the thresholds for all ratings (both systemproperties and characteristics) yearly' is present. The paper cites the 2018 Guidance for Producers: 'should not exceed 21.1%' [Vis18], and says 2017 had 'a threshold of 24.3%' [Vis17]. It adds 'Remeasuring the same systems again with the stricter benchmark thresholds results in overall lower maintainability scores.' Independent, newer source: SIG's own 2026 model-changes doc (raw.githubusercontent.com/Software-Improvement-Group/sigridci/main/docs/reference/quality-model-documents/2026-model-changes.md) says 'the metrics are recalibrated yearly to reflect the current state.' The same doc notes that users can pin the model version in scope configuration, so their systems 'will not automatically migrate', which supports the frozen-baseline inference. Caveat: unchanged code gets a lower rating only when thresholds tighten, which is typical but not guaranteed every year.

findings.claim: Quamoco's section 7 validation compared the base-model grades of 5 open-source Java systems with the Linzer Software-Verkostung ranking by 9 experts (Kendall's W = 0.6635). It found Spearman rho = 0.9 (p = 0.05), with two adjacent systems swapped. A second study showed grades improving over 4 versions (3.63 to 3.17) of one industrial system. The authors did not test whether fewer measures or other weights would give the same ranking.

sources.title: Wagner et al.: Operationalised product quality models and assessment: The Quamoco approach (IST 2015), local copy .local/geiger-research/sources/aggregation/quamoco2015.txt, section 7
sources.quote: Although the base model did not provide exactly the same ranking as the experts, the calculated Spearman’s rho correlation is r = 0.9

sources.title: Wagner et al.: Quamoco (IST 2015), section 7.1.4
sources.quote: We did not explicitly test whether the same results could be obtained with a smaller number of measures or product factors

findings.relevance: This is the only Quamoco evidence against an external criterion. The criterion is expert opinion rather than maintenance outcomes, n = 5, and weight sensitivity was not tested.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://arxiv.org/pdf/1611.09230 (saved at aggregation-check/quamoco.pdf). Section 7.1.3 quote verbatim: 'the calculated Spearman's rho correlation is r = 0.9'. The section says the hypothesis is accepted 'with a p-value of 0.05' and that two systems' 'places are switched'. Table 5 shows Log4j and RSSOwl swapped. Section 7.1.5 gives 'Kendall's W concordance coefficient, we get a value of 0.6635' and 'nine experts' over five Java systems. Section 7.2 Table 6 gives grades 3.63, 3.42, 3.27, 3.17 over 4 versions of one industrial (steel automation) system; lower is better. The 7.1.4 quote is verbatim, but the paper says 'measures or product factors', not weights. A grep for 'sensitiv' and 'robust' found no weight-sensitivity analysis, so 'did not test other weights' holds by absence.

findings.claim: Griffith, Izurieta and Huvaere (ESEM 2017) compared Quamoco and SQALE assessments of 20 C# projects (open source and US Army Corps of Engineers commercial). They found Cohen's kappa = 0.0 for maintainability, reliability and security, and Goodman-Kruskal gamma confidence intervals that include 0.

sources.title: Griffith, Izurieta, Huvaere: An Industry Perspective to Comparing the SQALE and Quamoco Software Quality Models (ESEM 2017)
sources.quote: The results of the Cohen’s κ analysis strongly indicates there is no agreement between the Quamoco and SQALE models in any of the three quality characteristics

findings.relevance: Two established aggregate models do not agree on which projects are good. A single repository number is a modelling convention unless it is validated against outcomes.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/ESEM_2017.pdf. The quote is verbatim (section V). Table IV gives kappa 0.0 for maintainability, reliability and security, and gamma 0.032 (CI -0.275, 0.327), -0.074 (-0.3411, 0.194), 0.038 (-0.238, 0.358). The paper says 'the 95% confidence interval for each characteristic includes 0.0'. The 20 projects are 18 random GitHub C# OSS projects plus 2 US Army Corps of Engineers CERL systems (SMS Outcome, SMS Fueler). Caveats the claim omits: SonarQube 5.6.5 was used, and the paper notes some agreement when both models give an A grade (Bangdiwala B).

findings.claim: Sjøberg, Anda and Mockus (ESEM 2012) studied 4 functionally equivalent Java systems built by different companies, on which 6 developers did 3 maintenance tasks each. The Maintainability Index, structural metrics and code smells were mutually inconsistent at system level. Only system size and low cohesion tracked effort, while 1/MI, OMMIC and Feature Envy correlated negatively with effort.

sources.title: Sjøberg, Anda, Mockus: Questioning Software Maintenance Metrics: A Comparative Case Study (ESEM 2012)
sources.quote: Results: The metrics were not mutually consistent. Only system size and low cohesion were strongly associated with increased maintenance effort.

sources.title: Sjøberg, Anda, Mockus (ESEM 2012)
sources.quote: at the entire system level, the simplest metric of size was the best predictor of maintainability.

findings.relevance: This is the only controlled system-level comparison found (same requirements, measured effort). The result is negative for composite surrogates and points to size as the confounder that any repository score must handle.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://www.mn.uio.no/ifi/personer/vit/dagsj/sjoberg.anda.mockus.esem.2012.pdf. Both quotes are verbatim (abstract; conclusion 'at the entire system level, the simplest metric of size was the best predictor of maintainability.'). Body: 'The only two metrics that are highly correlated with effort are size and the inverse of cohesion (1/TCC)... Three of them, 1/MI, OMMIC and FE, have a high negative correlation.' Minor detail: each of the 6 developers did the same 3 tasks on two of the four systems, so each system was maintained 3 times. The authors also note that 'having only four sample points' limits the analysis.

findings.claim: Borg, Ezzouhri and Tornhill (CodeScene; arXiv Aug 2024, ICSME 2024) benchmarked tools against Schnappinger et al.'s expert-labelled MainData. The dataset holds 519 files, 78% labelled maintainable, with experts disagreeing substantially on 17%. Code Health (AUC 0.95) matched state-of-the-art ML (0.97) and a line-count-only baseline (0.95). SonarQube's size-normalised TD Ratio scored AUC 0.60 and F1 0.12 at finding unmaintainable files, against 0.86 for its absolute TD Time. All of this is file-level.

sources.title: Borg, Ezzouhri, Tornhill: Ghost Echoes Revealed: Benchmarking Maintainability Metrics and Machine Learning Predictions Against Human Assessments
sources.quote: SotA ML (A), Code Health (B), and the LoC baseline (C) reach about 0.95. TD Time (E) and MS-MI (D) yield about 0.90. TD Ratio performs the worst

sources.title: Borg, Ezzouhri, Tornhill (2024)
sources.quote: maintainability prediction of source code files, Schnappinger et al. (2020) presented a manually annotated Maintainability Dataset (MainData) containing 519 files

findings.relevance: The Schnappinger dataset cannot validate a repository score because its labels are per file. Dividing debt by size, as SonarQube's debt ratio does, discarded most of the signal here. Any Geiger metric must beat a line-count baseline.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://arxiv.org/pdf/2408.10754 (v1, 20 Aug 2024). Both quotes are verbatim. MainData has 519 files, 'imbalanced with 78% maintainable files', and 'For 17% of the source code files, the experts disagreed substantially.' Table I AUC: SotA ML 0.97, Code Health 0.95, LoC 0.95, MS-MI 0.89, TD Time 0.86, average human expert 0.83, TD Ratio 0.60. UC2 (liability) F1: TD Ratio 0.12, TD Time 0.60, Code Health 0.83. The 0.86 is TD Time's AUC, not an F1. As written, the claim reads as if 0.86 were TD Time's F1 for unmaintainable files. The venue was confirmed on the researchr ICSME 2024 page as 'Industry Track Paper'. All three authors are CodeScene employees or affiliates, which is a vendor conflict of interest.
verdict.corrected_claim: Borg, Ezzouhri and Tornhill (CodeScene; arXiv 20 Aug 2024; ICSME 2024 Industry Track) benchmarked tools against Schnappinger et al.'s expert-labelled MainData. The dataset holds 519 Java files, 78% labelled maintainable, with experts disagreeing substantially on 17%. AUC was Code Health 0.95, state-of-the-art ML 0.97 and a line-count-only baseline 0.95. SonarQube's size-normalised TD Ratio scored AUC 0.60, and F1 0.12 at flagging unmaintainable files. Its absolute TD Time scored AUC 0.86, and F1 0.60 on the same task. All results are file-level, and the authors are from the vendor of the winning tool.

findings.claim: Borg et al. (CodeScene, arXiv Jan 2024) built their Code Health value model from file-level regressions only. They call project-level extrapolation future work and warn that a plain average is inflated by many small, healthy files. They propose a size-weighted average over high-churn files instead, but did not test it.

sources.title: Borg et al.: Increasing, not Diminishing: Investigating the Returns of Highly Maintainable Code
sources.quote: a project with numerous small, high-quality files would display an inflated average CH.

sources.title: Borg et al.: Increasing, not Diminishing
sources.quote: Extrapolating file-level results to project-wide averages is an important research direction.

findings.relevance: This confirms that no project-level outcome validation exists for average Code Health, and that the vendor's own preferred aggregation (churn-filtered, size-weighted) is untested.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.13407 (v1, 24 Jan 2024). Both quotes are verbatim (section 5.2). 'Our value creation model is based on file-level regression models.' The paper proposes 'A weighted CH average of files that at a given point in time have a relatively high level of churn would likely be a better option. We plan to explore this ... in future work.' Nuance: it adds 'the initial feedback from pilot runs has been positive.' That is informal pilot feedback, not a test against outcomes, so 'did not test it' stands.

findings.claim: Borg, Udayakumar and Tornhill (arXiv Dec 2024) analysed more than 1,000 proprietary projects. The size-weighted average Code Health had a mode of 9.5 and a 10th-percentile ('laggard') threshold of 5.9. Hotspot Code Health has a heavier low tail (laggard threshold 4.1). Counting each project equally versus weighting by project size changes the distributions markedly. No outcome data was used.

sources.title: Borg, Udayakumar, Tornhill: Industrial Code Quality Benchmarks: Toward Gamification of Software Maintainability
sources.quote: Due to the dominant probability mass around high scores, the leaderboard positions around the leaders might appear volatile. That is, small CodeHealth changes might cause big moves.

findings.relevance: Most projects sit near the top of the scale, which matches Geiger's template at 98/100. Near the ceiling, small score changes and choices of aggregation (raw, size-weighted, hotspot) dominate rank and pass/fail outcomes.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.06307 (v1, 9 Dec 2024; 'preliminary work'). The quote is verbatim. The paper analyses 'roughly 1,000 projects' and says 'a vast majority of projects are in the interval above 8 with a mode at 9.5 ... the laggards threshold can be seen at 5.9'; for hotspots, 'The laggard threshold is found at 4.1'. The paper also says 'The size-weighted blue curve in the figure shows a contrasting distribution'. Clarification: each project's average Code Health is SLoC-weighted across its files, but the mode 9.5 and thresholds 5.9 and 4.1 come from the raw distribution, where each project counts equally. They do not come from the project-size-weighted (blue) curve. No outcome data was used. The sample is CodeScene customers with at least 10 employees, and sampling details are undisclosed.

findings.claim: Zhang, Hassan, McIntosh and Zou (TSE, May 2017) studied 255 open-source projects and 11 method-to-file aggregation schemes (sum, mean, median, SD, CoV, Gini, Hoover, Atkinson, Shannon, generalised entropy, Theil). Sum alone gave the best defect-proneness model in 11% of projects and all schemes together in 40%. Mean (69%) and median (71%) were best for effort-aware ranking, and sum was adequate for predicting defect count or rank. Max and percentiles were not studied.

sources.title: Zhang, Hassan, McIntosh, Zou: The Use of Summation to Aggregate Software Metrics Hinders the Performance of Defect Prediction Models (TSE 43(5))
sources.quote: when constructing models for effort-aware defect prediction, the mean or median aggregation schemes yield performance values that are significantly closer to the best performance than any of the other studied aggregation schemes.

findings.relevance: This is the largest comparison of aggregators against outcomes. It is file-level, not repository-level. No single aggregator wins, and combining several preserves the most signal, which supports a multi-statistic profile over one mean.

verdict.evidence: Opened the SAIL PDF (TSE 43(5), May 2017, pp. 476-). The abstract quote is verbatim. It reports '11 aggregation schemes using data collected from 255 open source projects', summation alone best for defect proneness in 11%, and all schemes in 40%. Table 8 effort-aware: Mean 176 (69%), Median 180 (71%), Sum 79 (31%), All schemes 42 (16%); defect count: Sum 253 (99%), All 248 (97%); rank: Sum 56%, All 60%. Section 3.6 excludes only skewness, kurtosis and Kolm, and max and percentiles are absent from the 11 schemes. Caveat on the relevance note: 'combining several preserves the most signal' holds for defect proneness. It does not hold for effort-aware ranking, where all schemes together were best in only 16% of projects.

findings.claim: An unreviewed single-author preprint (Abou Assi, Queen's, 2015) on 12 releases of Eclipse, Ant and jEdit found the opposite. Sum-aggregated models beat the other aggregations, and adding all aggregation types gave no significant gain over sum.

sources.title: Abou Assi: Investigating the Impact of Metric Aggregation Techniques on Defect Prediction
sources.quote: Our results show that defect prediction models built using summation outperform those built using other aggregation techniques.

findings.relevance: This is conflicting evidence on a much smaller sample. Which aggregator is best depends on the dataset and the outcome, so Geiger should not claim one aggregator is validated.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.08504 and the PDF (saved under .local/geiger-research/sources/agg-fc/abou.pdf). The paper is single-author, from the School of Computing, Queen's University, submitted 29 Mar 2015 and listed only on arXiv/CoRR. It studies 12 releases (Eclipse 2.0-3.0, Ant 1.3-1.7, jEdit 4.0-4.3). The quote appears verbatim. Abstract: 'incorporating all aggregation types in the same model does not provide a significant improvement over using summation alone.' The tests are more nuanced. Table 8 shows All-vs-Sum MSE differences of p<0.001 on all 12 datasets, with negligible-to-small Cliff's d, and the differences point in both directions: 'the difference between the two sets of MSE values is statistically significant for all datasets. However, the effect size is negligible for most'. Section 5.1: 'We also applied aggregation at the file level only.' I could not check what 'the opposite' refers to, because the prior finding is not in this claim.
verdict.corrected_claim: An arXiv-only, single-author preprint (Rawad Abou Assi, Queen's University, 2015) aggregated method-level LOC, McCabe and Halstead metrics to file level in 12 releases of Eclipse, Ant and jEdit. Sum-aggregated models generally beat the other eight aggregations. A model with all aggregations gave no meaningful gain over sum. The differences were often statistically significant, but effect sizes were negligible to small and pointed in both directions. Aggregation was to file level only, never to package or repository level.

findings.claim: Vasilescu, Serebrenik and van den Brand (ICSM 2011) lifted SLOC from class to package level across the 106 Qualitas Corpus systems. Gini, Theil, Atkinson and Hoover were highly and significantly correlated, so choosing among inequality indices adds little information. No outcome variable was used.

sources.title: Vasilescu, Serebrenik, van den Brand: You can't control the unfamiliar: A study on the relations between aggregation techniques for software metrics (ICSM 2011), abstract
sources.quote: Our results indicate high and statistically significant correlation between the Gini, Theil, Atkinson, and Hoover indices, i.e., aggregation values obtained using these techniques convey the same information.

findings.relevance: This partly answers the earlier open question on Theil versus means. One inequality index is enough, but no study shows any inequality index tracks repository-level outcomes better than a LOC-weighted mean.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://research.tue.nl/en/publications/3bd12134-da86-489f-9f3d-ebeeb9fe7781. The abstract contains the quote verbatim. It describes 'an extensive correlation study of the most widely-used traditional and econometric aggregation techniques, applied to lifting SLOC values from class to package level in the 106 systems comprising the Qualitas Corpus', with evolution studied on 12 systems. The design correlates aggregation techniques with each other and names no outcome variable. Caveats: Kolm is not in the highly correlated group, and the authors 'discuss some of the rationale behind choosing between one index or another.' I could not open the full text, so 'no outcome variable' rests on the abstract.

findings.claim: In Eclipse 2.0-3.0 (Zimmermann, Premraj, Zeller, PROMISE 2007), maximum-aggregated metrics correlated with post-release defects at file and package level about as well as summed metrics. Examples: nested block depth max .483 vs sum .464, cyclomatic complexity max .451.

sources.title: Zimmermann, Premraj, Zeller: Predicting Defects for Eclipse (PROMISE 2007)
sources.quote: many cases the maximum metrics (_max) show correlation values comparable to the accumulated ones (except for PAR_max).

findings.relevance: Worst-case (max) aggregation keeps defect signal comparable to sum, so a max- or tail-based local gate is not obviously worse than a total. Evidence is from one project and correlations only.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://thomas-zimmermann.com/publications/files/zimmermann-promise-2007.pdf. The quote appears verbatim. Table 3 covers release 3.0 only ('Table 3 lists the correlation values for both, file and package level (release 3.0)') and gives separate columns for pre- and post-release defects. The cited .483 (NBD_max) and .464 (NBD_sum) are package-level correlations with PRE-release defects. For post-release defects at package level: NBD_max .467 vs NBD_sum .404, and VG_max .451 vs VG_sum .431. At file level, post-release: NBD_max .383 vs NBD_sum .392, and VG_max .385 vs VG_sum .401. All are Spearman correlations.
verdict.corrected_claim: In Eclipse release 3.0 (Zimmermann, Premraj, Zeller, PROMISE 2007), maximum-aggregated metrics often correlated with defects about as well as summed metrics; PAR_max was the exception. Post-release Spearman correlations at package level: nested block depth max .467 vs sum .404; cyclomatic complexity max .451 vs sum .431. At file level, max was slightly below sum (NBD .383 vs .392, VG .385 vs .401). The .483/.464 pair is for pre-release defects. The correlations cover one release, not 2.0-3.0.

findings.claim: Posnett, Filkov and Devanbu (ASE 2011) used defect and process data from 18 OSS projects to show the ecological-inference risk. Relations found at one aggregation level (file, package, module) can be misleading at another.

sources.title: Posnett, Filkov, Devanbu: Ecological inference in empirical software engineering (ASE 2011), abstract via OpenAlex
sources.quote: In other fields it has been found that choosing the wrong level might lead to misleading or fallacious results.

findings.relevance: File-level validations (Code Health, Zhang et al.) do not carry over to a repository average by default. A repository-level claim needs repository-level evidence.

verdict.evidence: Opened the OpenAlex record https://api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.1109/ASE.2011.6100074 and reconstructed the abstract. It contains the quote verbatim and states: 'using defect and process data from 18 open source projects to illustrate the risks of modeling at an aggregation level in the context of defect prediction, as well as in hypothesis testing.' Authors are Posnett, Filkov and Devanbu; ASE 2011, pp. 362-371, published November 2011.

findings.claim: Dawes (1979) showed that linear composites with non-optimal weights (equal, intuitive or random) predict a numerical criterion nearly as well as fitted weights, provided each weight has the correct sign and predictors are not negatively correlated (the 'flat maximum').

sources.title: Dawes: The robust beauty of improper linear models in decision making (American Psychologist 34(7))
sources.quote: In fact, unit (i.e., equal) weighting is quite robust for making such predictions.

sources.title: Dawes (1979)
sources.quote: The ways in which outputs are relatively insensitive to changes in coefficients (provided changes in sign are not involved)

findings.relevance: User-tuned weights are unlikely to destroy a score's overall correlation with outcomes if every component has the right sign. The 2019 SIG drop (agg-2) came from components with the wrong sign.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/dawes/the-robust-beauty-of-improper-linear-models-in-decision-making.pdf. Both quotes appear verbatim, as does 'Weights that are near to optimal level produce almost the same output as do optimal beta weights.' The non-negative intercorrelation condition is also there: 'as long as these intercorrelations are not negative'. Table 1 shows the random-weight claim is overstated. Random-weight models scored .30/.51/.51/.39 against cross-validated regression .46/.57/.57/.38 and optimal .46/.69/.69/.54. Random weights equalled the judges' models but often fell short of fitted weights. Equal weights (.34/.60/.60/.48) matched or beat cross-validated regression in 3 of 4 examples, but stayed below the optimal in-sample model. Dawes also requires standardized predictors ('Equal or random weighting of incomparable variables ... without prior standardization would be nonsensical') and conditionally monotone predictor-criterion relationships.
verdict.corrected_claim: Dawes (1979) showed that equal-weighted linear composites of standardized, correctly signed predictors predict a numerical criterion about as well as cross-validated regression weights; in 3 of 4 examples they did as well or better. They stay below the in-sample optimum, for example .60 vs .69. Random positive weights did only about as well as models of human judges and were often clearly below fitted weights (.30 vs .46 cross-validated). The 'flat maximum' covers near-optimal weights and requires predictors that are not negatively correlated.

findings.claim: The JRC's composite-indicator toolkit (Nardo, Saisana, Saltelli, Tarantola; EUR 21682, 2005) reports that weights and the aggregation method change unit rankings. With equal weights throughout, linear, geometric and multi-criteria aggregation of the Technology Achievement Index (23 countries) gave very different ranks, Finland placing 1st, 2nd and 3rd. Monte Carlo analysis gave an average shift of about 3 positions, up to 9.

sources.title: Nardo, Saisana, Saltelli, Tarantola: Tools for Composite Indicators Building (JRC EUR 21682)
sources.quote: Weights heavily influence the outcome of a composite indicator and countries ranking in a benchmarking exercise.

sources.title: Nardo et al. (JRC 2005)
sources.quote: Although in all cases we used equal weighting, rankings produced are very different.

findings.relevance: Weight changes leave population-level validity mostly intact (Dawes) but reorder individual units. A per-PR pass/fail threshold is a decision about one unit, so it is exposed to this.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://knowledge4policy.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/eur_21682_en_1.pdf (EUR 21682, 2005, Nardo, Saisana, Saltelli, Tarantola). Both quotes appear verbatim. Table 6.11 confirms Finland ranks 1 (LIN), 3 (MCA) and 2 (GME) across 23 countries. The uncertainty analysis varied more than weights. Its inputs were 'normalisation method, inclusion-exclusion of a sub-indicator, aggregation system, weighting scheme, expert selection'. The text says: 'The mean value is almost 3 positions ... The input factors affecting this variable the most are aggregation system plus inclusion – exclusion at the first order'. In Table 7.1 the weighting scheme has a first-order Sobol index of 0.038 and a total effect of 0.327, mostly through interactions. The 'up to 9' figure is an average shift across all countries, seen in some MCA runs: 'In some cases the average shift in country's rank when using MCA can be as high as 9 places.'
verdict.corrected_claim: The JRC toolkit (EUR 21682, 2005) says weights heavily influence composite rankings. With equal weights, linear, geometric and multi-criteria aggregation of the 23-country Technology Achievement Index ranked Finland 1st, 2nd and 3rd respectively. A Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis jointly varied normalisation, indicator inclusion, aggregation method, weighting scheme and expert selection. It produced a mean average rank shift of almost 3 positions, reaching 9 in some multi-criteria runs. Aggregation method and indicator inclusion drove most of the shift; weighting acted mainly through interactions (first-order Sobol 0.038).

findings.claim: Bakota et al. (ICSM 2012) related a system-level probabilistic maintainability score (Szeged group, ISO 9126/25010 based) to development cost on 3 proprietary and 2 open-source Java systems. They report an exponential maintainability-cost relationship and accurate cost prediction.

sources.title: Bakota et al.: A Cost Model Based on Software Maintainability (ICSM 2012), abstract
sources.quote: maintainability and development costs are in exponential relationship with each other. We also found that our model is able to predict future development costs with high accuracy

findings.relevance: This is another small (n = 5) repository-level outcome link, from the model's own authors. It supports the idea but not any particular aggregator or weights.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://www.inf.u-szeged.hu/~ferenc/publication/bhl12. The abstract contains the quote verbatim and says: 'We evaluated our model on three proprietary and two open source real world software systems implemented in Java'. Authors are Bakota, Hegedűs, Ladányi, Körtvélyesi, Ferenc and Gyimóthy (Szeged), ICSM 2012, pp. 316-325. The keywords include ISO/IEC 9126 and ISO/IEC 25000. The abstract does not say 'probabilistic'; that detail comes from the group's maintainability model, not this page.

findings.claim: Ulan, Löwe, Ericsson and Wingkvist (EMSE, June 2021) proposed setting metric weights without ground truth, using probability-based unsupervised weighting. Tested on about 200,000 code changes and 5,000 classes, it predicted defects about as well as supervised models. They note that expert weighting breaks down when metrics are interdependent.

sources.quote: The results show that our approach can be used as an agnostic unsupervised predictor in the absence of a ground truth.

findings.relevance: This offers a default weighting method for Geiger that needs no labelled outcomes. Only the abstract was read; the full text was blocked.

verdict.evidence: Opened the OpenAlex record https://api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.1007/s10664-021-09984-2 (published 2021-06-23, EMSE vol. 26, issue 5). The quote appears verbatim, as do 'one on ca. 200 000 code changes, and another ca. 5 000 software classes' and 'experts get confused if the metrics are not independent, which is rarely the case.' The abstract does not say the approach predicted defects about as well as supervised models. It says only that it 'can be used as an agnostic unsupervised predictor in the absence of a ground truth.' The full text (CC-BY, Springer and DiVA) was blocked by redirects and bot checks, so I could not verify any comparison with supervised models.
verdict.corrected_claim: Ulan, Löwe, Ericsson and Wingkvist (EMSE 26(5), published 23 June 2021) proposed unsupervised, probability-based weighted metrics aggregation. They evaluated it on defect prediction with about 200,000 code changes and about 5,000 classes. The abstract says it 'can be used as an agnostic unsupervised predictor in the absence of a ground truth.' It also says expert weighting does not scale and that experts get confused when metrics are not independent. Whether it matches supervised models is not stated in the abstract and remains unverified.

findings.claim: Inference: no repository-level aggregate (SIG stars, Quamoco grade, SQALE/SonarQube debt ratio, CodeScene average Code Health) has outcome validation beyond 4-10 systems. No study compares aggregators (mean, LOC-weighted mean, max, percentile, inequality index, risk profile) against repository-level maintenance outcomes. This rests on agg-1 to agg-14 and on the negative searches.

sources.quote: Previous research has shown that there is a positive correlation between the maintainability score measured by the SIG maintainability model and shorter issue resolution time.

findings.relevance: Geiger should present the repository score as a configurable convention and health signal, not as a validated predictor. Its strongest defensible claims are change-level (see the file and change evidence), not repository-level.

verdict.evidence: Opened https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-2510/sattose2019_paper_11.pdf. The quote appears verbatim. The original study 'assessed 10 open source systems looking at multiple snapshots', with 120 snapshots in Table 4. The negative claim is too broad as worded. Athanasiou, Nugroho, Visser and Zaidman (IEEE TSE 2014, DOI 10.1109/TSE.2014.2342227; abstract read via https://api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.1109/TSE.2014.2342227) validated a SIG-style, benchmark-based system-level test-code-quality rating against issue-handling outcomes: 'the test code quality model is applied to 18 open source systems'. Results: 'a significant positive correlation between test code quality and two out of the three issue handling metrics (throughput and productivity)'. That model is not one of the four named aggregates, so the restriction to those four may still hold. The web search budget ran out during this check. I could not independently re-run the negative searches for aggregator comparisons against repository-level outcomes, so that part stays unverified.
verdict.corrected_claim: Inference, limited to the named aggregates: none of SIG maintainability stars, Quamoco grade, SQALE/SonarQube debt ratio or CodeScene average Code Health has been validated against maintenance outcomes on more than about 10 systems. The largest found is the SIG model on 10 OSS systems (about 120 snapshots; Bijlsma/Luijten, replicated by Wijnmaalen et al. 2019). A related SIG-style system rating, the test code quality model, was validated on 18 OSS systems (Athanasiou et al., TSE 2014); it correlated with 2 of 3 issue-handling metrics. No study comparing aggregators (mean, LOC-weighted mean, max, percentile, inequality index, risk profile) against repository-level maintenance outcomes was found, but this negative was not independently re-verified.

findings.claim: Inference: for Geiger's per-PR budget (no PR may cost more than 0.2 points), user-tuned weights will mostly preserve the score's overall validity if every component keeps the correct sign (Dawes). They will still flip pass/fail decisions for marginal PRs, especially near a high baseline where scores bunch (JRC 2005; Borg et al. 2412.06307). Recalibration or new components can sharply reduce validity (SIG 2019 replication). Geiger should therefore (a) freeze weights and thresholds per baseline, (b) report each PR's decision under a range of weights or with an equal-weights cross-check, (c) check every component's sign and compare it with a line-count baseline, and (d) keep hard gates outside the weighted sum.

findings.relevance: This turns the evidence into design rules for user-weighted scoring and the PR gate.

verdict.evidence: Both quotes appear verbatim in https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/sds/docs/dawes/the-robust-beauty-of-improper-linear-models-in-decision-making.pdf and https://knowledge4policy.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/eur_21682_en_1.pdf. Dawes supports overall robustness for correctly signed, standardized components. JRC rank shifts came mainly from aggregation method and indicator inclusion, with weighting as a first-order effect of only 0.038 (Table 7.1). Opened https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.06307 (Borg, Udayakumar, Tornhill; Gamify 2025 workshop; 1,000+ proprietary projects). Its bunching concerns average CodeHealth across projects ('a vast majority of projects are in the interval above 8 with a mode at 9.5'). Its volatility concerns leaderboard ranks across projects ('the leaderboard positions around the leaders might appear volatile'), not per-PR decisions within one repository. Wijnmaalen et al. support the recalibration point: 'The overall maintainability correlation with defect resolution time decreased significantly'. Recommendations (a)-(d) follow as reasonable design rules. The claim that weights flip marginal pass/fail decisions is true by construction for any threshold on a weighted sum, and needs no empirical citation.
verdict.corrected_claim: Inference: user-tuned weights will probably keep the score's overall correlation with outcomes if components are standardized and correctly signed (Dawes 1979). Any threshold on a weighted sum, including a 0.2-point per-PR budget, will still flip decisions for marginal PRs when weights change. JRC 2005 shows that aggregation-method and component-inclusion choices move rankings even more than weights. Borg et al. 2024 (arXiv 2412.06307) found average CodeHealth bunched near the top across 1,000+ projects (mode 9.5), so small changes move leaderboard ranks a lot. That is cross-project evidence and only an analogy for per-PR decisions. Recalibrating the model sharply reduced the SIG rating's correlation with defect resolution time (Wijnmaalen et al. 2019). Design rules (a)-(d) follow as prudent choices, not tested results.

open_questions: Would a LOC-weighted mean, a churn-weighted mean, a tail statistic (p90/max) and a SIG-style risk profile rank the same repositories in the same order, and which tracks issue resolution time or change effort best? No study tests this; Geiger could test it on OSS Rust workspaces.
How much do Geiger-style per-PR pass/fail decisions change under plausible weight perturbations (Monte Carlo over the weight simplex) near a 98/100 baseline?
Does the Bijlsma correlation survive controls for project size, team size and activity? Volume alone correlated 0.29-0.39, and no study adjusted for confounders.
Schnappinger's 2020 dataset and later work are file-level. Is there any expert-labelled repository-level maintainability dataset beyond Quamoco's 5-system Linzer ranking?
Would CodeScene's untested churn-filtered, size-weighted project average validate against project outcomes? The authors list this as future work.

areas.title: Which Rust-specific signals (Clippy warning density by lint group, unsafe usage, panic sites such as unwrap/expect/indexing, clone and Rc<RefCell<_>> density, typestate or newtype use) have an empirical link to defects, vulnerabilities, review effort or maintenance cost, and which crates.io-wide distributions exist to calibrate Rust thresholds the way Alves et al. calibrated Java and C#?
areas.summary_before_verification: Only two Rust-specific signals have outcome-linked evidence: unsafe code and panic sites. Even for these, the evidence comes from bug-cause studies, which report what share of known bugs involve the construct. No study tests whether a higher density of the construct predicts later defects. For unsafe code: all memory-safety bugs studied require unsafe code (Xu et al., 186 bugs; Qin et al.). Vulnerable code has significantly higher ratios of unsafe functions and blocks than other code (Zheng et al., 433 RustSec vulnerabilities). Still, 95% of affected functions are safe functions, and most memory bugs also involve safe code. So counting unsafe finds where to look but does not measure the risk. For panic sites: 107 of 110 panic bugs were in safe code; 39 came from unwrap/expect and 12 from out-of-bounds indexing (Qin et al., TSE). The same study's checkers found 7,259 potential assertion sites, so counting raw panic sites would mostly measure noise. For Clippy warning density, clone density, Rc<RefCell<_>> density and newtype or typestate use, I found no study that links them to defects, vulnerabilities or review effort. Clippy's maintainers moved cognitive_complexity into the restriction group so that it would not be used as a measurement tool. A 31-person survey reported many false positives. Tadesse et al. (2026) show Clippy misses panic and thread-safety risks in non-idiomatic code. A case study (a bachelor thesis) suggests size and Halstead metrics penalize typestate and newtype designs that experts judged better. For calibration there are no crates.io-wide per-function or per-file metric distributions comparable to Alves et al. What exists: binary per-crate unsafe prevalence (Evans 2020: under 30% of crates; Rust Foundation, May 2024: 19.11% of about 127,000 crates). There is also a single pooled Clippy mean of 21 warnings per KLOC (Li et al.). That mean was computed under each project's own lint configuration, and one restriction lint, default_numeric_fallback, accounts for over 50% of the warnings, so it cannot serve as a baseline. Available outcome labels: RustSec, Zheng et al.'s 433-vulnerability dataset, RustXec (102 reproducible vulnerabilities), Panic4R (102 panic bugs). The AI-agent quality studies barely cover Rust: the Cursor DiD study has 24 Rust repositories and disclaims generalization beyond JS/TS/Python. Geiger would have to build its own Rust benchmark and validate it before any Rust threshold can be claimed as evidence-based.

findings.claim: Li et al.'s 21 Clippy warnings/KLOC for crates.io is a pooled mean: 8,095,259 warnings over 374,424,742 LOC in the latest releases of 94,715 crates. Each crate was linted with its own configuration, and one lint accounts for over 50% of all warnings. It is neither a per-crate distribution nor a fixed-configuration baseline, and the paper does not link it to defects.
findings.relevance: The only crates.io-wide Clippy density figure is not usable as a Geiger threshold. A Rust benchmark must fix one lint configuration and report per-crate percentiles.

verdict.evidence: Opened arxiv.org/pdf/2310.11738 (v1, 2023-10-18, unrefereed preprint; the PDF still carries the ACM template header 'Conference acronym XX, June 03-05, 2018'). All three quotes are in the text. Also verified: '94715 projects on Crates-IO, which has 374,424,742 LOC for their latest release'; 'Altogether we found 8,095,259 instances of 403 types of warnings'; 'The largest category default_numeric_fallback'. 8,095,259 / 374,424.742 KLOC = 21.6, which matches the '21 per KLOC' figure, but the paper only says 'On average' and never states how it computed the number. It gives no per-crate distribution, no snapshot date and no link to defects. Problem with the methodology: the paper says it used each project's own configuration, yet 4,887,114 warnings (over 50%) come from default_numeric_fallback. That lint is in the allow-by-default restriction group (confirmed in Clippy's source), and few crates are likely to enable it, so the two statements are hard to reconcile. The actual lint setup is underspecified.
verdict.corrected_claim: Li et al. (arXiv 2310.11738 v1, 2023-10-18, unrefereed preprint) report 'On average, 21 per KLOC' for crates.io: 8,095,259 warnings over 374,424,742 LOC in the latest releases of 94,715 crates (snapshot date not given). The figure matches a pooled ratio (about 21.6), but the paper does not say how it averaged. The paper says each crate's own configuration was used. However, its top lint, default_numeric_fallback, is an allow-by-default restriction lint and accounts for 4,887,114 warnings (over 50%). That casts doubt on whether the warnings really reflect per-crate configurations; the lint setup is underspecified. The figure is neither a per-crate distribution nor a fixed-configuration baseline, and it is not linked to defects.

findings.claim: The lint that dominates Li et al.'s count, default_numeric_fallback, is in Clippy's allow-by-default restriction group. Clippy's README says the restriction group should never be enabled as a whole. Clippy has over 800 lints in groups with different default levels: correctness is deny, suspicious/style/complexity/perf are warn, pedantic/restriction/nursery/cargo are allow. Warning density therefore depends mainly on which groups a project enables.
findings.relevance: A Geiger soft metric based on Clippy must be computed per lint group with a fixed group selection. Otherwise scores are not comparable across repositories.

verdict.evidence: Fetched raw README.md from rust-clippy master on 2026-11-07. It says 'There are over 800 lints included in this crate!' and its category table matches the claim: correctness deny; suspicious/style/complexity/perf warn; pedantic/restriction/nursery/cargo allow. Exact wording: 'The `restriction` category should, *emphatically*, not be enabled as a whole. The contained lints may lint against perfectly reasonable code'. The claim's 'never' paraphrases 'emphatically, not'. default_numeric_fallback.rs on master declares 'pub DEFAULT_NUMERIC_FALLBACK, restriction,'. Its docs add 'which results in many false positives and false negatives'. Li et al. name default_numeric_fallback as 'The largest category'. The closing sentence, that density depends on which groups are enabled, is an inference, and it follows from these facts.

verdict.evidence: arxiv.org/pdf/2310.11738 contains: 'Surprisingly, a lot of (42%) participants complained that Clippy produce relatively many and frequent false positives.' and 'we gathered a total of 31 responses from developers'. The 31 respondents were 11 Master's students, 2 community experts and 18 employed developers. The longitudinal study covers four rust-lang projects (RustFix, Log, Git2-Rs, CC-Rs): 'the number of warnings in RustFix, Log, and Git2-Rs decreases significantly' and CC-Rs 'has exhibited an upward trend'. The paper measures no defect outcome. It is an unrefereed preprint.

findings.claim: Tadesse et al. (Jan 2026) studied seven GNU coreutils programs translated by C2Rust, C2SaferRust, TranslationGym and humans. Clippy reported zero warnings in the categories runtime panic risk, thread safety, error handling and compatibility for every translation. GPT-4o flagged substantial numbers of issues in those categories, and manual analysis confirmed examples such as unsynchronized static mut. Clippy works best on idiomatic code.
findings.relevance: A Clippy-only soft score can show a clean result for C-style or agent-written unidiomatic Rust that still carries panic and concurrency risk. This matters for Geiger's use as an agent constraint.
